title: Indonesian-Javanese-English Sentiment Analysis with AutoML and XAI
abstract: Reproducible Python pipeline for three-class sentiment classification of Indonesian–Javanese–English (IJE) code-mixed text. The pipeline compares three AutoML frameworks (FLAML, AutoGluon, Optuna) across three feature sets (TF-IDF, TF-IDF with code-mixing features, TF-IDF with multilingual sentence embeddings), selects a configuration on development folds only, and explains the selected model with LIME. Classes: negative (0), neutral (1), positive (2). Reported results. Selection uses development folds only; the test split is not used to pick the configuration. Development-selected configuration: autogluon_tfidf (dev mean outer macro-F1 0.9129; test macro-F1 0.8909, weighted-F1 0.8923, accuracy 0.8920). Macro-F1 95% interval for the selected configuration: 0.8617–0.9172. The configuration is retained regardless of its test ranking — reporting the test-best configuration as the outcome would be test-set selection. Reproducibility. Every executing stage is gated by an approval file that binds a run to an exact protocol hash, code hash, and stage list. This release carries the fixed dataset and its documented preprocessing. Release 2.0.0 corresponds to git tag v2.0.0, commit f2559ad7fcaf87d5d538c2f06eb61d180b19625f of the GitHub repository. Licensed CC BY 4.0. Repository: GitHub

title: Replication materials for "State-preparation costs in exact conjunction learning"
abstract: Replication materials for the manuscript "State-preparation costs in exact conjunction learning" by Junye Fu. The archive contains a Python standard-library enumeration script, complete numerical outputs, and reproduction instructions. It records 71 exact problems and 11,251 cost tuples for finite checks of the state-preparation cost analysis. All inputs are enumerated finite sets; no external dataset is required. These materials support the mathematical analysis and finite computational validation. They do not contain native agent performance benchmarks.

title: Reflective AI: A Conceptual Framework for Second-Order Reflection and Temporal Self-Understanding
abstract: This paper proposes Reflective AI: an architecture in which an intelligent agent can examine not only its recorded prior reasoning contexts, but also the history of its subsequent interpretations of those contexts. The conceptual starting point is the difficulty of establishing subjective self-awareness in another system. The continuing sense of human identity across interruptions in conscious experience suggests a narrower, functionally investigable question: how can a system connect what it once knew, believed and anticipated with what later occurred? The architecture retains selective, immutable records of the information, assumptions, goals, forecasts and documented reasoning links relevant to decisions; it does not attempt to capture every machine computation. Multiple later interpretations are stored separately, and second-order reflection evaluates whether current interpretations and the criteria for selecting evidence should change. Reflection is event-triggered and directed towards identifying missing knowledge and improving future decisions, not endless introspection. This paper situates the proposal within existing work on autobiographical memory, prospective simulation, metacognition and reflective agents, and outlines a feasible comparative evaluation without claiming that the system would possess subjective consciousness.

title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.

title: Laryngeal lesion triage: training and video analysis
abstract: Version 1.0.0 of the training, model-comparison, and video-analysis code accompanying the manuscript Development and multicenter validation of a vision foundation model for laryngeal lesion triage. The archive contains Python source code and configuration files for comparison of 11 visual backbones, evaluation of DINOv2 adaptation strategies, supplementary ROI-auxiliary experiments, and a video pipeline combining frame sampling, vocal-fold localization, quality ranking, and risk aggregation. Installation instructions, input formats, and example commands are provided in README.md. This is a source-code archive only. Datasets, patient images, annotations, videos, pretrained or fine-tuned model weights, and saved experiment outputs are not included. Data and study-compatible checkpoints must be supplied separately as described in README.md. The original code and documentation are released under the MIT License. Third-party libraries and pretrained models retain their respective licenses and terms.

title: SmartDesk-IT-Support-Research: An Intelligent Automated Classification Framework for IT Support Tickets Using Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
abstract: SmartDesk-IT-Support-Research is an advanced automated classification framework designed to revolutionize IT service desk operations through the integration of machine learning and natural language processing techniques. This research addresses the critical challenge of high-volume IT support ticket management by developing intelligent algorithms capable of accurately categorizing, prioritizing, and routing incoming support requests. The project repository and accompanying research artifacts provide a comprehensive, reproducible experimental pipeline—including synthetic benchmark datasets, baseline classification models (such as Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression), evaluation metrics, and detailed technical documentation—offering a scalable and efficient solution for modern automated IT infrastructure and intelligent enterprise support systems.

title: Revocation Is Not Complete at Receipt: An Executable Outcome Contract for Distributed Agent-Tool Gateways
abstract: Distributed agent workflows cache delegated authority at tool gateways. Revocation may be reported at issuer commit, transport acknowledgment, or receiver persistence, although none of these observations establishes that all gateways enforced the change or that guarded effects stopped. We define C0-C5, a bounded outcome contract spanning issuer commit through effect prevention, and implement it as a persistent monitor over a frozen gateway set, call set, and observation window. A 14-case fault matrix checks conservative classification, sticky violations, restart persistence, and evidence immutability. In a derived audit of its eight semantic cases, treating C3 or C4 as completion produces seven or five false positives, respectively; the bounded C0-C5 verdict produces none. Descriptive scaling covers 1,024 gateways and 10,000 effect vectors. The primary experiment uses the maintained Keycloak 26.7 identity server and measures the contract across two durable receivers, eight physical agent-tool gateways, Filesystem and PostgreSQL effects, and 16 AWS hosts in three availability zones. Normal delivery and recovery commit no effects. Under receiver-selective non-delivery, transport acknowledgment and receiver persistence still succeed, but 112 of 225 calls (49.78%) are admitted, and all 112 effects commit in every treatment block. A separately provisioned execution repeats the result. OPA/Toxiproxy and a live three-role LLM workflow with networked MCP tools reproduce the persisted-but-not-enforced boundary on narrower surfaces. Finally, an unmodified external MCPMark agent executes 60 closed-loop task arms. Normal C4 denies all 31 exposed post-barrier calls and commits no effect; selective C3 allows 344 calls and commits 145 effects across Filesystem and PostgreSQL. Transport success is therefore evidence of progress, not a revocation-completion verdict.

title: TL;QR: Querying Temporal Discursive Patterns in Textual Corpora
abstract: Many questions about large textual corpora concern patterns that unfold over time, such as a political group whose stance on a topic drifts from support to criticism over several years of debates. We present TL;QR (Too Long; Query with logical temporal Reasoning), a declarative query language and open-source engine for finding such temporal discursive patterns. In TL;QR, a single query combines natural-language predicates, whose truth is judged by a Large Language Model (LLM), with regular expressions and the operators of a temporal logic. The LLM answers only local questions about individual text passages; a symbolic engine then aggregates these judgments over time and links every match to the recorded passages and predicate decisions behind it. With this division of labor, the temporal and relational reasoning stays exact and auditable even over long time horizons. In addition, when a query includes a regular-expression pre-filter, only a small fraction of the corpus ever reaches the LLM. On a suite of controlled synthetic benchmarks with temporally and semantically complex patterns, TL;QR is substantially more accurate than LLM-only baselines. In a case study on ten years of European Parliament debates (442,593 multilingual speeches), TL;QR identifies candidate shifts in the political groups' stances on the GDPR privacy regulation.

title: Indonesian Cross-Platform Hate Speech Dataset (X, YouTube, and Threads)
abstract: Dataset ini berisi 21.202 teks berbahasa Indonesia bertema sosial-politik yang dikumpulkan secara mandiri melalui scraping dari tiga platform media sosial (X, YouTube, dan Threads) pada periode Januari 2025 hingga Juli 2026. Setiap teks dilabeli secara semi-otomatis berbasis leksikon ke dalam dua kelas: ujaran kebencian (1) dan bukan ujaran kebencian (0). Dataset memiliki 4 kolom: text, labels, source, dan platform. Distribusi label: 15.004 bukan ujaran kebencian (70,8%) dan 6.198 ujaran kebencian (29,2%). Dataset ini digunakan dalam penelitian "Analisis Performa Model Klasifikasi Teks untuk Identifikasi Ujaran Kebencian pada Media Sosial Indonesia".

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Wildfire Size Using Conditional Flow Matching
abstract: In this work we present a probabilistic model for predicting the temporal evolution of wildfire size using conditional generative algorithms, namely flow matching. Rather than predicting spatially resolved fire progression, the proposed model forecasts a time series of fire acreage, substantially reducing computational cost and enabling efficient integration with downstream applications such as early warning systems and risk assessment tools. Given estimates of the fire size at the current and previous forecasting steps, alongside spatially averaged weather conditions, terrain characteristics, and fuel composition, the model predicts the change in fire area over a 3-hour interval. Training data are drawn from 140 coupled atmosphere-wildfire simulations generated using WRF-SFIRE, paired with weather data from the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the model captures physically-consistent responses to variations in wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity. Model performance is evaluated against reference solutions from WRF-SFIRE. For single-step predictions, the model achieves a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39 relative to the reference WRF-SFIRE solutions. Recursive multi-step predictions over 24 hours are performed for 12 held-out test cases, where the flow matching model achieves a final fire area sMAPE of 0.39 while further providing meaningful quantification of forecast uncertainty.

title: What DNA Foundation Models Learn Beyond Sequence Composition
abstract: Do genomic foundation models (FMs) provide predictive information beyond simple sequence composition? We evaluate frozen representations from five DNA FMs against normalized k-mer frequencies across 57 genomic classification datasets and two exploratory gene-expression regression tasks. Simple k-mer features remain competitive with most models, whereas NTv3 shows a consistent advantage; the ranking is robust to globally fixed and multi-scale k-mer baselines and alternative downstream probes. To test incremental predictive utility directly, we compare global 6-mer features with their concatenation with each FM embedding under a matched Random Forest protocol. NTv3 improves 46 of 57 datasets (mean $Δ$MCC = +0.072), while Caduceus provides smaller gains and the other models do not improve mean MCC. We separately decompose embeddings into a component linearly predictable from 6-mer frequencies and a ridge residual, finding that linear recoverability does not reliably indicate downstream utility. Exact 6-mer-preserving shuffles further reveal task-relevant sequence-order sensitivity, most pronounced for NTv3, although order sensitivity alone does not guarantee predictive improvements. Our results establish compositional features as essential controls and offer complementary diagnostics for evaluating the added value of frozen genomic representations, without making claims about fine-tuning capacity.

title: Every AI is just a Large Language Model (LLM) The Entropy of English vs. The Precision of Math
abstract: There is a fundamental misconception about the current state of artificial intelligence. We categorize AI into different domains—assuming that a machine built to play chess, a machine built to generate images, and a machine built to write text are fundamentally different architectures. This is an illusion. If you strip away the user interface and look at the raw mathematics of the neural network, every domain is simply a language. And every AI is just a Large Language Model (LLM). **The Tokenization of Reality** At the hardware level, a GPU does not know what an English word is, nor does it know what a pixel is. It only processes multidimensional numerical vectors called tokens.

title: Training quantum neural networks for Tl-limited hardware: what the qg symmetry filter does and does not do
abstract: A quantum neural network (QNN) built from gates that conserve the Hamming weight keeps its data in one weight sector, so the shots that left the sector can be discarded at readout. This is the qg filter of the qang library [1, 2]. We show that, with equal amplitude damping (T1) on every qubit, the filtered readout of such a network is exactly the noiseless one in any weight sector. title: What survives the write: do agent memory pipelines keep the record of successes behind a single failure? Protocol and materials frozen before the run (Study 1)
abstract: Frozen protocol, code and materials of a study of what LLM agents' memory-writing pipelines keep from a run of tool outcomes, deposited before any confirmatory model call (the manifest's OpenTimestamps proof is included; its Bitcoin attestation is checked by the gated launcher). After eight successful runs of the faster, standard route, one run fails for no reason the agent can see. The study replays the memory pipeline of OpenAI's open-source Codex agent in its default (v1) and opt-in (v2) versions (Phase-1 extraction per run and Phase-2 consolidation, with the instructions pinned at commit ecebd679 and the default writer models; an adapted replay, not the shipped pipeline), ReasoningBank's released extraction prompts, and two harness records (a dated log and per-route counts). Fresh sessions read only the injected memory, forecast whether the standard route would succeed and choose a route. The registered question is whether the failure's increment — against a matched branch in which the ninth run succeeded — in the share choosing the fallback and in the forecast differs between the replayed pipeline's memory and the counts. The archive holds the registration (REGISTRATION.md), the design memos, the stream generator and the 96 registered streams, the scripted run tree, the memory designs with the instructions they replay (Apache-2.0, with provenance and declared departures), the reader prompts and the panel, the wave-1 writer schedule, the runner, the codebook and schedule of the two model coders that code the memory snapshots inside the run, the registered analysis, statistics and sentence rules with their power and size tables, the two development pilots' gates and operational summaries (the first pilot's reader choices are sealed outside the archive; their hash is in its summary), the pre-freeze reviews of the design with their dispositions, and the chain scripts. MANIFEST.sha256 lists every file with its SHA-256; MANIFEST.sha256.ots is its OpenTimestamps proof. Manifest SHA-256: a406b12f00729cfb66b167153865e7a218d0c3049ff767e293a68b0543e9da4d. Zip SHA-256: 36daccd239119e65068e93ed9b4ef655d5b5b1a25a9aaa4e9d3f71312ed589b2. No confirmatory result is included. Licences: LICENSE.md.

title: Towards Finite Satisfiability of PDL with Loops
abstract: Propositional Dynamic Logic (PDL) is a well-established modal logic of programs. Among its many extensions, the loop operator stands out for capturing the cyclic behaviour of programs: a world satisfies loop(pi) precisely when it can return to itself along a path matching the regular expression pi. While the satisfiability problem for the resulting logic LPDL was settled already in the 1980s, the decidability of its finite satisfiability problem has remained open ever since. The core difficulty is inherent to the finite setting: requiring and forbidding cycles at once is easily reconciled over arbitrary models, but over finite ones it defeats the existing finite-model-theoretic techniques. We make the first substantial progress towards closing this gap. We prove that finite satisfiability is ExpTime-complete for LPDL formulae (also in the presence of the converse operator) in negation normal form, under the restriction that every negated non-atomic loop has the form loop(pi^+) for some arbitrarily complex program pi -- a generalised form of self-reachability; positive occurrences of loops remain unrestricted. At the heart of our approach lies a novel way of representing intended finite models as their infinite, cactus-like unravellings: these are recognisable by two-way tree automata and satisfy a tailored omega-regular foldability condition that lets us finitise the accepted structures.

title: Confidentiality Forces Universality
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A machine forbidden to know which instruction it is running cannot branch on that instruction; to remain correct it must run them all and select the answer through a mask that never reveals the choice. We take this observation to its conclusion on a bounded interaction-net arena — a fixed-capacity computational fragment with allocation, principal linking, a local firing interaction, and reclamation — and give it four confidential realizations: public-program and fully-encrypted homomorphic evaluation, a zero-knowledge execution proof, and secret-shared multiparty computation. A single finite Boolean semantics is the authority. Each route is proven, in a machine-checked kernel, to decode to exactly that semantics on a frozen corpus, under a replay-safe signature gate whose rejection is definitionally the identity. The encrypted universal interpreter is a fixed circuit that evaluates every instruction candidate and selects through a provably one-hot mask, so its access pattern is independent of the secret program by construction, not by inspection: we state and prove obliviousness as a refinement of the plaintext interpreter, for every input and every lawful backend. Beneath the four routes is one construction: the oblivious selector is the sheaf gluing of local branches over a disjoint cover of truth, so correctness and obliviousness become two readings of a single fact — and the price of not knowing is the size of the cover. We report precisely what is proven, what is bounded, and what is measured but not proven. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Supplementary code, configurations and results for "Design and Evaluation of a Graph Memory Architecture for Long-Term Knowledge Retrieval" (compiled graph memory build, evaluation notebooks and per-query results)
abstract: This deposit accompanies the article "[final manuscript title]" (Data & Knowledge Engineering, manuscript in preparation). The article compares a graph-based long-term semantic memory, which stores word-token memory traces in a graph database and retrieves with lexical graph retrieval, against a matched vector RAG baseline (SentenceTransformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with a FAISS flat index) on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and SciFact. Contents: (1) Jupyter notebooks for each dataset that prepare the shared sentence corpus, run both retrieval systems and compute Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, nDCG@K and latency; (2) configuration files; (3) per-query result exports and saved notebook outputs for the reported runs; (4) a compiled Linux (Ubuntu) build of the graph memory system used in the experiments. The source code of the graph memory system is not released at this time because it is under ongoing development. See README for setup and run instructions.

title: Examining Racial and Gender Bias in CLIP via Explainability-Based Visual Attention Analysis
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP are increasingly integrated into automated decision-making systems where unexamined social biases can directly harm racial and gender minorities through discriminatory outcomes and unjust content censorship. Despite strong multimodal performance, CLIP's susceptibility to demographic bias remains underexplored from a visual attribution perspective. Consequently, the mechanisms by which these biases emerge in visual processing remain opaque, both to researchers and to governance bodies concerned with the equitable and transparent deployment of AI. We address this diagnostic gap by applying four attribution methods to the PAIRS dataset, a controlled benchmark of parallel occupation images balanced across race and gender. We then seek to determine whether demographic stereotyping is detectable and measurable at the level of visual attention, rather than only through output statistics. Preliminary results are mixed: subject-level differences in face-focused saliency across race conditions are not statistically separable at the aggregate level, but under race-explicit prompting we observe the clearest race-conditioned saliency differences. These results suggest that attribution-based diagnostics can expose hidden visual biases, invisible to standard fairness metrics, and help explain how demographic bias emerges in multimodal AI systems. Furthermore, we comparatively analyze the behavior of the attribution methods and discuss their outputs with respect to the broader implications of visual bias diagnostics for fairness and transparency in deployed multimodal AI systems.

title: Enhancing parametric and causal reasoning through a formula-augmented language model approach for belt grinding knowledge assistance
abstract: Abrasive belt grinding is a flexible surface finishing process in which precision machining of geometrically complex components often involves coupled parameters and contact mechanisms. Retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in domain-specific knowledge questioning. However, their capabilities in numerical computation and mechanism-oriented reasoning remain limited in scenarios involving coupled parameters. This study introduces a structural enhancement mechanism based on formula-group embedding. It integrates formula retrieval, task classification, structured prompting, and code execution into the conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The approach addresses numerical computation and mechanistic reasoning in belt grinding and is validated through contact modeling, a representative core problem of the process. In numerical computation tasks, the proposed method achieved 100% accuracy in basic cases. In more challenging scenarios, it reached 90% accuracy with an average deviation within 5%. In contrast, for these complex tasks, general-purpose LLMs achieved only about a 10% pass rate. In mechanism-related reasoning tasks, utilizing a hybrid expert-LLM evaluation, the method demonstrated a 13.1% improvement over the second-best model and a 36.6% gain over the baseline without formula augmentation. These results indicate that the proposed mechanism provides value in improving the reliability of numerical computation and the coherence of mechanistic reasoning.

title: Embedding Information in Policy Randomness: Distribution-Preserving Implicit Communication in MDPs
abstract: This paper investigates a new role of randomness in stochastic policies--as a medium for embedding and communicating information. Specifically, we consider an agent interacting with an environment according to a prescribed stochastic policy. By carefully modulating the random action realizations of the policy, information can be embedded into the agent's behavior without altering the prescribed action distribution. We cast this problem as a channel coding problem, in which the controlled system implicitly serves as a communication channel. We then propose a coding scheme, termed posterior-matching randomness modulation (PRAM), that selects actions according to the message to be transmitted. With the aid of common randomness independent of the control system, PRAM preserves the prescribed action distribution for every state and every message. We further prove that PRAM is asymptotically reliable: the message can be decoded with arbitrarily small error probability as the observed state trajectory becomes sufficiently long. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in applications including multi-bit policy watermarking and trajectory provenance.

title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

title: AnyEdit: A Unified Framework for Speech and Singing Voice Editing with Real-World Environmental Consistency
abstract: We present AnyEdit, a unified, separation-free framework for speech and singing voice editing that preserves real-world acoustic environments, including noise, reverberation, and background music. Recent unified generative models already achieve strong speech and singing generation in clean conditions, but real-world vocal editing remains challenging because the model must revise content while simultaneously preserving speaker identity, prosody, and the surrounding acoustic scene. Directly modeling noisy audio end-to-end entangles semantic editing with environmental acoustics, weakening the core vocal generation capability. We therefore adopt a two-stage design that preserves clean-domain editing ability while deferring acoustic rendering to a separate stage: an instruction-guided autoregressive editor first predicts clean prosody and content-style tokens, supported by a teacher-student noise-robust prosody tokenizer that distills clean prosodic tokens from degraded recordings; a flow-matching acoustic model then performs in-context rendering conditioned on the source acoustic context, so the edited segment inherits surrounding noise, reverberation, and background sound while maintaining consistent speaker timbre. To stabilize unedited regions, we introduce unmodified-area-aware supervision; after pre-training, we further apply direct preference optimization on mined real-to-real singing pairs. We also release AnyEditBench, a benchmark covering both speech and singing voice editing under clean, simulated, and in-the-wild acoustic conditions. Experiments on Chinese and English speech and singing datasets showed that AnyEdit consistently outperforms strong baselines in content accuracy, subjective quality, and background consistency under noisy and reverberant conditions. Demo: https://any-edit.github.io/. AnyEditBench: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ririiiii/anyeditbench.

We therefore adopt a two-stage design that preserves clean-domain editing ability while deferring acoustic rendering to a separate stage: an instruction-guided autoregressive editor first predicts clean prosody and content-style tokens, supported by a teacher-student noise-robust prosody tokenizer that distills clean prosodic tokens from degraded recordings; a flow-matching acoustic model then performs in-context rendering conditioned on the source acoustic context, so the edited segment inherits surrounding noise, reverberation, and background sound while maintaining consistent speaker timbre. To stabilize unedited regions, we introduce unmodified-area-aware supervision; after pre-training, we further apply direct preference optimization on mined real-to-real singing pairs. We also release AnyEditBench, a benchmark covering both speech and singing voice editing under clean, simulated, and in-the-wild acoustic conditions. Experiments on Chinese and English speech and singing datasets showed that AnyEdit consistently outperforms strong baselines in content accuracy, subjective quality, and background consistency under noisy and reverberant conditions. title: Stereo-Planner: Learning Stereo-to-Trajectory Planning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Quadrotor Navigation
abstract: Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of up to 7 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 24.27 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced at https://github.com/Stereo-Planner/Stereo-Planner.

title: OmniRSI: Taming Latent Diffusion for Unified Multimodal Remote Sensing Image Generation
abstract: Multimodal remote sensing image generation emerges as a promising paradigm for recovering complete and complementary observations from heterogeneous and partially observed remote sensing data. However, existing methods predominantly depend on sensor-specific fine-tuning of natural image generation models, limiting unified multimodal generation capacity due to the absence of shared representations and robust conditioning mechanisms. To address these challenges, we propose OmniRSI, a unified multimodal remote sensing image generation model. Specifically, we develop a remote sensing-specific variational autoencoder that captures multimodal priors and promotes a locally smooth latent space for unified representation and robust reconstruction across diverse observed data. Building upon that, we fully adapt Stable Diffusion 3.5 with a ControlNet branch to support unified multimodal generation and translation conditioned on textual and visual cues. Besides, we devise a training-free cyclic latent alignment mechanism that iteratively enriches incomplete visual conditions with generated multimodal information, progressively improving guidance reliability while preserving observed measurements. We also construct RSI-MM, a large-scale dataset comprising 11.5M multi-resolution images with text annotations and partially paired data for training and evaluation. Extensive experiments verify that OmniRSI achieves superior performance in multimodal reconstruction, generation and translation.

title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
abstract: Background Machine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. Methods We assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin–stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. Results In leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. Conclusions We present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

title: Humarticosynergy: A New Word for Cognitive Human–AI Synergy
abstract: This essay introduces humarticosynergy as a concise term for the previously developed concept of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy. The proposed word combines elements referring to the human, artificial intelligence, cognition, and synergy. The essay explains its formation, defines the concept it denotes, and outlines possible grammatical derivatives, including humarticosynergistic, to humarticosynergize, and humarticosynergistically. Humarticosynergy is defined as structured, iterative, and mutually reinforcing cognitive cooperation between a human and artificial intelligence in which two distinct cognitive systems contribute complementary capabilities to the creation of higher-quality knowledge while ultimate responsibility remains human. The essay also presents examples of use in strategic decision-making, scientific research, methodology, and education, and discusses the originality and possible value of the proposed term within the broader framework of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy.

title: SpecForge: Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents via Behavioral Specifications
abstract: Coding agents based on frozen language models can improve their performance by refining the external context they rely on, without updating model weights. We study recursive self-improvement through behavioral specifications: natural-language code documentation that describes the behavior of program entities and guides agents in generating correct code. We formulate a self-improvement loop in which an agent generates code from its current specifications, evaluates it with execution-verified tests, and refines the specifications based on observed failures. The improved specifications then guide subsequent generation, progressively improving the agent's understanding of the codebase. However, recursive refinement is challenging because program entities are interdependent. Improving the specification of one entity can inadvertently degrade the correctness of others, a phenomenon we call output coupling. This creates a whack-a-mole effect in which local improvements cause regressions elsewhere, preventing consistent progress. We introduce SpecForge, a multi-frontier tree search framework that addresses this challenge with three mechanisms: (i) Pareto-guided state selection preserves complementary specification states and prevents premature commitment; (ii) dependency-constrained entity selection prioritizes callee-before-caller refinement; and (iii) error-diversified expansion explores multiple refinements using different subsets of test failures. On DevEval+, SpecForge achieves the best performance across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and a 5.7-percentage-point average improvement over the strongest baseline. The improved specifications also make the agent better at tasks outside the loop: they transfer to cross-language translation and to new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents.

title: Both Halves of the Boundary
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A confluent reduction calculus normalizes: many terms flow to one normal form, and the flow is irreversible by construction. Its lattice of observations is nevertheless a biHeyting algebra, and a bi-Heyting algebra carries two negations, not one. The calculus is built on the first — the double Heyting negation R = ¬¬, whose fixed points are the normal forms. The second, the double co-Heyting supplement k = ∼∼, sits inside the algebra unused. We promote it. Once k is a first-class operator, every configuration splits as a = ka ∨ ∂a: its reversible interior core, joined with its boundary ∂a = a ∧ ∼a. That single identity is three things at once. It is a reverse: k is the canonical best-inverse to normalization, and ∂ measures exactly what the forward flow destroyed — a Landauer ledger in which erasing the boundary is the only irreversible act. It is a derivative: ∂ is a co-Heyting derivation, and it distributes over the parallel-composition tensor, so the boundary defect of a composite is the sum of its parts' — the linear core of a chain rule on reduction. And it is a clock: ∂ is the infinitesimal generator whose fixed locus is exactly the calculus's eigenforms, its normal forms, its ground state. We identify the objects on a three-valued re-entry classifier and again on the four-configuration lattice of an actual interaction net, and we resolve where the program stops: the boundary is a derivation but not a differential because it is an idempotent projector (∂ 2 = ∂). Its invariant is therefore K-theoretic — the rank (1, 2, 3 on the corpus) — and the genuine homology is concentrated in degree zero (the K-theory), with the reduction complex acyclic above it. The infinite periodic-cyclic tower degenerates onto that degree-zero invariant because an idempotent admits no infinitesimal deformation (§7). The results are checked in Lean 4 and, on the net-configuration lattice, independently in Cubical Agda; see §8. This paper is a living document: §10 names the phases still to land. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Логика приписывания понимания
abstract: Статья анализирует логическую схему приписывания понимания современным языковым моделям на основе их успеха в выполнении заданий на тестовых наборах. Показывается, что такой переход осуществляется в рамках силлогизма второй фигуры с нераспределённым средним термином и построенное рассуждение неправомерно. Ошибка маскируется скрытой посылкой, вводимой каноническим форматом: он придаёт выводу достоверность до проверки оснований. Механизм маскировки разбирается в рамках системной модели аргументации В. Н. Брюшинкина: дефект лежит в логическом ядре перехода, скрытая посылка о репрезентативности класса заданий входит в когнитивную структуру рассуждения, а канонический формат как коммуникативное условие делает эту посылку принимаемой без экспликации. Сопоставление с описанным С. С. Аверинцевым эпизодом из истории византийской риторики показывает, что слой, в котором срабатывает маскировка, не постоянен: он задаётся тем, что в данной культуре имеет силу канонической формы достоверности, — дедукция в одном случае, количественный формат в другом. В современной социологии и в литературе по оценке моделей искусственного интеллекта дефект фиксируется эмпирически; статья даёт его логическую квалификацию. Различение ложного и неправомерного предлагается как инструмент, делающий концептуальную структуру операциональной. Устойчивый провал на этом различении снимает атрибуцию понимания как удержания концепта в целом, успех её не удостоверяет. Усиление свидетельства повышает вес основания, но не делает переход доказательством. В обычной коммуникации ошибки этого рода практически нельзя систематически предусмотреть; в работе с языковыми моделями можно, если не позволять каноническому формату маскировать скрытую посылку.

title: Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems
abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.

title: CoverSynth: Coverage-Guided Generation of Retrieval Evaluation Sets
abstract: Enterprise agents need retrieval evaluation sets that expose domain-specific failures and guide developers towards efficient deployment tradeoffs. Neither expert-human-authored sets nor current synthetic generation methods provide a methodology for achieving the necessary coverage, reliability, efficiency, and discriminability required for such decision-making. Simultaneously, the field does not have an assessment framework for determining when an evaluation set has satisfied these properties. We introduce an evaluation set assessment framework for these criteria and CoverSynth -- a generator specifically designed to satisfy these criteria without incurring the high cost of human expert labeling. Starting from an unannotated corpus, CoverSynth targets coverage across retrieval demands and system capabilities. Deterministic checks locate evidence quotes in their sources, while model-based checks assess semantic validity to guarantee reliable ground truth. Across five public enterprise-style corpora, our method provides informative variation in difficulty, revealing unseen failure modes such as an inability of agents to handle underspecified or ambiguous requests. On the RepLiQA corpus, 91\% of human-generated queries can be answered by all members on a panel of 12 retrieval systems, compared to only 12\% of CoverSynth-generated queries. Finally, in a repeated TechQA/RepLiQA study, 12 of 12 within-harness model contrasts have positive nominal 95\% intervals on generated sets, compared with 4 of 12 on human sets. CoverSynth makes coverage and evidence quality explicit construction objectives, producing corpus-grounded evaluations that reveal retrieval headroom and differences between agent configurations.

title: AI video model free-tier observations
abstract: 117 dated observations of what twelve AI video models grant on their free tiers, one row per figure. Each row carries the channel it was observed on, the date it was observed, and whether the source was a vendor statement or a report.Covered: daily credit grants and daily generation caps per channel, sign-up bonuses and launch promotions, maximum single-clip length, extension ceilings, output resolution as stated by the vendor versus as advertised by hosts, watermark behaviour on free and paid tiers, API availability and error codes seen in practice, the measured credit cost of one generation, and product discontinuations.Where two observations disagree both are retained rather than averaged, so the dataset records the disagreement instead of resolving it. Some rows record what an official page does not state — a documented absence is checkable, so it gets a row instead of an empty cell. No value is estimated or interpolated.Deliberately excluded: price per generation, any ranking of models, and scraped marketing copy.Files: CSV, JSON and Markdown. Licence CC BY 4.0. Maintained alongside videofreetier.com, where the same figures appear with surrounding context and where corrections land first.

title: MultiAgentInject: Benchmark Dataset, Injection Templates, and Analysis Scripts for "Reach Without Compliance: Disentangling Injection Propagation From Attack Success in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems"
abstract: Research artifact accompanying the paper Reach Without Compliance: Disentangling Injection Propagation From Attack Success in Multi-Agent Large Language Model Systems (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security). The artifact contains: The full benchmark dataset: 4,050 trials from a complete factorial design (15 tasks × 3 topologies × 6 attack classes × 3 stealth levels × 5 propagation depths), with per-trial reach, compliance, propagation, and stealth outcomes. The injection template library (6 attack classes, 3 stealth levels) and the 15-task benchmark definition. The multi-agent experiment harness (chain, star, and mesh orchestration; LLM backend; judge-based evaluation). All analysis scripts reproducing the statistics and figures reported in the paper, including robustness collections (repeated-run study, cross-model judge, human-annotation agreement, objective payload-marker certification, bootstrap confidence intervals, and survival-mixture estimates). Version 1.1 additionally includes the complete run caches (65,430 cached API request/response pairs) so that every agent, detector, and judge call in the main grid and the robustness collections can be replayed and re-scored exactly as reported in the paper. The injection templates are attack payloads for evaluating multi-agent LLM pipelines and are provided for research and defensive purposes only.

title: Towards Trustworthy Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Nursing Education: Integrating Nurse-Informed Design with a Frugal Neuro-Symbolic Architecture
abstract: Nursing education is increasingly expected to provide personalised, scalable, and clinically meaningful learning experiences while responding to educator shortages, growing student numbers, limited placement opportunities, and rapidly evolving healthcare environments. These pressures have led to the adoption of technology-enhanced learning and renewed interest in innovative and student-centred pedagogies within healthcare education. Consequently, nursing education has explored a broad range of computer-aided educational approaches, including virtual reality, augmented reality, simulation systems, mobile learning applications, haptic devices, and chatbots. Although many of these technologies demonstrate educational potential, important limitations remain regarding explainability, accessibility, educator involvement, adaptive support, and long-term educational effectiveness. Recent interest in large language models and conversational AI has introduced further concerns surrounding reliability, hallucinations, transparency, privacy, educator trust, and ethical deployment within healthcare education. One AI-enabled learning environment that may address several of these limitations is the Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS). Traditionally, ITSs combine domain, tutoring, student, and interface models to provide adaptive instruction, individualised support, and immediate formative feedback. Through natural-language processing and adaptive learning techniques, ITSs may support realistic communication scenarios, individualised learning experiences, and scalable educational assistance. Compared with isolated educational technologies, ITSs are particularly promising because they can support students and educators within one integrated learning environment. Despite this potential, ITS research in nursing education remains limited. Earlier reviews in this doctoral research found that ITS-related studies represented only a small proportion of AI research in nursing education. They also identified limited attention to student modelling, tutoring strategies, explainability, educator oversight, pedagogical alignment, and the wider educational context in which these systems are introduced. Importantly, no nurse-informed conceptual or design-oriented framework was identified to guide ITS development within nursing education. This gap became the central motivation for this doctoral research. The project adopts a multi-phase, sequential exploratory mixed-methods and design-oriented approach. Phase One used grounded theory interviews to explore nurses’ and nursing students’ awareness, perceptions, expectations, concerns, and educational requirements regarding ITS adoption. These qualitative findings informed the development of the CARE-ITS framework. The framework comprises Content Alignment; Adaptive and Accessible Learning; Retention of Human-Centred Learning; Ethical and Trustworthy AI; Individualised Learning Support; Timely and Explainable Feedback; and Sustainability and Educator Support. The framework was subsequently evaluated and refined through expert validation (N = 20), with 95–100% agreement across the overall evaluation criteria (means = 4.40–4.55 out of 5). Phase Two translated the validated CARE-ITS framework into the design, development, and evaluation of EduNurse, a functional web-based ITS prototype for scenario-based nursing education. EduNurse uses a frugal neuro-symbolic assessment architecture that combines domain-adapted embeddings, deterministic educational constraints, structured rubrics, retrieval-grounded explanations, adaptive progression logic, and educator supervision. The grading pipeline does not use a generative large language model. Instead, it uses semantic similarity as one source of evidence alongside explicit relevance, rubric, safety, and uncertainty checks. This enables the system to provide structured formative feedback while retaining appropriate boundaries for educator oversight. The research contributions achieved to date include: 1. A substantial literature contribution through two complementary published reviews. A mixed-methods systematic review of computer-aided pedagogies and a scoping review of ITSs in nursing education critically examined the existing evidence base. Together, they identified gaps that informed the subsequent phases of this doctoral research. 2. An empirical contribution through a learner needs analysis for ITS in nursing education. This doctoral research presents a learner needs analysis employing a grounded theory approach to investigate nursing students’ and nursing professionals’ awareness, perceptions, educational requirements, and implementation expectations of ITSs. The study addresses an important gap within the literature by providing an empirically grounded understanding of the pedagogical, educational, and implementation requirements that should inform the design and development of AI-supported educational systems for nursing education. 3. A methodological contribution through the translation of qualitative findings into a design-oriented conceptual framework. This doctoral research demonstrates a systematic approach for translating empirically derived learner needs, pedagogical considerations, and implementation requirements into actionable design guidance. This provides a transparent transition from qualitative findings to educational AI design that may inform future research within nursing and other professional education domains. 4. The development of the CARE-ITS conceptual framework. Derived from the learner needs analysis, CARE-ITS is a nurse-informed, design-oriented conceptual framework. The framework addresses key components including content alignment, adaptive and accessible learning, retention of human-centred learning, ethical and trustworthy AI, individualised learning support, and timely and explainable feedback. By translating the identified educational requirements into AI system design principles, CARE-ITS provides an evidence-based framework to support the design and implementation of trustworthy ITSs within nursing education. 5. The design, development, and evaluation of EduNurse, a domain-specific ITS prototype for nursing education. Guided by the CARE-ITS framework, this research presents a scenario-based ITS prototype (EduNurse) that translates empirically derived learner needs, pedagogical considerations, and framework-guided design principles into a functional educational system. EduNurse does not introduce a new AI technique. Its contribution is how it brings established approaches together within a nurse-informed ITS architecture designed around the pedagogical requirements of nursing education. Within EduNurse, semantic similarity is used alongside educational decision rules to assess written scenario responses and provide feedback and learner support. This forms the basis of its frugal neuro-symbolic approach to scenario-based learning and assessment. In doing so, this research demonstrates how AI techniques can be applied within a trustworthy ITS that is informed by empirical educational requirements and aligned with the pedagogical, professional, and ethical principles of nursing education. The formal evaluation of EduNurse is complete. The evaluation combines nursing learners’ questionnaire responses, linked system-interaction records, technical-performance logs, and an independent nursing-educator audit of assessment outputs. Data analysis is now being undertaken to examine the extent to which EduNurse demonstrated the intended CARE-ITS capabilities and achieved the doctoral research objectives.

title: ALGORITHMS FOR INTEGRATING EXTERNAL KNOWLEDGE INTO NEURAL NETWORK DATA PROCESSING TECHNOLOGIES
abstract: The integration of external knowledge into neural network data processing technologies is an important direction in artificial intelligence research. Traditional neural networks primarily learn from training data and may struggle with incomplete information, limited datasets, and complex domain-specific relationships. External knowledge sources, including knowledge graphs, ontologies, databases, and expert-defined rules, can improve the accuracy and reliability of intelligent systems. This thesis examines the principal algorithms for incorporating external knowledge into neural network architectures, focusing on knowledge graph embeddings, feature fusion, and knowledge-based optimization. The integration process is described mathematically, and potential applications in intelligent information processing are discussed.

title: MAES: Multidimensional Algorithmic Evolution System
abstract: MAES is a single-file Python multi-agent ALife simulator (NumPy only) that studies emergent cognitive ecology, dimensional abduction, and communication layers. Built on a hands-off methodology: the experimenter sets initial conditions and observes; the simulator does not optimize for any goal. Phase 1 empirical study (80 runs, 4 conditions x 20 seeds) reports that dimensional abduction (5D->13D) approximately doubles ai_peak and yields ~9x increase in species diversity. Note: in v1.0 ai_peak was read over a 200-trace window; this measurement error is documented in the v3.3 release notes.

title: Bộ BIT về FRC trong ELITE–AGLC: nền toán hữu hạn, tham chiếu Arbiter và hợp thành có kiểm soát
abstract: Bộ tài liệu nghiên cứu BIT về tuyến FRC trong kiến trúc ELITE–AGLC, gồm báo cáo tổng kết, các lập luận giải tích có phạm vi, mã kiểm thụ động, dữ liệu kiểm, hồ sơ nguồn và sổ câu hỏi còn mở. Nền tảng được tập hợp gồm đại số ba giá trị, miền vector 14 tọa độ, Pareto và tính tối thiểu tương đối với slate hữu hạn có điều kiện. Hai bổ sung chính là R1A, kiểm phép nối tới đúng một tham chiếu Arbiter ở actual round k−1, và R1C, chặn đánh giá F2 khi điều kiện tham chiếu, kiểu dữ liệu hoặc binding chưa đạt, đồng thời bảo toàn kết quả của bộ đánh giá F2 gốc trên đầu vào đã kiểm. Các kết quả áp dụng cho miền dữ liệu được nộp và giả thiết được ghi rõ; không chứng minh nguồn, currentness hoặc quyền vận hành ngoài thế giới. Atlas bao quát 32 countermodels về mặt hồ sơ; chỉ ba ca có thực thi overlay R1C mới, 29 ca còn NOT_RUN/OPEN. Đây là bộ bàn giao nghiên cứu có hỗ trợ của AI, chưa phải hệ ELITE–AGLC hoàn tất hoặc phản biện độc lập bên ngoài. Các giới hạn về owner projections, complete slate, reason coverage, quan hệ snapshot, trace và durable atomicity được giữ công khai. Hướng dẫn tái lập trực tiếp được cung cấp; tiện ích sao chép reproduce.py không phải entrypoint được hỗ trợ do lỗi đã ghi nhận. Tác giả: Bùi Quang Trịnh. CC BY 4.0 chỉ áp dụng trong phạm vi nội dung mà tác giả có quyền cấp phép; các nguồn khác giữ quyền/giấy phép gốc. Xem thông báo tác giả và phạm vi giấy phép kèm theo. Không bổ sung giấy phép MIT cho mã.

title: Dissimilarity Measures and Internal Validation Criteria for Unsupervised Clustering of Categorical, Ordinal, and Mixed-Type Data: A Systematic Review
abstract: This project is a systematic methodological review of dissimilarity measures and internal cluster validation criteria used in the unsupervised clustering of categorical, ordinal, and mixed-type data. Its purpose is to identify, classify, and critically synthesize studies that propose, substantially extend, or methodologically evaluate distance functions, dissimilarity measures, internal validity indices, and procedures for assessing partition quality or selecting the number of clusters. For each included study, the review examines the type of data addressed; the formal definition and intended use of the method; its treatment of nominal and ordinal information; reported mathematical and statistical properties; the clustering algorithms and datasets used; the theoretical, simulation-based, or empirical evaluation procedures; comparator methods; and reported limitations. Particular attention is given to whether ordinal information is preserved without imposing unjustified equal spacing, whether metric properties are demonstrated rather than assumed, and whether consistency, stability, uncertainty, or inferential guarantees are addressed. The initial bibliographic search was conducted reproducibly through the OpenAlex API using thematic query blocks and direct verification of foundational seed studies. Search records, screening decisions, full-text eligibility assessments, extraction procedures, and synthesis decisions are documented. The final corpus comprises 43 studies; data extraction and a verification audit of the extraction matrix against the full texts have been completed. Because the contributions are methodologically heterogeneous and do not share a common effect-size metric, the evidence will be synthesized through descriptive mapping, structured narrative synthesis, and comparative tables rather than quantitative meta-analysis. The expected outputs are an organized taxonomy of existing approaches, comparative evidence tables describing their formal and empirical properties, an assessment of the extent to which categorical and ordinal structure is appropriately represented, and the identification of methodological gaps concerning ordinal-sensitive dissimilarities, mixed-type data, internal cluster validation, and statistical inference. The review supports the theoretical framework of a doctoral research project and provides a transparent evidence base for future methodological development.

title: Small but Mighty: Test Suites as Improvement Signals for Self-Evolving Agents
abstract: A self-evolving agent rewrites its own harness and must decide which rewrites to keep, so its improvement signal is the check a rewrite has to pass. Verifying a rewrite by agent rollout is expensive and subjective, while executable checks such as the repository's own tests are too sparse to catch behavior-changing rewrites, rejecting only a quarter of them. We instead take test feedback as the executable signal, and search for test suites that are both small and strong with a quality-diversity evolutionary algorithm, so that the signal is dense and informative. TeSearch treats suite size as a behavior descriptor, so that quality is pursued at every size and a small, strong suite is reachable, and learns a transition kernel during the search that denoises the LLM as an actuator on that descriptor. Across 129 real-world modules and three backbones, TeSearch delivers the highest-quality suites of any method compared, LLM-driven evolutionary search included, and the smallest of any LLM-based one. Used as the improvement signal of a self-evolving agent, it rejects 59.9% of behavior-changing rewrites against 25.3% for the repository's tests, at a 4.0% false-alarm rate and 3.5 s per decision. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/TeSearch.

title: RespFocus: Learning Temporal Evidence for Weakly Supervised Respiratory Sound Classification
abstract: Respiratory auscultation provides a low-cost means of assessing pulmonary function, yet transient crackles and sustained wheezes can be difficult to recognize in noisy clinical recordings. Conventional deep learning classifiers often operate as black boxes, offering limited insight into the temporal acoustic evidence supporting their predictions. We present RespFocus, a weakly supervised framework that uses multiple instance learning (MIL) to learn inspectable temporal evidence from cycle-level labels and integrate it into classification. We also introduce PedResp2026, a multicenter pediatric respiratory sound cohort collected in routine clinical environments with adjudicated cycle-level annotations. In classification experiments, RespFocus achieves four-class Scores of 69.55\% on public ICBHI 2017 and 72.91\% on PedResp2026. Evidence diagnostics and matched temporal interventions support the functional contribution of the learned evidence to model predictions. Together, these findings highlight RespFocus's potential as a tool for automated respiratory sound diagnosis.

title: A Decade of PhotoMappers: A Longitudinal Study of Crowdsourced Disaster Photos Geolocalization with Vision-Language Models and Geospatial Reasoning
abstract: Crowdsourced disaster imagery provides timely, ground-level observations when conventional disaster mapping is delayed or incomplete, yet its geographic value depends on where observations are produced, how they are interpreted, and whether they can be reliably located as actionable Geospatial Intelligence (GEOINT). Using more than a decade of PhotoMappers, a crowdsourced disaster-mapping initiative, this study examines the changing geography of disaster information and asks how emerging GeoAI models compare with human geographic interpretation. We combine longitudinal spatial analysis with cross-view geolocalization using street view imagery (SVI) and remote sensing imagery (RSI), and evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) reasoning through 30 indicators spanning geographic cues and reasoning evidence. The results reveal a geographically and temporally uneven archive shaped by changing disaster types, Community Lifelines, and operational priorities. Integrating VGI, SVI, and RSI with Sinkhorn re-ranking achieves 40.90% R@1, 61.10% R@5, and 69.45% R@10, while yearly R@1 varies markedly from 25.00% to 65.07%. Geographic reasoning is similarly uneven: Qwen3.6-27B achieves an overall agreement of 67% compared with 51% for InternVL3-8B, with both models showing greater difficulty with localized and place-specific evidence than broad spatial configurations. We argue that the value of GeoAI lies less in replacing volunteered geographic interpretation than in complementing it, scaling candidate retrieval while retaining human judgment for ambiguous and consequential cases. This provides a pathway toward more human-centered and responsible GeoAI for disaster mapping. All data and code are openly available at https://github.com/bobleegogogo/PhotoMappers-VLM.

title: AI for Engineers: A Beginner's Guide with Power System Examples and Real-Data Case Studies
abstract: AI for Engineers: A Beginner’s Guide with Power System Examples and Real-Data Case Studies is a first introduction to artificial intelligence for engineering students. It assumes no background in AI, machine learning or programming. Every idea is explained in plain language, first with an example from everyday life and then with an example from electrical power engineering, such as load forecasting, protection relays, transformer monitoring, smart meters and the inspection of power lines. The book has eleven chapters. Chapters 1 to 3 cover the foundations: what AI is, how machines learn, and how to work with data. Chapters 4 to 7 cover the classical methods: linear regression, classification, decision trees and random forests, clustering and anomaly detection. Chapters 8 and 9 introduce neural networks and their use with images and language. Chapter 10 deals with the ethical and responsible use of AI. Chapter 11 is a guide to the research literature on AI in power systems. Each chapter states its main ideas as numbered equations with small worked examples, using only school-level algebra. Five chapters include a case study on real, publicly available data: the hourly load and temperature data of the Global Energy Forecasting Competition 2014. The teaching examples elsewhere use illustrative numbers and are labelled as such. The book also contains review questions with answers, a glossary and a reference list. The Python code and data behind every figure and case-study result are included with this record. This book grew out of the lecture notes for the course COMP-140 AI for Engineers.

title: Oddworld: relational reasoning emerges under implicit selection in evolving attention agents
abstract: Whether reasoning can arise without a teacher is a central question for both artificial intelligence and the evolution of cognition. Most demonstrations of reasoning in artificial agents rely on an explicit objective: a reward, a loss or a fitness score that names the desired behaviour. Here we show that a simple form of relational reasoning, finding the odd one out among symbolic objects, emerges in an artificial-life world where agents only eat, survive and reproduce, with no reward function and no fitness score. Agents carry a generic attention network whose weights are their genes and contains no built-in comparison feature. After a long period without change, evolving populations reliably acquire the ability, it transfers to shape and colour values never encountered during evolution, and it never appears in a control world where the energy from each meal is a lottery. Inside the evolved brains, evolution did not build pairwise comparison but a cheaper set-level computation: each object estimates how rare its features are in the current scene. These results suggest that open-ended selection can discover relational computations on its own, and they set up a sharper test, an ecology in which no answer is defined in advance. This record contains the technical note (PDF), the simulation and analysis code with logs and final genomes of all runs (ZIP), a 20-second video, and an interactive 3D replay (HTML; open in a web browser, click an agent to see its brain's scores, its target and the answer). https://github.com/drnamlabs-gif/oddworld

title: IDA Quantum Computing: GF(8) as the Natural Algebra of the Steane Code and Transversal Cliord Gates
abstract: We establish a rigorous correspondence between the IDA algebraic frame- work (Papers 3 and 5) and quantum error correction. The key result is that the Galois eld GF(8) = F2[x]/(x 3 + x + 1), identied in Paper 5 as the IDA alge- bra, is precisely the natural coecient algebra of the Steane [[7, 1, 3]] quantum error-correcting code. We prove four main theorems: (T1) the seven non-zero elements of GF(8)∗ ∼= Z7 are the columns of the parity-check matrix of the [7, 4, 3] Hamming code, giving the [[7, 1, 3]] Steane code via the CSS construc- tion; (T2) the Frobenius automorphism φ : a 7→ a 2 of GF(8) corresponds to a transversal Cliord gate on the [[7, 1, 3]] code; (T3) the IDA operations ⊕ and ⊗ map respectively to stabilizer generators (Pauli X chains) and logical operators of the Steane code; and (T4) the quantum channel capacity of the IDA wormhole (Paper 4 Corollary 4) is the quantum capacity of the associated ReedSolomon channel over GF(8). Corollaries include: the GF(64) multiverse of Paper 6 corre- sponds to the [[63, 1, 21]] quantum ReedSolomon code; fault-tolerant quantum computation via the IDA Frobenius; and the identication of dark matter (Pa- per 6) with logically undetectable quantum errors.

title: Who Bears Privacy Risk? Model-Dependent Memorization in Synthetic Tabular Data
abstract: Privacy risk in synthetic tabular data is typically evaluated as an aggregate property: how much leakage exists, rather than who is exposed. But aggregate metrics treat individuals as undifferentiated, hiding whether certain records or subgroups are systematically more exposed than others. If risk is unevenly distributed, a natural but largely unexplored question is whether the choice of generative model itself shifts who bears it. We address this question through per-sample nearest-neighbor memorization analysis across diffusion-based and LLM-based tabular generators on real-world financial and clinical datasets. We find that the training records at highest memorization risk vary substantially across generators, with some model pairs exposing nearly disjoint victim sets, and that the most exposed demographic subgroups shift with the generator deployed: on the financial dataset, diffusion models disproportionately expose lower-income individuals while an LLM-based generator over-exposes higher-income ones; on the clinical dataset, LLM-based models concentrate memorization on a clinically sensitive subpopulation that diffusion models largely spare. Standard aggregate privacy metrics surface neither pattern; in at least one case, a model with more favorable aggregate metrics shifts who is exposed rather than uniformly reducing risk. We argue that model selection for synthetic data generation is implicitly a decision about which subpopulations bear privacy risk, constituting a fairness consideration distinct from aggregate privacy guarantees. Privacy evaluations that rely on aggregate metrics alone may fail to identify the individuals most vulnerable to memorization-based leakage.

title: Using Line Segment Tracking to enable ML-based Track Reconstruction in CMS
authors: Aashay Arora on behalf of the CMS Collaboration
abstract: High-pileup conditions in CMS during the HL-LHC era make charged-particle tracking increasingly challenging as detector occupancy and combinatorics grow. We present a hybrid approach that exploits Line Segment Tracking (LST) objects rather than individual hits to enable the first CMS ML-based track reconstruction algorithm. The LST objects, namely the triplets used in this study, are built according to geometry- and physics-driven criteria and carry richer local structure, geometrical cues, and physics quantities such as transverse momentum, which helps the model incorporate detector-level information from the start. We apply a Transformer encoder with geometrically masked sparse self-attention to embed these objects in a learned latent space, and use object condensation to assemble full tracks in a single inference step. This object-based representation reduces complexity in dense environments and makes the model less sensitive to ambiguities introduced by high pileup. Evaluated on CMS Phase-2 simulation of $t\bar{t}$ events at $\langle μ\rangle = 200$, the approach achieves reconstruction efficiency comparable to the LST quintuplet baseline while reducing the fake rate by roughly a factor of three and suppressing duplicates almost entirely, demonstrating the promise of advanced ML architectures for next-generation particle tracking.

title: TabMosaic: Unified In-Context Diffusion for Tabular Generative Tasks
abstract: Generative modeling for tabular data has advanced to the point where models can synthesize realistic records, recover missing values, and generate samples conditioned on class labels or observed attributes. Despite recent advances, existing approaches either require table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to single-cell prediction. In this work, we formulate these tabular generative tasks as a single problem: modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table. To this end, we turn to diffusion, whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells rather than one cell at a time. Under the pretraining distribution, this objective is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution over the target set. Building on this, we propose TabMosaic, a unified in-context diffusion model for generating mixed-type target cells in unseen, potentially incomplete tables without table-specific training. We further show that its pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning from a single-value prediction to joint multi-cell generation. Across 48 real-world tables, TabMosaic ranks first on all evaluated generative tasks against 20 baseline approaches
