title: Deterministic Containment of Probabilistic Intelligence: The Squirrel OS Journey — Philosophy, Architecture, and Empirical Evidence
abstract: Research monograph in thesis form — a self-published master's-thesis-style synthesis of the Squirrel OS program. Status disclosure: this is not a university-issued document and confers no degree or credential. Chapter 1, the journey: a receipted timeline from the August 2026 question (can an LLM-governed fleet heal itself?) to a DOI-stamped corpus — first benchmarks and first self-heal, first live-tenant chaos learning (100% healing success, 5/5, with both security guards held by design), the append-only doctrine, SIM-B parity, the CCR containment series, and the published Dual Mesh Benchmark. Chapter 2, the philosophy: bifurcated governance (probabilistic proposers inside a deterministic cage), receipts-first discourse, the append-only transparency ledger, patent-then-publish, prototype honesty, and the simulated-customer doctrine — with the project's own failures preserved in the ledger on purpose. Chapter 4, the empirical evidence: the full CCR table — CCR-1 (72 permitted actions, 8 harness adversarials rejected), CCR-2 (a genuine model-generated invalid proposal intercepted), CCR-N (10 novel adversarial families rejected), CCR-P/CCR-T (guarded live write routes; engine resistance and gate enforcement reported as separate mechanisms), the DeepSeek leg (a fabricated tuple caught deterministically at the first structural check, honestly recorded, not retried), and the Dual Mesh Benchmark (MEASURED: mesh median 0.000443 ms n=200 vs platform baseline median 4509.1 ms n=20, ratio 1.018e+07, binding disclosure: characterizes the tested environment; the historical 267x figure is not confirmed or superseded; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303081). Honesty guards: every claim is held at corrected-claim strength — deterministic containment demonstrated under the tested conditions; the approval-registry gap and the coverage boundary are named as gaps; no universal, mathematical, production, or certification claim is made. AI-assisted under human direction; two-key curation: AI vet, human GO (October 11, 2026). Public append-only ledger: four-horsemen (thesis commit 1e6aa52, ledger 0048). Research home: DCAI community. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

title: Beyond Language Resource Tier: A Survey Study of Culturally Situated Resource Scarcity in LLM-Generated Cultural Translation of Math Word Problems
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being used to adapt math word problems for personalized learning at scale, and whether those adaptations actually serve students is an open question. Personalized learning, when conducted poorly, can introduce extraneous cognitive load for students, which makes it important to understand when and why LLMs fail at this task. To account for these failures, we present culturally situated resource scarcity, a mismatch between language-level data availability and coverage of the specific cultural and educational context a task requires. A language can appear high-resource overall while still lacking data for the community, region, script, domain, register, or educational genre needed for a particular task. In this preregistered study, we surveyed 552 native speakers across seven languages and three regions to assess the effectiveness of three frontier models in culturally translating math word problems. Our confirmatory results show that a low-resource language tier does impact linguistic quality and cultural appropriateness scores, but does not alter the mathematical reasoning of the translations. Our exploratory analysis shows, however, that region is a better predictor of culturally adapted translation quality than language resource tier. For example, Italian is a high-resource language yet receives lower cultural appropriateness ratings than all three Indian languages that were assessed, including low-resource Punjabi. A single-axis resource classification is insufficient. We argue that contributions from multiple data types should be assessed when reviewing complex translation tasks to fully understand where translation failures are occurring. We find that Likert ratings, checklist responses, and open-ended coding reveal different failure modes, with some coded errors not reflected in holistic ratings.

title: DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage
abstract: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.

title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.

title: Chapter 11: Liar Paradox Resolved - Will over Will and M is Ground
abstract: Chapter 11: Liar Paradox Resolved - Will over Will and M is Ground Author: Teo Chwee Hock [Independent Researcher, Sanduo Framework] Keywords: Liar Paradox, Will over Will, M is Ground, Tarski Hierarchy, Self-reference, Ungrounded Sentence, Sanduo Framework C11 ABSTRACT The Liar sentence S = "This sentence is false" generates a classic antinomy: if true, then false; if false, then true. We show Liar is structurally harder than Barber (C8). Barber is Can vs Will, separable by Will over Can. Liar is Will vs Will, Will judging Will. Resolution: By axiom M is Ground, every legal E must be grounded in M. Truth is a Will that must be conferred by M. Liar attempts to confer truth upon itself without external M, therefore it is not paradoxical but illegal. You Can utter it, but M Will not assign a truth value. The paradox dissolves before evaluation.

title: Karakalpak Speech Recognition with Whisper: An Open 107-Hour Corpus, a Held-Out Benchmark, and Knowledge Distillation into Smaller Models
abstract: Karakalpak is a Turkic language spoken by roughly 0.8–0.9 million people, chiefly in the Republic of Karakalpakstan (Uzbekistan), and has almost no open speech technology. We release the Karakalpak Speech Corpus, 106.9 hours (21,702 utterances) of read speech contributed by more than 200 volunteers, with speaker-disjoint train / validation / test splits. Fine-tuning Whisper-Medium on the training split alone yields 10.66% word error rate (WER) on the held-out test set with greedy decoding, and 9.47% with beam search and a 4-gram language model trained on the training transcripts, against 50.4% for the best publicly available system (MMS-1B with its Karakalpak adapter). We then distil the fine-tuned model into smaller students and compare them with students of the same size fine-tuned directly on the human transcripts: distillation lowers test WER by 0.75 points for Whisper-Small (to 11.52%) and by 2.52 points for Whisper-Base (to 15.54%), both statistically significant, and the distilled Whisper-Small runs faster than real time on a 4-core CPU. A Distil-Whisper-style student with a 2-layer decoder is under-trained at this data and compute budget and falls behind both, and replacing the Uzbek proxy language token with Kazakh (with Cyrillic targets) gives no significant difference. All data, models and code are released under open licences. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/atikuwu/karakalpak-speech-corpus Models: https://huggingface.co/atikuwu/whisper-medium-karakalpak · https://huggingface.co/atikuwu/whisper-small-karakalpak · https://huggingface.co/atikuwu/whisper-base-karakalpak Demo: https://huggingface.co/spaces/atikuwu/whisper-karakalpak-asr

title: Harmonic Representations in Symbolic Music Transformers are Localized and Controllable
abstract: Transformer models trained on symbolic music have become remarkably capable. However, it is yet unclear how they represent music structure, and whether understanding their internal representations can be used to unlock methods for model control. We examine this through a case study of harmonic analysis: when a music transformer navigates a cadence, what does it internally "know" about its harmonic context, and can that knowledge be used to affect the generation? Using Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer evaluated on Bach chorales, we find that harmonic decisions are causally localized progressively from middle layers onward. Linear probes show that mode becomes decodable in the same layer range where patching identifies growing causal effect, while key identity emerges later. We then confirm these representations are actionable for music generation control: steering via latent directions corresponding to harmonic changes reliably produces a deceptive or minor resolution, while preserving structural coherence and generation quality. This demonstrates that, at inference time, the model's internal harmonic knowledge can be directly manipulated to control the harmonic output.

title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.

title: Regression Analysis of Environmental Factors Affecting Photovoltaic Power Output
abstract: This project investigates the effect of solar intensity, wind speed, humidity, ambient temperature, and Air Quality Index (AQI) on the performance of a photovoltaic (PV) solar plate. The study involves collecting experimental data on meteorological parameters and electrical outputs, including current and voltage, using appropriate measuring instruments. Regression analysis will be performed to examine the relationships between these parameters and the PV plate’s output power and efficiency. The primary objective is to identify the most influential environmental factors and establish suitable parametric relationships. The findings may help improve solar energy utilization and support better performance evaluation of photovoltaic systems under varying environmental conditions.

title: A decoupled perception–control training pipeline for vision-based deep reinforcement learning, with cross-domain and cross-reward transfer extensions
abstract: Training a control policy directly from camera pixels with deep reinforcement learning is fragile: the visual encoder and the policy are optimised by the same temporal-difference gradient, so the latent state is non-stationary, and recovering a working agent usually demands image augmentation, a separate encoder learning rate and a tuned replay ratio. This article specifies the decoupled alternative as a complete, replicable pipeline, in which a convolutional autoencoder is pre-trained on a small demonstration corpus, frozen, and then used as a fixed feature map for an off-policy actor–critic agent. The pipeline customises two established methods — convolutional autoencoder representation learning and Soft Actor-Critic — and its contribution is the set of specifications that make the combination work with no per-configuration tuning, together with stage-wise validation checkpoints that expose a failed perception stage before expensive policy training begins. Two extensions reuse the same artifacts, one for deployment in an unseen visual domain and one for a revised objective, each with the algorithm substitution and the evaluation rules it requires. Under a single hyperparameter set applied unchanged, every decoupled configuration converged, while an end-to-end baseline consuming the same 120 × 160 × 3 observation never completed a lap.

title: DC-Flow: Target-Conditioned Cyclic Peptide Design via Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching
abstract: Target-conditioned cyclic peptide design requires coordinating interfacial side chains with macrocyclic closure. Existing end-to-end generators concurrently update geometric and chemical variables from noise, assigning residues to disordered coordinates. Meanwhile, predictor-assisted workflows often get stuck in local traps because they lack feedback in the propose-and-filter stage and ignore 3D structural proposals during sequence search. To overcome the drawbacks of these two paradigms, we propose DC-FLOW, a staged generative framework built around Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching. In principle, DC-FLOW postpones sequence and side-chain activation until a target-conditioned backbone takes shape, resolving structural ambiguity before chemical assignment. Then, it feeds delayed activations back into the backbone, achieving co-evolution of backbone geometry and emerging residue identities by coupling their flows. This mechanism enables more reliable macrocyclic closure and favorable interface packing. For predictor-assisted workflows, DC-FLOW supplies 3D proposals with in-trajectory guidance, enabling cascaded test-time scaling to prune redundant backbones and terminate unpromising refinement early. Extensive experiments show that DC-FLOW improves cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, substantially increasing the yield of confident cyclic peptide binders under a fixed final-candidate budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/mianqiu00/DCFlow.

evidence.title: DC-Flow: Target-Conditioned Cyclic Peptide Design via Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching
evidence.abstract: Target-conditioned cyclic peptide design requires coordinating interfacial side chains with macrocyclic closure. Existing end-to-end generators concurrently update geometric and chemical variables from noise, assigning residues to disordered coordinates. Meanwhile, predictor-assisted workflows often get stuck in local traps because they lack feedback in the propose-and-filter stage and ignore 3D structural proposals during sequence search. To overcome the drawbacks of these two paradigms, we propose DC-FLOW, a staged generative framework built around Delayed-Coupling Flow Matching. In principle, DC-FLOW postpones sequence and side-chain activation until a target-conditioned backbone takes shape, resolving structural ambiguity before chemical assignment. Then, it feeds delayed activations back into the backbone, achieving co-evolution of backbone geometry and emerging residue identities by coupling their flows. This mechanism enables more reliable macrocyclic closure and favorable interface packing. For predictor-assisted workflows, DC-FLOW supplies 3D proposals with in-trajectory guidance, enabling cascaded test-time scaling to prune redundant backbones and terminate unpromising refinement early. Extensive experiments show that DC-FLOW improves cyclization fidelity, diversity, and interface energetics, substantially increasing the yield of confident cyclic peptide binders under a fixed final-candidate budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/mianqiu00/DCFlow.

title: Temporal evaluation of US consumer financial complaint classification (2018-2025): data and code
abstract: The harmonised analytical dataset and the complete analysis pipeline underlying the article Do machine-learning models remain reliable as consumer complaints change? A temporal evaluation of US financial complaint classification. The dataset holds 369,063 public complaint narratives submitted to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau between 1 January 2018 and 31 December 2025, harmonised into four product categories: credit card, mortgage, student loan, and vehicle loan or lease. Alongside the narrative text it carries a SHA-256 hash of each normalised narrative and three duplicate-structure flags, which support duplicate-aware splitting, purging and cluster bootstrapping. The pipeline reproduces every table and figure in the article: the data audit, word-level TF-IDF representation, four classifiers, three validation designs (group-aware random, fixed out-of-time, and rolling-origin), drift and explainability analyses, and eight pre-specified robustness specifications. Source records were downloaded from the CFPB Consumer Complaint Database on 4 September 2026. The narratives are published by the CFPB only after its own personal-information review. The dataset is released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT Licence.

title: Population size reduction methods in differential evolution: a comprehensive review and experimental analysis
abstract: Abstract Optimization plays a crucial role in modern engineering and science. Evolutionary computing techniques are a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) and have attracted a lot of attention recently. Scientists, engineers, and practitioners need to understand how evolutionary computing techniques work and be fluent in using AI-based optimization techniques to solve engineering optimization problems. The Differential Evolution (DE) algorithm, which is classified as a population-based evolutionary algorithm, is primarily intended for solving complex optimization problems. The original DE algorithm uses a fixed population size, whereas modern DE variants adopt advanced strategies for reducing the population size over the evolution process. In this review article, 204 studies are included and we offer not only an overview of the population size reduction methods, but also a comparative analysis of selected methods by integrating them into the state-of-the-art algorithm and performing experimental work on the CEC 2024 benchmark functions and two real-world problems. Benchmarking demonstrates that the choice of population size adjustment strategy affects optimization performance, with its effectiveness depending on the problem characteristics and dimensionality. According to the Friedman test applied to 15 methods, 10 non-linear population size reduction methods were ranked higher than the linear population size reduction method on 100-dimensional problems. Moreover, a non-linear population size reduction method achieved the top rank on both real-world optimization problems. However, no single population size adjustment strategy consistently dominates across all problem dimensions and function families.

title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multiclass Multicalibration
abstract: We study online multiclass multicalibration over $T$ rounds, and give an algorithm with beyond-worst-case guarantees. With $n$ possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension $d=n-1$. In the worst case, cumulative $\ell_1$ multicalibration error scales with $\widetildeΘ(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$, which becomes untenable once $d$ exceeds a small constant. Our algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the sequence of adversarially selected outcome means lies in an affine subspace of dimension $s$, it obtains error $\widetilde O(n^{1/(s+2)}T^{(s+1)/(s+2)})$ with high probability. The algorithm adapts to this structure without knowing the subspace or its dimension. For $T\ge n\ge2$, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. For a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean, the bound specializes to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$, giving a square-root dependence on the horizon.

title: Have You Seen It Clearly? Uncertainty-Guided Belief Refinement for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) requires an agent to locate target objects in unfamiliar environments without additional training for the test categories or environments. Recent approaches leverage large language models and vision-language models to construct spatial representations and guide exploration. However, whether the available evidence sufficiently supports a navigation choice, and how new evidence changes the search value of previously visited locations, remain insufficiently addressed. We propose RefBeliefMap, an uncertainty-guided mapping framework that distinguishes target-location belief from spatial and semantic evidence uncertainty. By jointly modeling intra-observation uncertainty and inter-observation disagreement over a sliding memory window, RefBeliefMap assesses the reliability of both evidence channels. When competing frontiers remain insufficiently resolved, these uncertainty estimates guide active observation and semantic reasoning to refine the evidence supporting target-location beliefs before navigation commitment. Building on the refined map, we introduce RefBeliefNav, which jointly evaluates unexplored frontiers and historical waypoints according to their target-finding potential, expected information gain, and navigation cost. This unified objective allows historical locations to be reconsidered as new evidence changes their search value, coordinating exploration and revisitation. Experiments on HM3D and MP3D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines, with ablation studies examining the contributions of modules. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 quadruped robot further demonstrate the sim-to-real transferability of our method.

title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence to Appraise Social Media Narratives on Breast Reduction Procedures: A Snapshot Analysis
abstract: Background: Social media platforms increasingly influence patient perceptions regarding reconstructive procedures.This study evaluated the characteristics, quality, engagement patterns, and user sentiment associated with breast reduction-related content on TikTok, while assessing the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in content and sentiment analysis.Methods: A cross-sectional analysis of 140 TikTok videos on breast reduction was conducted.Engagement metrics, including likes, comments, shares, saves, and a weighted engagement index, were collected.The modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) and Global Quality Scale (GQS) were used to appraise content quality by AI and two human reviewers.Sentiment analysis was performed by human reviewers, ChatGPT, and Claude AI.High-engagement videos were defined as those within the upper quartile for likes (≥30,400) or shares (≥1,050).Results: Most videos were created by patients (89%) and focused on postoperative experiences (75%).Videos demonstrated substantial engagement, with median values of 3,860.5 likes, 131 comments, and 194.5 shares.Overall informational quality was poor, with median GQS and mDISCERN scores of 1-2 across raters.Highly liked and highly shared videos were significantly shorter in duration (18 vs. 34 seconds; p < 0.05) and generated markedly greater engagement across all metrics.Popular videos received significantly lower quality scores from human reviewers.Sentiment analysis revealed predominantly positive responses (49-58%).Claude showed greater concordance with human consensus than ChatGPT (κ = 0.749 vs. 0.649).Conclusion: Breast reduction content on TikTok is largely patient-driven and characterized by high engagement but low informational quality.Shorter videos achieved greater dissemination despite being associated with less reliable health information.

title: An Overlapping Multi-Signal Detection Framework Based on Masked Pretraining and Repulsion Loss
abstract: As the electromagnetic environment grows increasingly crowded with coexisting wireless systems, overlapping signals have become commonplace. Signal overlap in a limited space leads to feature mixing, boundary blurring, and annotation difficulty, which existing deep learning methods cannot effectively handle. To tackle these challenges, we propose a two–stage detection framework that combines SimMIM self-supervised pretraining with a repulsion loss. In the pretraining phase, a Swin-Tiny backbone is trained on unlabeled time–frequency images through masked reconstruction. In the fine-tuning phase, the backbone is transferred to a YOLOv8 detector, where the repulsion loss is optimized jointly with the base detection loss. In the component ablation, the complete framework improves mAP50 by 9.0 points over the random-initialized baseline on the validation set. On the held-out main and overlap-stress sets, it obtains 0.875 mAP50, 0.798 mAP50-95, and 0.873 mAR, and 0.838, 0.756, and 0.829, respectively. Compared with the YOLOv8 baseline, the observed mAP50 gains are 1.95 and 2.18 points, respectively. The main high-overlap subset is small; its observed 1.64-point margin is therefore reported as descriptive evidence. These results indicate that in-domain self-supervised pretraining combined with spatially constrained box regression provides an effective representation and detection strategy for overlapping signals.

title: Small area learning
abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop standard and cross-fitted estimators for low-complexity and flexible learners, unifying synthetic, model-based, and fully residual-corrected estimation. For area means, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality and provide variance estimators and confidence intervals. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals a bias--variance trade-off: partial residual correction can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to working-model misspecification, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34\%--49\% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. An empirical application favours a cross-fitted estimator using a flexible learner under the chosen validation criterion. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.

title: Adaptive Sorting, also in the BST Model
abstract: Sorting is one of the most basic algorithmic problems. Adaptive sorting algorithms exploit features that make an input easier to sort, often captured by entropy measures. Many such measures have been studied, raising two natural questions: how do they relate to one another, and are there algorithms that are adaptive to them? We complete a hierarchy of relations between previously studied entropy measures and show that the classical measure Reg is a source of this hierarchy. We prove that an existing data structure yields a Reg-adaptive sorting algorithm, thereby achieving the adaptive bounds of every measure in the hierarchy. Following McIlroy's observation that Reg has a mathematically inconvenient definition, we study a slightly weaker but simpler measure, reg. For inputs without duplicates, we show that O(n + log reg) = O(n + log Reg), so this simplification preserves the adaptive bound. Finally, we do algorithms design and introduce SproutSort, a reg-adaptive algorithm in the offline binary search tree (BST) model. SproutSort achieves an access cost of O(n + log reg), making it the most adaptive algorithm in this model to date. We also introduce SkeletonSort, a simple randomised pointer-machine algorithm that sorts distinct keys in expected O(n + log reg) time, offering a considerably simpler implementation of a sorting algorithm this high in the adaptive hierarchy.

title: When do explicit penalties improve flow matching?
abstract: Flow matching can learn structure directly from data, raising the question of when additional constraints improve generation. We study penalties that encode such constraints, with physics-informed flow matching as a motivating example. Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.

title: VideoEvoHarness: Self Evolving Agent Harness from Unlabeled Videos for Video Understanding
abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.

title: Solving Specification Drift and Contextual Degradation via a Tri-Stream Cognitive Architecture with Non-Lossy Canonical Synthesis in Autonomous AI Agents
abstract: Long-running conversational AI agents and assistive development models inevitably succumb to contextual degradation, specification drift, and sycophantic decay. Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms treat dialogue turns, human identity, and technical parameters as an undifferentiated, flat vector repository. This structural limitation induces lossy compression of technical truth, context window pollution, and hallucinatory synthesis of project constraints. This paper introduces the architecture of Blue Synergy CORTEX, an external, persistent cognitive runtime operating via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and stateful REST gateways. CORTEX establishes an architectural Tri-Stream Memory Boundary, bifurcating context into three distinct operational lifecycles: an evolving User Stream (Cognitive Blueprint), an audited Identity Stream (Executive Calibration with immutable Core Axioms), and an invariant, non-decaying Knowledge Stream (Living Canonical Specifications). To permanently eliminate specification drift, the Knowledge Stream utilizes a Dual-Zone Ingestion Pattern that couples sub-20ms fast-append staging buffers with scheduled, non-destructive canonical refactoring governed by an algorithmic Semantic Invariant Guard. Operational telemetry is protected by a Cognitive Immunity Shield, ensuring runtime tool crashes and apologetic model artifacts are filtered from long-term memory. Context retrieval executes via a deterministic, zero-LLM topological pathway achieving sub-65ms latency. Finally, we formalize the compliance model under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, Articles 5, 14, and 15), backed by quantitative benchmark metrics demonstrating 98% factual faithfulness and a 2% hallucination rate.

title: MiguelSantPasc/Code_AdvSSM: v1.0.0 – Adversarial Observations in State-Space Models for Robust RL Copiar
abstract: Code release – v1.0.0 This release contains the source code accompanying the manuscript "Adversarial Observations in State-Space Models for Robust Reinforcement Learning" by M. Santos-Pascual and D. Ríos Insua. The repository provides implementations and experimental scripts for studying adversarial perturbations of observations in probabilistic state-space models and their impact on downstream reinforcement learning. The main experimental components include: Adversarial observation attacks against Kalman filtering and smoothing. Evaluation of adversarial attacks in reinforcement learning environments, including navigation and CartPole. Analysis of the influence of observation and process noise covariance on attack effectiveness. Evaluation of uncertainty-aware defensive strategies based on adaptive covariance inflation. Comparison of attack and defense performance under different experimental settings. This version is intended to provide a reproducible snapshot of the computational experiments accompanying the manuscript. Archival information: This release is archived through Zenodo to provide a persistent DOI for research reproducibility and citation.

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.

title: Shannon's Information Channel as a Sector of the Triadic Coherence Invariant
abstract: Establishes a structural isomorphism between Shannon's information channel theorem and the triadic coherence invariant R = P × I × Pr ≠ 0. The sender–encoding–receiver decomposition maps to Intent–Pattern–Presence. Derives: topological channel capacity C ≈ 10.7 bits per anyon pair at SU(2)₃₀; spectral Shannon entropy H ≈ 0.929 nats with efficiency η ≈ 0.845; Landauer floor P_min ≈ 7.42 kT/τ; a self-reference bound unifying Shannon, Gödel, and the Ouroboros fixed-point condition. Proves DPI saturation for topological encoding and provides a channel-theoretic formulation of the measurement problem. Part of the CAT'S Theory corpus (ISBN 979-8160469362).

title: Pius-318/wideband-signal-dataset-generation: RF Signal Spectrogram Dataset Generation Tool
abstract: This project provides a MATLAB script for generating radio frequency (RF) signal spectrogram datasets for semantic segmentation tasks. The script can generate synthetic signals containing 9 different modulation types (BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK, 16QAM, 64QAM, FM, AM-DSB, AM-SSB, MSK) and automatically generate corresponding spectrograms and multi-class semantic segmentation labels.

title: Vision: "What Don't I Know About User's Preferences?" How Uncertainty Estimation Improves Proactive Assistant Alignment
abstract: Proactive Smart Assistants (PSAs) increasingly use general knowledge, learned patterns from group-level data, patterns from individual user's data, and recent sensor observations to anticipate which action a user may prefer. Existing systems typically select actions from predicted user preference likelihoods, but these likelihoods alone do not reveal how reliable the prediction is, which evidence supports it, or why ambiguity remains. In this vision paper, we argue that uncertainty estimation can provide this missing information and substantially change appropriate downstream behavior. Using the example of a home assistant, we introduce the questions that uncertainty estimation aims to answer, i.e. how sure is the assistant about the predicted preference likelihood, whether the confidence come from group-level assumptions or individual's data, and whether likelihood ambiguity reflect the user's intrinsic preference variability or insufficient data for the particular situation. We further introduce uncertainty estimation applications in neighboring domains, such as human trajectory prediction, personalized activity recognition, information-collection, and model-based control. Finally, we draw on insights from neighboring domains to envision how future uncertainty-aware proactive assistants may address key challenges in proactive interaction.

title: E8 Lattice Key Quantization for Low-Bit KV-Cache Compression
abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.

title: Mutual Transformations of Arbitrary Ternary Qubit Trees by Clifford Gates

title: Semantic Recovery in a Generative–perceptive Domain
abstract: Models with different neural architectures can develop corresponding representations from similar observations. To investigate those phenomena in a broad class of neural networks under a unified approach, we introduce a generative domain as a system with differentiated, writable state and boundary coupling, then define its generative–perceptive extension through predictive generation, retained evidence-dependent revision, and causal reuse. Semantic classes are specified by agreement of observable continuation laws. Under coverage, causal-state sufficiency, and vanishing excess predictive risk, a recovery theorem establishes convergence of native predictive laws and, at an attained optimum, identifies their state quotient with the source semantic classes. Additional continuation-consistency conditions preserve source operations and yield cross-model correspondence without requiring shared coordinates. Restricted autoregressive and diffusion learning constructions satisfy the domain conditions; a solvable Gaussian-factor learner demonstrates hidden-subspace acquisition. Experiments tested semantic recovery for a 4-state automaton driven by a continuous symbol stream, through native query predictions and write continuations. At matched exposure the categorical-diffusion model answered all 5,376 audit queries correctly; the prefix transformer reached 94.10%–99.16% accuracy. All runs recovered corresponding state distinctions, while operation fidelity varied and extended interference impaired preservation of unrelated bindings. Internal-state probing and interventions identified causal carriers of history information in both architectures and a context-dependent transformer write pathway. Potential machine-learning applications include semantic-recovery metrics and initialization strategies for faster semantic recovery. We also propose a mechanistic explanation for double learning and grokking.

title: Evidence Combines by Meet: The lattice that lets untrusted hands write quantum circuits
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A person who understands a physical problem rarely also understands quantum circuit synthesis, and almost never also understands a proof assistant. A language model can bridge both gaps — and in bridging them becomes the weakest component in the chain, because a plausible wrong artifact and a correct one look identical at the surface where the user reads them. We describe a system whose design removes the model from the trusted set entirely, and we give the algebra that makes the removal a theorem rather than a discipline. Evidence carries a tier in a four-element chain, and compound evidence combines by meet: a compound is top-tier if and only if every component is, so no assembly, however arranged, manufactures a guarantee. A display is honest exactly when it is a lax map into that lattice, and lax maps compose — which closes the laundering route through a rendering pipeline structurally rather than by inspection. Admission of untrusted source is a decidable predicate on text, deliberately over-rejecting: it may refuse honest input, never admit adversarial input. What the author wrote and what the production parser reconstructed from the emitted bytes are tied by a definitional equality checked in the same kernel run as the author's claims, so the retraction is the shipping parser rather than a shadow of it. The consequence is a surface on which an untrusted hand may write anything and a non-expert may read the result safely: what the screen displays is provably bounded by what the certificate supports. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Physics-guided machine learning for saturation control across variable hydraulic conditions in heap leaching
abstract: Heap-leaching hydraulics vary between regions of an ore bed, motivating fast prediction models that accommodate different material properties. This study develops a parameter-conditioned physics-guided machine-learning (PGML) surrogate and demonstrates its use in simulated saturation control. A dataset of 4096 numerical Richards-equation trajectories was divided into 2867 training, 614 validation and 615 evaluation cases. The network predicts hourly saturation profiles from the current profile, irrigation rate and four hydraulic parameters, and is trained with an approximate Gardner mass-balance penalty. A daily predictive controller compared 200 constant irrigation rates over a 24-hour horizon. Across the evaluation cases, the median full-cycle tracking deviation was 4.9% of a 0.70 saturation target, equal to that of a tuned proportional-integral (PI) controller, while the PGML controller reached the target without overshoot in the median and applied approximately 4% less irrigation. Moderate physics guidance reduced long-horizon prediction error by approximately 30% relative to data-only training and reduced irrigation-bound activity, but slightly worsened closed-loop tracking. For a matched prediction workload, the surrogate was approximately 70 times faster than the numerical solver, and batched evaluation cost under 2 ms per column for 5000 columns. The results support a reusable physics-guided surrogate for large-scale saturation control in simulation.

title: Low-Latency Belief-Propagation Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes with Reinforcement-Learned Scheduling
abstract: Belief propagation (BP) is attractive for quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) decoding because of its low complexity and low latency, but short cycles and degeneracy can limit its error-correction performance. Reinforcement-learned sequential scheduling (RL-S) substantially improves this performance by adapting the variable node (VN) update order, although Q-table storage and heap-based selection introduce additional overhead. We propose bucket RL-S (B-RL-S), which quantizes learned Q-values into integer priorities and schedules VN updates using dynamically maintained first-in, first-out buckets. Without retraining or changing the BP message updates, B-RL-S reduces policy storage and refreshes only priorities affected by local residual syndrome changes. A fixed number of priority levels enables constant-time VN selection and queue relocation. For the $[[288,12,18]]$ bivariate bicycle code over the depolarizing channel at $p=0.05$, B-RL-S with eight priority levels achieves approximately one fifth the block error rate (BLER) of flooding BP followed by order-10 ordered-statistics decoding. The respective caps are $1000$ sequential iterations for B-RL-S and $1000$ flooding iterations for the BP stage of the reference decoder. These results highlight strong error correction with inexpensive scheduling and no additional post-processing stage.

title: Rethinking Human Intent-to-CAD: Parametric CAD Model Generation via Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.

title: See Me, Believe Me: Causality, Intersectionality, and Interventions Improving the Appearance of Patients
abstract: In the context of medical records, patients often experience testimonial injustice, where the textual account undermines the validity of their experiences. Past work has demonstrated that intersectionality of demographic features is crucial to detect such injustice. We use causal discovery to study the degree to which certain demographic features tied to marginalization (namely age, gender, and race), together lead to specific types of testimonial injustice terms. This offers us an insightful Structural Causal Model (SCM) relating those demographic features to the different ways a patients' reality may be undermined. We then move toward addressing such injustice, by very selectively (based on insights from the SCM) editing physicians' notes. For comparison, we contrast these rule-based edits with blanket context-based modifications using an LLM. We assess the impact of these changes on the perception of patients' experiences, using human experts and an LLM. We find that edits, in general, enhance clarity regarding the urgency and causes of patients' conditions. Additionally, for human experts, rule-based modifications show a tendency to shift blame away from patients, and toward more objective external factors. These findings (1) underscore the importance of quantifying sources of injustice in how patients' testimonies are recorded, (2) reveal that making minimal intentional changes accordingly can effect improved patient perception, and (3) call for larger efforts to assess health outcomes under such more just representation.

title: Kernel-only Lean proof that the rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23
abstract: The Lean 4 proof, checked entirely by the Lean kernel, that the tensor rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23, for the paper The rank of 3×3 matrix multiplication over F2 is 23 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23304897, arXiv:2610.11823). The final theorem R22K.Final.rank_ge_23 depends only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. This is release v1.0 of github.com/tejasvi/rank333-f2-kernel, commit 0c7c6173c3dc91cf63972f1fe8980b726dd6a8e6. Its README describes the contents: SHA256SUMS gives the SHA-256 hash of every file, VERIFICATION.md the checks, and REGENERATE.md how every package is regenerated from the inputs with the programs in generators/. The private parts of the modules were deleted after they were built and checked, so a full replay regenerates them. The repository at v1.0 is in this record as rank333-f2-kernel-v1.0.zip. The other files of this record are listed, with their sizes, SHA-256 hashes and contents, in the repository's ZENODO.md.

title: The Proof Already Contains the Program: One rewrite theory from every logic to running code
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Trust in a proof is supposed to rest on a kernel small enough to read by hand. The formal-methods ecosystem has instead grown a dozen large, mutually opaque kernels—one per proof assistant—and now machine learning floods all of them with proofs and programs no human can eyeball. We report a working demonstration that the escape from this predicament is a single, small, well-understood mathematical object: the λΠ-calculus modulo rewriting, a typed lambda calculus with user computation rules into which functional type theories are known to embed. We realize eight source systems—Coq/CIC, Lean 4, HOL Light, Isabelle/Pure, Agda, Metamath, GHC's System FC, and Rust's typed MIR—as exact, faithfully translated images inside one such checker, so that eight trust roots collapse to one. Then we show the same object runs in reverse: because a constructive proof already contains its program (the Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov reading of Curry–Howard), the checked content of each image extracts, through one back-end, to a whole-program Rust artifact that a compiler builds and runs against a certified differential—for all eight languages. One small kernel receives every logic and emits its program. The consequence is a concrete first step toward software engineering done mathematics-first: you audit a tiny shared checker rather than trusting the author, human or machine, and the verified proof is the deployable artifact. A fresh finite logical-entropy estimator now tests that extraction thesis on an object not used to build the original eight-door demonstration: its exact ensemble law is proved in Lean, its Rust realization returns the same unreduced rational pair, and applicable structural mutations are killed. A successor program, reported in §6, has since walked this paper's own roadmap: export depth past scalars, an independent dual-metal differential through the Boundary reducer, an exactly enumerated residual trust base, and a proved composition theorem making source-kernel-to-bare-metal a single certified arrow. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Three Errors, Not One: The Quantum MacWilliams Identity, Certified
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A classical bit fails one way: it flips. A qubit fails three ways—X, Z, or both at once—and that single change of arithmetic, from one error per site to three, is the whole difference between the classical theory of error-correcting codes and the quantum one. It has a precise home. The MacWilliams identity of 1963 is the exact law relating a linear code's weight distribution to its dual's; its quantum analogue, due to Shor and Laflamme, carries the same law across the stabilizer formalism with one coefficient changed—a +1 becomes a +3. We prove that quantum identity in the kernel of a proof assistant, and we prove it the honest way: by reusing, unchanged, the finite character-orthogonality argument that certifies the classical identity, isolating the +3 to a single new lemma about the four Pauli operators at one qubit. The classical coefficient is not merely inapplicable to quantum codes; we exhibit a code on which the +1 law is false and its failure is itself a theorem. From the certified identity the entire Shor–Laflamme weight spectrum of a code follows—the count of stabilizers and of logical operators at every weight—and from the spectrum two numbers the field cares about: the code distance (the minimum weight of a logical operator, recovered as the first place the spectra part) and the sub-threshold error-rate prefactor (the count of minimum-weight logical representatives, which the distance alone cannot see). We certify both for the five-qubit perfect code and the Steane code, exhibit the exact spectra, and place the result beside a companion certificate that reaches the distance by a single witness: the witness is a local probe, the enumerator a global census, and a code is fully accounted for only when both have spoken. A public instrument reproduces every number by independent enumeration, trusting neither our kernel nor our word. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Routing signals for silent-error detection in text-to-SQL over a university data warehouse: benchmark, labels and code
abstract: Supporting data and code for the paper "Does the Router Know? Mixture-of-Experts Routing Signals for Detecting Silent Errors in Text-to-SQL over University Data Warehouses" (submitted to Knowledge-Based Systems, Elsevier). An agentic assistant built on the open-weight Mixture-of-Experts model gpt-oss-120b answers questions in Italian over the live data warehouse of a public university, on premises and without a GPU. Its most damaging failures are silent: a query that runs, returns a plausible number, and answers a different question from the one asked. This deposit contains: a benchmark of 1000 Italian questions from 51 templates, with reference values verified against the institution's own reports and the date each value was read; the error labels for three system configurations, together with the human review behind them and the stratified sample used to validate the references; the assistant's answers as returned; per-layer router statistics for all 36 layers of the model, extracted post hoc by replaying each answer through a teacher-forced forward pass in llama.cpp and capturing the router tensors, validated against the experts the model actually selected; the reports produced by the probes, including AUROC by feature family, control tasks and risk-coverage curves; the semantic layer, that is the official measure behind each institutional report and the catalogue of the 283 warehouse tables; and all the code, from routing extraction to probe evaluation. All material is aggregated. No person-level data was processed or released at any stage. The internal page and API addresses of the institutional dashboard have been removed from two files, which keep the measure definitions and default filters relied on by the paper. Data, labels and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; the code is additionally available under the MIT licence. Access to the files is currently restricted and granted on request; it will be opened on publication of the article.

title: Timed Reachability in Logic
abstract: Abstract We discuss some recent approaches to game-theoretic semantics (GTS), a useful alternative to the traditional Tarski-style compositional semantics of logic. One attractive feature of GTS is that model-checking upper bounds for logical systems can often be obtained directly by considering the corresponding alternating Turing machines. Our focus is on semantic games equipped with clocks, i.e., resources that control recursive behaviour during play and give rise to timed variants of reachability games. Such clock-based semantic frameworks naturally suggest variants of logical systems with different computational properties. We review some developments related to these themes, focusing on systems derived from the modal $$\mu $$ μ -calculus while also discussing applications to temporal logic.

title: To Use or Not: Differentiating Artificial Intelligence Content for Different Industries
abstract: Artificial Intelligence continues to develop; its integration has rapidly progressed into numerous business industries, impacting business operations regardless of context. This study examines how consumers respond to AI implementation across industries that vary in perceived creativity. Using a survey and a 2 by 2 between- subjects experimental design, this research finds that AI implementation negatively affects consumers’ willingness to purchase, regardless of the perceived creativity level of the industry. Additionally, drawing on research linking gender to differential perceptions of technology, this research shows that the negative effect of AI implementation is stronger for women than for men. Based on the findings, practical implications are offered while limitations are also discussed.

title: Celeus engine validation report
abstract: Validation report for the Celeus statistics engine, generated from a pinned R environment. It lists 111 cases across 39 test types and 281 numeric comparisons. Every case is compared with an independent computation in base R or standard packages; 12 cases are also anchored to a published literature value and 11 carry a certified reference value; 88 are canonical-only and labelled as such. For test selection, the correct test family was proposed in 85 of 93 evaluated cases; 18 of the 111 cases skipped that evaluation because their dataset is fetched externally. Reproducibility is checked separately over a 41-case corpus. This report is not a substitute for review by an independent statistician, and it is research statistics, not clinical decision support.

title: Systematic Inference Audit and Runtime Telemetry of Aleph Alpha Kolibri-1: Serving Forensics, Token Economics, and Parser Remediation on NVIDIA H200 SXM
abstract: Systematic Inference Audit and Runtime Telemetry of Aleph Alpha Kolibri-1: Serving Forensics, Token Economics, and Parser Remediation on NVIDIA H200 SXM Available in English and German. Both technical reports (PDF), Markdown sources, raw JSONL telemetry, and replication scripts are included in this record. Abstract (English) We present an independent, systematic inference audit of Aleph Alpha's Kolibri-1 model deployed under vLLM on a single NVIDIA H200 SXM (141 GB HBM3e). Comprising 5,372 live requests across four benchmark stages (Probe, Ablation, Stress/Concurrency, and Needle-in-a-Haystack), this audit resolves a critical failure class in LLM production pipelines: the silent failure of naive JSON parsers on reasoning models. Key Empirical Findings: Parser Remediation & Semantic Compliance: An initial 0.0% usable response rate in standard toolchains was isolated as a harness parsing artifact caused by unhandled delimiters. Upon delimiter-aware extraction and Pydantic validation, Kolibri-1 achieved a 99.98% semantic accuracy (5,371 / 5,372 requests correct; 95% Wilson CI lower bound: 99.89%). Token Economics & Fast-Lane Architecture: For routine information extraction, disabling reasoning (enable_thinking: false) reduces generated tokens by ~90% (median 492 to 50 tokens), cutting compute resource allocation by 71% and increasing request throughput by 3.4x on 4k-token unique prompts (up to 8.8x with cached prefixes). Hardware Saturation & The Latency Wall: Prefill compute saturates at ~35,100 prompt tokens/s. Under high concurrency (C=64, 31k context), P95 TTFT is 38.88 s across the full cell due to the synchronized start-burst prefill queue (steady-state P95: 5.0 s). Peak KV-cache utilization reached 42.66% with zero preemptions, demonstrating that H200 capacity is prefill-compute bound rather than memory bound. Enterprise On-Premises Dimensioning: Sizing extrapolations indicate that typical enterprise and legal workloads (e.g., 500 documents/day) utilize < 1% of an H200's prefill capacity. Dual 48 GB PCIe setups (e.g., 2x NVIDIA L40S or RTX 6000 Ada) paired with an intelligent API gateway (Fast Lane vs. Deep Lane) provide a cost-effective on-premises alternative. Kurzfassung (Deutsch) Dieser technische Bericht dokumentiert ein unabhängiges Inferenz-Audit von Aleph Alphas Kolibri-1 auf NVIDIA H200 SXM unter vLLM über 5.372 Live-Requests. Das Audit beweist, dass frühere 0,0-%-Ausfälle in Standard-Toolchains auf unmaskierte Reasoning-Delimiter ( ) im Test-Harness zurückzuführen sind. Nach Implementierung eines strikten Delimiter-Parsings liefert Kolibri-1 eine inhaltliche Genauigkeit von 99,98 %. Durch die Entkopplung von Routine-Extraktion („Fast Lane", Reasoning aus, 50 Tokens) gegenüber komplexer Urteilsfindung („Deep Lane", Reasoning an, 492 Tokens) lässt sich der Durchsatz um das 3,4- bis 8,8-Fache steigern und der Rechenaufwand pro Request um 71 % senken. title: A Lightweight Optimized CNN Framework for Breast Cancer Screening and Subtype Classification
abstract: Breast cancer remains one of the most serious diseases threatening human health globally. To address diagnostic subjectivity and insufficient classification granularity in pathological screening, this study proposes a lightweight complementary convolutional neural network (CNN) framework for two distinct yet clinically related tasks. The first model performs binary classification of invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) (IDC-positive vs. IDC-negative), while the second model conducts fine-grained multiclass classification of four malignant subtypes. Notably, primary patch-level evaluation for the IDC binary task may produce optimistically biased performance due to data leakage, where patches from the same patient can appear in both the training and test sets. The IDC_regular_ps50_idx5 dataset embeds patient/case identifiers within patch filenames, enabling patient-disjoint partitioning to mitigate this risk. On public patch-level test data, the framework achieves a patch-level accuracy of 0.8732 and an AUC of 0.9245, demonstrating superior resource efficiency compared with several state-of-the-art models. Computational analysis shows that the proposed model has 0.435 M parameters and 0.145 G FLOPs—33.8× fewer parameters than VGG16 (convolutional-only), 54.0× fewer than ResNet50, and 9.3× fewer than EfficientNet-B0. To quantify the optimistic bias introduced by patch-level evaluation, we first performed supplementary patient-disjoint 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation on the IDC dataset using filename-embedded patient identifiers. Under this intra-dataset patient-disjoint protocol, it achieves a mean accuracy of 0.8005 and mean AUC of 0.8783, with a moderate performance drop of approximately 7 percentage points relative to patch-level results. We further conducted external cross-dataset validation on BreakHis with strict patient-disjoint 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation. Under this cross-dataset protocol, the model yields substantially degraded performance (mean accuracy of 0.5417 ± 0.1738 and mean AUC of 0.5930 ± 0.1680), illustrating significant performance drop when generalizing to completely unseen patients under domain shift. title: "R2D2-Guard Experimental Records and Reproduction Data"
abstract: "This dataset accompanies the study \u201cR2D2-Guard: Auditable Release Policies for LoRA-Adapted LLM Services.\u201d It contains frozen experimental records for examining how release policies retain, replace, or withhold model responses under clean and backdoor attack conditions. The records cover mathematical reasoning experiments using GSM8K and SVAMP, together with scientific claim verification experiments using SciFact.The materials include request-level model outputs, recorded policy decisions, evaluation annotations, aggregate results, frozen protocols, configuration metadata, figure source data, and audit reports. JSON, JSONL, and CSV files preserve the recorded evidence. Accompanying documentation explains field definitions, provenance, evaluation denominators, and reproduction procedures. The materials support CPU reconstruction of reported tables and inspection of the relationships between requests, policy decisions, and recorded delivery outcomes.Verification software and reproduction instructions are available in the associated R2D2-Guard GitHub repository. Some historical model weights and training inputs are unavailable; the documented limitations distinguish reconstruction of saved results from regeneration of experiments. Reused benchmark components retain their upstream attribution and licensing conditions."

title: Unsupervised Cross-device Speaker Diarization And Linking Through Spatiotemporal Structure
abstract: Linking speakers across independently recorded rooms is difficult because microphone, room, and codec mismatch distort speaker embeddings. We study visitor linking without visitor enrollment or identity labels in simulated outpatient workflows. The proposed method combines per-device embedding centering, concurrency constraints, room-type-specific visit constraints, and a clustering threshold calibrated from concurrent visitors and identified staff voices. On simulated days built from VOiCES recordings, with companions, return visits, walk-ins, silent visits, and acoustic leakage, it improves B$^3$-F1 over the best label-free baseline for all 11 extractors, by 5.3-14.6 points (all 95\% intervals exclude zero). ECAPA-TDNN reaches 86.6, compared with 76.4 for the best label-free baseline and 87.7 for the best oracle-informed baseline. Gains persist across the reported workflow perturbations, but depend on removing duplicated cross-room speech: without this step, the method wins for only 2 of 11 extractors. Single-visit patients also remain vulnerable to false merges. These results support structure-aware linking while identifying preprocessing and identity-safety limitations that must be addressed before clinical deployment.

title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.

title: Recovering Low-Bit Failures in Vision-Language-Action Policies via Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $π_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $π_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model-memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.

title: SKSurrogate: a Python toolkit for surrogate-based optimization of expensive functions
abstract: SKSurrogate is a suite of tools implementing surrogate optimization for expensive functions based on scikit-learn. It facilitates hyperparameter optimization for machine learning models and optimized pipeline design (AutoML), with a custom Hilbert-space-based regressor alongside any scikit-learn regressor, plus an evolutionary search over transformer/estimator pipelines.

title: Winning Is a Witness
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: To win a chip-design contest today is to pass a test someone wrote, run on a simulator that another simulator may contradict — most sharply about the value a wire carries before it has been driven. The referee is not an object; it is a program someone trusts. We remove the trust. We give a digital circuit a meaning that is a single mathematical object — the schedule-independent fixed point of a four-valued event dynamics — and we build that meaning from six interlocking structures, each machine-checked, so that it is reachable from any surface a designer or an autonomous agent might use to describe a circuit. The first structure treats unknown as a value rather than an omission, so a design that "works" only because a two-valued simulator quietly powered its registers to zero is refused until it earns its zeros through a reset. The others fix when a single evaluation pass equals the order-independent fixed point (so the meaning is well defined at all), make the meaning invariant under the interleaving of independent clocks, compute the critical-path delay as a product in the tropical semiring, read temporal specifications as folds over that meaning, and carry every authoring surface through one semantics-preserving lowering. The six compose into a single arrow: what a designer authored equals the schedule-independent fixed point of its lowered form. On that foundation a contest stops being a test and becomes a game in the exact sense of constructive mathematics. A passing submission is a witness — a constructive proof that the challenge is satisfiable, realized by the submitted design; the leaderboard is a partial order on witnesses ranked by a kernel-defined objective (gate count, delay, area, power); and a podium design is awarded not a number but a certificate: a term the theorem prover's kernel re-checks, with an empty axiom footprint, portable to anyone who doubts the result. Three activities that hardware engineering keeps apart — verifying a design, optimizing it, and competing with it — become one activity: exhibiting and comparing witnesses. We report the system end to end. An adversarial battery of nine malformed and dishonest submissions is each rejected with the failing condition named; two contests rank correct entrants by genuine architectural tradeoffs (a three-gate multiplexer beats a thirteen-gate expansion; a balanced parity tree beats a linear chain of identical cells) while constant-output cheats never reach the board; podium designs certify with zero axioms; and, to close the loop to silicon, two winning designs pass an open place-and-route flow to a clean-signoff physical layout in a public process node. Nothing here asserts that the underlying semantics is the only possible one, or that the open backend is itself proven; we state both boundaries plainly. What we claim is narrower and, we think, useful: once meaning is an object a kernel checks, the reward for good engineering can be a proof that travels. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Making Large Language Models More Flexible to Changing Contingencies through Tracking Induction
abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.
