title: DiffNash: Finding Nash Equilibrium in High-Dimensional Continuous Action Spaces with Diffusion Policies
abstract: Computing equilibria in high-dimensional continuous games requires learning and representing rich, multi-modal strategy distributions, something conventional neural policies struggle to achieve. Diffusion models offer a natural solution, but standard diffusion training requires direct samples from a fixed target distribution, which are generally unavailable under iterative game-solving updates. We propose a diffusion-based framework for equilibrium computation that enables diffusion-based variants of Online Mirror Descent (OMD) and Fictitious Play (FP). Our approach derives a reweighted score-matching objective that trains diffusion policies without requiring direct samples from each updated policy. Our main method, DiffNash, combines the fast convergence of OMD with the sample efficiency of FP by reusing past actions through a replay buffer. To correct the resulting distribution shift from sample reuse, we derive an unbiased estimator of the difference between current and past policies' Evidence Lower Bounds, whose exponential provides a tractable proxy for the corresponding importance weight without evaluating diffusion likelihoods. We evaluate our approach on forest protection games and continuous Colonel Blotto games, reducing the Nash gap over the strongest baseline by 35.6% and 24.7%, respectively, with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

title: An Efficient and Privacy-Preserving Framework for Edge AI Using Federated Learning and Homomorphic Encryption
authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Sanjivani Zite
Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
abstract: Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) supports intelligent processing close to where data is generated. However, training machine-learning models across edge devices is difficult when devices have limited memory, processing power, battery capacity, and network bandwidth. Federated learning (FL) addresses one important concern by allowing devices to train a shared model without sending their raw records to a central repository. Nevertheless, model updates may still expose information, while repeated communication and encryption can increase training time and resource use. This paper reviews an integrated architecture that combines federated learning, homomorphic encryption (HE), client clustering, update pruning, adaptive quantization, and convergence-aware stopping. In the architecture, each client trains locally, removes low-impact update values, compresses the remaining update, and encrypts it before transmission. The server aggregates encrypted updates and coordinates the next training round. The source study reports that its FLHC-QPR approach improves accuracy and reduces latency and memory overhead compared with selected comparison methods on a Human Activity Recognition task. The paper explains the architecture, workflow, potential applications, evaluation measures, limitations, and future research directions. The discussion is based on the supplied research article; performance values are reported from that study and are not presented as newly measured results.

title: Research on an Efficient Authentication Scheme for Vehicle Networking Broadcast Messages Based on Attribute Encryption
abstract: ABSTRACT To address the issues of insufficient privacy protection strength, as well as low computational and communication efficiency in existing vehicular network broadcast message authentication schemes, a highly efficient attribute‐based encryption solution for broadcast message authentication is proposed. The scheme innovatively integrates elliptic curve cryptography with the LSSS access structure, establishing an attribute‐based encryption mechanism that does not require bilinear pairings. By associating identity information with attribute sets, dynamic privacy protection for messages is achieved without exposing specific identities in resource‐constrained environments. Simultaneously, the key generation process is optimized by pre‐generating part of the keys during the offline registration phase, significantly reducing the interaction frequency and communication delay between vehicles and trusted institutions. Security analysis confirms that the solution meets multiple security requirements, including vehicle identity privacy protection, message unforgeability, attribute revocation, and malicious node tracking. Performance test results demonstrate that, compared with existing typical solutions, the proposed scheme reduces computational overhead by 88% and communication overhead by 66%, offering a practical solution for secure and efficient message communication in IoV environments.

title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
abstract: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.

title: Quantum circuit representation and incomplete Bell measurements in Compton scattering
abstract: We formulate massless tree-level Compton scattering as an effective two-qubit operation on electron and photon helicities. In the Bell basis, the scattering map separates into two parity sectors and admits a simple quantum circuit representation with one nonunitary filter. After Kraus normalization, this filter defines an unsharp incomplete Bell measurement that distinguishes the two Bell-parity sectors but not the relative Bell label within each sector. We further show that the incomplete measurement alone does not surpass the classical teleportation threshold, whereas a subsequent complete Bell-basis readout enables unit conditional teleportation fidelity.

title: Examining the Effect of Explanations of AI Privacy Redaction in AI-mediated Interactions
abstract: AI-mediated communication is increasingly being utilized to help facilitate interactions; however, in privacy sensitive domains, an AI mediator has the additional challenge of considering how to preserve privacy. In these contexts, a mediator may redact or withhold information, raising questions about how users perceive these interventions and whether explanations of system behavior can improve trust. In this work, we investigate how explanations of redaction operations can affect user trust in AI-mediated communication. We devise a scenario where a validated system removes sensitive content from messages and generates explanations of varying detail to communicate its decisions to recipients. title: Sealed Judge Enumeration Exhibit
abstract: Supplementary dataset for a preregistered reproducibility exhibit comparing exact linear-programming vertex enumeration with a typed probabilistic judge on a frozen blending problem. A 3-variable LP was solved exactly offline: 35 candidate triples reduced to 7 feasible vertices (A-G), with optimum candidate G at x=(9.2, 6, 4) and objective M*=14480. The feasible vertices, the sealed choice-type question, and the reading criterion were committed to a public repository before any judge call (preregistration commit 8133d0e; frozen state sha256 17e2c5593c9628f527cb4b8f88f630086bd10859d07599443a002f19bfe339c2). Five judge calls with model jev-1.13.0 pinned (no temperature control exposed; provider defaults apply) were driven through the identical preregistered state by a stdlib-only runner with verbatim request/response logging. All 5 runs selected candidate G (5/5 agreement with the exact optimum, 5/5 modal consistency, 0 fallback envelopes); under the sealed reading criterion this is a finding of stability, not quality, and n=5 supports no claim about calibration. Includes the enumeration core and tests, the frozen state, the preregistration, raw request/response records, the call log, the sealed analysis with per-run agreement scores, and the reading criterion. The protocol author maintains the judge tool under test; findings are about this exhibit, not any product.

title: Multitask Salience Learning for Position-Aware Extractive Summarization
abstract: This study proposes a multitask position-aware extractive summarization framework that jointly learns binary sentence selection and continuous sentence salience. BERT representations are enhanced through inter-sentence contextual modeling and positional information, while fused classification and regression scores guide redundancy-aware sentence selection. Experiments on 20,000 CNN/DailyMail documents show that the synonym-augmented model achieves ROUGE-1/ROUGE-2 scores of 0.3549/0.1420, improving over Lead-3 by 6.9%/10.3%, with statistically reliable gains. The improvement reaches 13.2% in ROUGE-1 for the longest documents. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining discrete extraction and continuous salience learning for robust, source-grounded extractive summarization.

title: Athenaeum: A Modular Language Architecture with a Shared Knowledge Pool, a Catalog Layer, and a Dedicated Truth Compartment
abstract: Current language models perform many distinct language operations, summarization, classification, translation, completion, structural analysis, through a single undifferentiated mechanism: next-token prediction steered by prompting. They also lack any internal representation of truth, treating facts and non-facts as identical sequences of tokens, which makes hallucination the default behavior rather than a malfunction. This paper specifies Athenaeum (working title), a modular language architecture that addresses both problems. Task families are assigned to fixed compartments at design time, each trained only on its own family. All compartments share a growing but bounded knowledge pool: a shared embedding space, a shared key-value memory, and shared layers. Compartments identify their contributions with distinctive fixed markers rather than fixed dimensional blocks. A catalog layer indexes compartment capabilities as bookmarks; compartments never connect directly to each other, and all sharing is mediated by the pool and the catalog, keeping inter-compartment wiring linear instead of quadratic. A dedicated truth compartment stamps claims as true, false, or unknown, and these stamps propagate through the system with provenance rules. The paper defines the write rule governing what enters the pool, the training procedure, the inference path, and conflict resolution. A formal mathematical specification, explicit input and output contracts, a glossary of terms, and an edge-deployment profile for on-device inference are included to make the architecture reproducible. A reference CPU prototype with three trained compartments validates the mechanics end to end, and the paper closes with the open research questions that remain.

title: Multi-Horizon Explainable Queue Forecasting and Resource-Aware Decision Support for Intelligent Border Control Using LightGBM
abstract: Border crossing points are stochastic service systems in which traffic demand, traveler categories, registration status, inspection requirements, staffing, and lane availability interact on multiple time scales. This paper extends an earlier multimodal queue-management framework by introducing an implementation-oriented, multi-horizon forecasting and decision-support architecture based on Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) models. In contrast to a single forecasting block, the proposed approach constructs horizon-specific regressors for 15, 30, 60, and 120 min forecasts and jointly estimates future waiting time and queue lengths. The models operate on temporally lagged traffic, service, density, and queue features, while an operational layer incorporates lane compatibility, officer availability, possibly degraded resources, traveler category, preregistration information, and human-approval constraints. Quantile LightGBM models provide 95\% prediction intervals for waiting-time forecasts. Beyond prediction, the framework produces machine-readable recommendations, alerts, aggregate key performance indicators, confidence information, and integration outputs suitable for border resource-management and decision-support systems. The results establish a reproducible synthetic-data baseline and a practical interface for subsequent validation with operational border-crossing data.

title: P-BFM: Perceptive Behavioral Foundation Models for Humanoid Control via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) provide humanoids with reusable repertoires of whole-body behaviors; in real-world humanoid control, the same behavioral intent may require fundamentally different motions under different terrain constraints. Covering such variation with terrain-matched demonstrations requires enumerating a combinatorial space of behaviors and terrain geometries. We introduce P-BFM, a perceptive behavioral foundation model that factorizes humanoid control into terrain-invariant intent and terrain-conditioned realization. A forward-backward representation maps motion references, target states, and reward functions into a shared intent space without terrain information, while a perceptive policy learns how to realize each intent under the surrounding terrain geometry. We further identify a complementary limitation of purely latent control: behavioral latents can preserve local motion patterns while losing precise global progress. We therefore introduce Explicit Root Instructions (ERI), which separates global transport (e.g., heading and planar velocity) from behavioral intent, while leaving local whole-body adaptation to the perceptive policy. This decomposition leads to a characteristic capability absent from conventional BFMs: one fixed intent induces different, terrain-appropriate behaviors, including changes in step height, stride, posture, foothold placement, and contacts, without terrain-specific demonstrations. Across challenging terrains, P-BFM improves motion fidelity, root-control precision, and perturbation recovery over strong baselines. A single frozen policy further supports motion tracking, goal reaching, reward inference, teleoperation, and terrain-aware recovery, and transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 using onboard depth sensing.

title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.

title: Homology You Can Run: The Topology of Quantum Codes, from the Logical-Qubit Count to the Phase Transition
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A CSS quantum error-correcting code is, on the nose, a length-three chain complex over F2 : the commutation law HZ H⊤ X = 0 that makes the code valid is exactly the condition ∂ 2 = 0 that makes a chain complex. We take this identification literally and show that the entire working theory of a quantum code is one homological object the same engine computes, at scale, and certifies. The number of logical qubits is the first Betti number, k = dim H1 = n − rank HX − rank HZ = b1 ; the code distance is the systole, the shortest non-contractible cycle. We reproduce the published parameters of state-of-the-art codes exactly—the toric and hypergraph-product families and the IBM bivariate-bicycle codes [[72, 12, 6]], [[144, 12, 12]], [[90, 8, 10]]—cross-validated four independent ways and kernelcertified for the small cases in Cubical Agda, on CPU and GPU. The two scale certificates—the Betti count b1 and the rank-derived logical count k—are themselves kernel-proved to be a single first-homology certificate (a DescentCertificate both readings factor through), closed terminally through a fixed-point engine. We then run the code, not just measure it. (i) The Union-Find decoder is the engine's connected-components reduction, and "a logical error occurred" is the engine's coboundary decision (the residual cycle has nonzero winding); decoding the toric code at growing distance recovers the accuracy threshold near 9.5%, and the optimal (maximum-likelihood) threshold near 11% is the engine's two homology sectors competing as the domain-wall free energy of a random-bond Ising model on the Nishimori line. (ii) A code's distance scaling is its Tanner-graph spectral expansion: the second eigenvalue λ2 versus the Ramanujan bound is a computable certificate (Sipser–Spielman), exact on the topological tier where the spectral gap obeys γ d2 → 4π 2 . (iii) The full chain complex carries metachecks—redundancies among the parity checks—and we compute them: the bivariate-bicycle codes have six, the engines of single-shot error correction; the 4-dimensional toric code's homology (1, 4, 6, 4, 1), with k = b2 = 6, is the tensor of four circle complexes. (iv) The logical error-rate prefactor is the multiplicity of the systole, A = 2L for the toric code, which we compute exactly. (v) Finally the engine measures a topological phase transition: as random noise thickens, torus-wrapping "giant" cycles appear in a sharp homological-percolation transition at pc ≈ 0.5 that sharpens with system size—the same homology machinery now detecting when noise spontaneously writes a logical operator. (vi) The engine runs over any coefficients: qudit (Fp ) codes are chain complexes over Fp , and the integral homology, computed by the Smith normal form, exposes torsion—so a code's logical-qudit count can depend on the qudit dimension, an extra logical appearing exactly when p divides a torsion coefficient (reproducing the known homology of the torus, the Moore spaces, the Klein bottle, and RP2 ). We are careful to fence what is not claimed: minimum distance is NP-hard in general and we compute it only on the systolic tier; the giant-cycle transition is the random-cluster one, distinct from the maximum-likelihood decoding threshold of the random-bond Ising model. The thesis is singular and operational: a quantum code's parameters, its decoder, its quality, its higher-dimensional structure, its performance prefactor, and its phase transition are not six theories but one—homology you can run. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Sistema Geométrico de Interpretación, Compresión y Análisis de Secuencias
abstract: Este trabajo presenta un sistema geométrico diseñado para interpretar, comprimir y analizar secuencias mediante la transformación de cualquier entrada —texto, números o datos arbitrarios— en una representación binaria estructural basada en símbolos densos y ligeros. El sistema permite identificar estabilidad, transición y ruido, además de realizar compresión estructural mediante la reducción de bloques consecutivos a unidades esenciales. Se introduce el concepto de semilla estructural, que clasifica el comportamiento global de la secuencia, y se define una medida de entropía geométrica que evalúa la variación interna. El modelo permite afinación estructural, predicción de comportamiento, detección de patrones ocultos y análisis universal independiente de la semántica. title: When Trackers Fail: VLM-Guided Verification and Recovery for Robust Video Object Segmentation
abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.

title: FIDE evidence archive: streaming privacy gateway conformance specifications, reports, and reproduction records
abstract: Supporting data for the article "Testing LLM Privacy Gateways on the Wire: Fragmentation-Induced Detection Evasion" (Ninad Phalak, submitted to IEEE Software, special issue "Building Trustworthy Software in the Time of AI", 2026). This is the open-access mirror of the IEEE DataPort dataset 10.21227/1kjn-0436; the two archives are byte-identical (see SHA256SUMS.txt inside). Every number in the article's text, Table I and Table II is computed from a JSON report in this archive, and the README maps each statement in the article to its file. The archive holds the frozen evidence (specifications v1.0.0, v2.0.0 and v2.1.0; 168 schema reports and ten aggregates produced by a deterministic conformance harness from real HTTP traffic against five gateway configurations and three library wrappers; the harness source at the revision that produced them), the reproduction kit and CI workflow that an independent third party ran on 2026-10-03 with the artifact of that run, the reviewer supplement, and the scripts and raw results of an Azure OpenAI default-streaming measurement with the vendor case outcome. All corpus values are synthetic and generated from a seed; no real personal data, live credential or customer traffic appears anywhere. Nothing in the archive was produced by an AI system. How to use: unzip and open README.md first. To verify, run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt; then re-run the reference controls with the reproduction kit (CPython 3.11 to 3.14, no network, about two minutes: lay reproduction-kit/ over evidence-round-8/, pip install ./pii-leak-benchmark, python benchmarks/reproduce_fragmentation.py --out reproduction; the Presidio track needs Docker and --policies presidio-chunk-local,presidio-retention). Every report carries instrument.inspector_sha256 = 94262e29a492ab6a; a report with a different inspector digest was scored by different code and is not comparable. Source mirror: Git tag v2-evidence-round-8 at https://github.com/ninadphalak/LLM-Shield-Proxy. Version 2 (2026-10-12) adds incidence-2026-10/, a production-incidence measurement made on 2026-10-11 and 12: 100 synthetic values of each of the eight corpus types tokenized with seven public tokenizers, and 3,000 raw SSE streams from five live models (DeepSeek, Claude Haiku, two Gemini models and gpt-5.4-mini, each with the value at the start of the answer and again mid-passage) asked to repeat a value, with every event's character and byte offsets. Its README.md explains the captures, and the tables re-derive from them with python scripts/layer2_analyse.py layer2 raw/*.jsonl, with no API key. Every version-1 file is byte-identical (the version-1 zip's MD5 was 50cd229819cd77da156da6110f8be0b1).

title: Descent Is a Reduction: A Kolmogorov–Arnold Network That Proves Its Own Training, Down to the Silicon
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A training step is usually a number that goes down on a plot. We make it a theorem. We exhibit a finite rational Kolmogorov–Arnold network whose evaluation, squared-error loss, and least-squares gradient are each a composition of a single primitive — the binary integer-arithmetic active pair, the smallest local rewrite of an interaction net — and we prove that one gradient step strictly decreases the loss, the decrease computed entirely by that primitive, with an empty axiom footprint, that the network's output equals the reduction of its own net, and that a network with a wrong parameter is carried by one exact step to the correct network with zero loss. The gradient that drives the step is itself reverse-mode backpropagation: we prove the backward pass — the chain rule — is the same active-pair reduction, its per-edge backward maps summing to the network's gradient, and that one exact gradient step trains an entire one-parameter family of wrong networks to zero loss. Because the network is a net, the verified object and the executed object coincide. The same arithmetic nets the proof reduces are reduced on graphics-processor silicon, and the result read back is identical, byte for byte, across an ordinary processor, a discrete accelerator, and a unified-memory device, and equal to the value the proof predicts. The three artifacts of trustworthy learning — the specification of the algorithm, its verification, and the kernel that runs it — collapse to one structure observed at three resolutions. We argue this is the natural home for a small but load-bearing class of learning systems: those whose correctness must be a theorem about the thing that actually runs. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: WiseBuild building-monitoring reproducibility artifacts: semantic modelling and virtual access
abstract: Reproducibility materials accompanying the manuscript “Semantic modelling for building energy monitoring: measurement attribution and virtual query performance”, prepared for Journal of Building Engineering. The archive contains executable synthetic competency-query fixtures for BEMO and Brick, the controlled SQL/view/semantic evolution pilot, evaluation outputs and negative controls, the archival set of 25 query-workload artifacts, mapping and ontology snapshots, and documentation. Both ontology implementations use the same five analytical conventions; the evolution pilot records 43 correct outcomes in 45 attempts, including two expected direct-SQL failures. These are controlled synthetic evaluations and archival workload evidence, not new production measurements. Private building telemetry, credentials and connection settings are excluded. The archive does not establish physical calibration of the original active/reactive energy register units. Register-based estimates in the manuscript remain at source register scale. Version 1.0.0. Original new materials are released under CC BY 4.0. Bundled Brick ontology materials retain their BSD 3-Clause license, and BEMO retains its existing CC BY 4.0 license. See LICENSE.md and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the archive. Earlier BEMO and WiseBuild releases remain separately identifiable; this deposit is the reproducibility supplement for the present journal revision.

title: Adaptive Confidence Sets for Nonparametric Density Estimation under Local Differential Privacy
abstract: In nonparametric density estimation without privacy constraints, it is known that a confidence set whose coverage holds uniformly over a `rough' class of regularity $r\geq0$ can simultaneously attain, in $L^2$-diameter, the minimax rate over a smaller, smoother class of regularity $s>r$ if and only if $s \le 2r$. We study such adaptive honest confidence sets under non-interactive $α$-local differential privacy (LDP) constraints. Our main result is that, for bounded $α$, such `smooth-rate adaptation' is now possible if and only if $s \le 4r/3$. In this smaller range we construct an honest private confidence set whose diameter is of the private minimax order on each of the two classes. As in the non-private case, the threshold arises because an honest set cannot, at a smooth density, be narrower than the separation rate arising in a related testing problem. Under LDP we prove that this private testing rate is of order $(nα^2)^{-2r/(4r+3)}$, which is at most the private estimation rate $(nα^2)^{-s/(2s+2)}$ over the smooth class exactly when $s \le 4r/3$. For $s > 4r/3$, however, we show that smooth-rate adaptation becomes possible once one discards from the rough class the densities that lie outside the smooth class but within an $L^2$-radius of the order of the private testing rate.

title: Understanding when and how knowledge graphs add value to EHR-based clinical prediction across Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and chronic pain
abstract: Abstract Biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) have emerged as a promising approach for incorporating biological knowledge into machine-learning models trained on electronic health record (EHR) data. However, their large scale and heterogeneous structure impose substantial computational cost, and it remains unclear whether their benefits generalize across diseases or depend on how the graph is constructed. We systematically evaluated KG integration across three diseases spanning distinct biological and clinical characteristics: multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and chronic pain. For each disease we compared five modelling strategies, spanning EHR-only features and graph diffusion over concept-level, cohort-derived, disease-anchored, and full SPOKE (Scalable Precision Medicine Open Knowledge Engine) subgraphs, asking whether graph construction affects predictive performance and computational cost, whether KG integration improves classification over EHR-only models, and what the graph does to model behavior. Cohort-derived subgraphs, comprising roughly 45% of SPOKE’s nodes and one-fifth of its edges, matched or modestly exceeded the full graph’s performance while substantially reducing computational cost in all three diseases. The predictive benefit of KG integration, however, was strongly disease-dependent: it improved classification in Parkinson’s disease, had no measurable effect in multiple sclerosis, and reduced performance in chronic pain. These differences were not explained by the amount of biological information incorporated: the disease with the largest shift toward molecular features showed no improvement, the sole beneficiary showed only a modest shift, and the disease with no molecular shift was penalized. Mechanistically, graph diffusion redistributed each disease’s existing signal across many correlated features rather than adding independent biological signal, so that any gain depended on whether it added information beyond the EHR. These findings show that cohort-derived subgraphs offer a computationally efficient alternative to full-scale knowledge graphs, and that KG integration functions less as a universal accuracy booster than as a data- and disease-dependent transformation of the patient representation.

title: EL-RAKHAWI CRYPTOGRAPHIC NEURAL INTERFACE SECURITY PROTOCOL (C-NISP) A Hardware-Integrated, Temporally Encrypted Authentication Framework for Brain-Computer Interfaces
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Cryptographic Neural Interface Security Protocol (C-NISP) (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23305238) presents a groundbreaking hardware-integrated security architecture for brain-computer interfaces, comprising three non-separable modules: (1) Temporal Cryptographic Key Generator (TCKG) utilizing AES-128-GCM or post-quantum lattice-based algorithms to generate dynamic, session-specific authentication pulse sequences; (2) Hardware-Enforced Signal Gating (HESG) requiring exact bitwise and temporal matching to transition from high-impedance (closed) to low-impedance (open) state, physically controlling neural signal transduction; (3) Anomaly-Driven Neural Isolation (ADNI), an air-gapped independent monitoring circuit triggering irreversible hardware latch within 2 milliseconds upon detecting non-compliant input patterns, independent of software overrides. The protocol establishes absolute neural data sovereignty by shifting security from vulnerable software layers to immutable hardware-enforced cryptographic gating. Published as sovereign defensive prior art under WIPO/TRIPS norms, the specification explicitly invalidates future patent claims on this temporal cryptographic authentication and hardware neural gating integration. title: Pragmatic Explainable Machine Learning
abstract: My PhD thesis, "Pragmatic Explainable Machine Learning: Philosophy, Methods and Applications," develops a pragmatic, context-aware approach to explainable AI (XAI) and AI ethics for high-stakes settings. The extended abstract describes three interconnected research strands. First, a pragmatic-rhetorical account of XAI that evaluates explanation methods by how well they achieve context-specific goals within particular rhetorical situations. Second, technical and theoretical contributions to XAI research, including causal dependence plots (CDPs), theoretical limitations of non-causal XAI for fairness auditing, and fairness detectability as a quantitative diagnostic for evaluating explanations against causal baselines. Third, qualitative research on how AI ethics is shaped across societal contexts, including media discourse analysis and collaborative, value-driven responsible AI design with a nonprofit supporting survivors of gender-based violence.

title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.

FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.

title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
abstract: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.

title: (Short Paper32) Language Generation Process and Analog Dy namic Recording Model of the Life Code in the In Vivo Analog Quantum Synchronizer (BioQPU) Paradigm: Trial and Error and Weighting Based on Active Rejection of Phase Noise and Chemical Triggers
abstract: The process by which humans spin words and construct long sentences has aspects that cannot be fully explained by the simple search and output model of discrete digital information in classical brain science. In this paper, we first overcome the metaphor of viewing life as a “computer” computing specific algorithms, and redefine the medium on which all memories in the biological system are recorded as an analog “life code (drive recorder of life)” that actively rejects phase noise based on LUCA’s Theorem (phase synchronization with environmental waves), proposing this as a verifiable hypothesis. Building on this, we model the language generation process as an iterative loop of analog resonance optimization. In this loop, waves from this continuous stream, along with their past contexts, are summoned into a quantum entangled space, and words are determined through “forced decoherence (conversion to particles)”—sublimating decoherence, which is considered an error in artificial machines, into a function via chemical triggers from the autonomous analog tuner (Glial OS) in the left brain. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of “selective decoherence” mediated by neurotransmitters via the Glial OS to explain the freedom of human analog memory retrieval. Finally, we consider the physical mechanism by which the time series process of trial and error in sentence construction itself is irreversibly carved onto the life code as “analog dynamic tag weighting,” independent of the computer metaphor.

title: Explaining Time Series Classifications Counterfactually: A Human-Centered Evaluation
abstract: Counterfactual explanations can promote accountability, fairness, and transparency in AI-supported decision-making by demonstrating how changes in input data can alter outcomes, offering actionable feedback for users to revise unfavorable decisions. However, the majority of counterfactual algorithms focus on tabular and image data, ignoring many high-stakes scenarios that rely on time series data. Furthermore, user studies of counterfactuals for time series are exceedingly rare. We address this research gap by proposing a novel methodology that advances carefully-controlled tests of counterfactual explanations for time series classification. In two experiments, participants were asked to classify time series plots and provide confidence ratings, before receiving feedback on the correct classification along with an explanation. The studies manipulated the explanation strategy used and the visualization used. Results indicate that counterfactual explanations elicit improved domain understanding and higher confidence in people in comparison to factual explanations. Wider implications for explanation in time series domains are discussed.

title: Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks
abstract: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.

title: Video-Based Sexual Harassment Detection Using Fine-Tuned Video Transformers
abstract: Sexual harassment represents a pervasive societal challenge, with a substantial proportion of incidents remaining unreported due to insufficient evidence and delayed intervention mechanisms. Smart surveillance systems capable of detecting such incidents in real-time could assist law enforcement and serve as a deterrent. However, video-based harassment detection poses significant challenges, including variations in clothing, illumina- tion, partial occlusions, low resolution, and diverse camera view- points. Despite its social importance, this problem has received limited research attention, primarily due to the scarcity of large- scale annotated video datasets. To address this gap, we extend the Sexual Harassment Video (SHV) dataset to 600 short video clips sourced from YouTube and annotated into harassment and non-harassment categories using consistent labeling guidelines. We fine-tune three state-of-the-art video transformer models, VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer, pretrained on Kinetics- 400, for binary harassment classification. Experimental results show that all three models achieve competitive classification performance, with TimeSformer attaining the highest test accu- racy of 92.27%, outperforming VideoMAE 91.71% and ViViT 91.16% on the extended SHV test set. Our analysis reveals that performance is notably influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling strategy, and model architecture. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of modern video transformers for this sensitive real-world task.

title: Scalable and Explainable AI Architectures for Intelligent Decision-Support Systems: Systematic Literature Review Protocol
abstract: Protocol of a systematic literature review, registered before the searches are run. The review maps how AI-based decision-support systems integrate data pipelines, machine-learning and relational inference, explainability, decision-support interaction, and human oversight, to ground a reference architecture for scalable and explainable decision support. It follows Kitchenham and Charters (2007) and will be reported according to PRISMA 2020. The protocol defines three research questions (layers integrated; how explainability and human oversight are realized; levels of evaluation), six databases (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, OpenAIRE Graph) plus Google Scholar and citation searching, five supervisor-approved search strings with five documented supplementary strings and their pilot results, eligibility criteria, a double-screened 20% sample with Cohen's kappa, a five-item quality assessment, a data-extraction form, and the synthesis plan. Appendix A gives the exact query for every database.

title: Ai-powered Chess Analysis System for Skill Development: a Case Study Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals
abstract: Chess players often face difficulties in identifying their mistakes, understanding positional weaknesses, and improving their playing skills through traditional training methods. This research proposes an AI-powered chess analysis system that uses chess engine evaluations and game analysis to identify errors, assess player performance, and recommend personalised training activities. The study also explores how AI-based chess learning can support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting accessible, personalised, and technology-driven learning. The proposed system aims to provide a structured approach to chess skill development through data-driven feedback and targeted practice.

title: We Need Explanation Cards to Connect Explanation Algorithms to the Real World
abstract: Algorithmic explanations are intended to help stakeholders understand opaque algorithmic decisions, but in practice, they often fall short. First, the meaning of algorithmic explanations is often not what one might intuitively expect, so expert knowledge is required to interpret them correctly. Second, recent work has shown that popular explanation algorithms are uninformative about the behavior of complex decision functions. Together, these issues create a gap between what explanations appear to convey and what they actually provide. In this work, we propose Explanation Cards for Explanation Algorithms, which augment standard explanations with complementary information about robustness and validity, as well as clear instructions for interpretation. The complementary information can render otherwise uninformative explanations practically useful, while also helping to detect cases where they are not. Importantly, the interpretation instructions in explanation cards shift responsibility from users to providers: Rather than expecting users to recognize what can and cannot be concluded from an explanation, providers must make this explicit upfront. Using counterfactual explanations and SHAP as examples, we demonstrate how providers can construct explanation cards and that these cards provide users with the guidance needed for sound interpretation. We further argue that explanation cards provide a practical framework for adhering to the explainability provisions of the EU AI Act. Overall, explanation cards are a significant step toward making explanation algorithms fit for real-world use cases.

title: RINO: Renormalization Group Distillation with No Labels
abstract: Supervised machine learning in high-energy physics (HEP) requires training on labeled simulations of particle collisions, which are known to be unfaithful to the underlying physics. This leads to significant inaccuracies and biases in the transfer of trained models to real data, limiting the power of deep learning methods. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a promising alternative for pretraining directly on real, unlabeled data. However, existing techniques largely operate with inductive biases inspired by domains such as images and natural language. We propose RINO (Renormalization Group DIstillation with NO Labels), which, for the first time, exploits the fundamentally multi-scale renormalization group structure of high-energy jet formation as a physically grounded source of SSL views. We define teacher-student representations across energy scales using different levels of hierarchical clustering, aligned via DINO-style self-distillation. To mirror the background-dominated nature of real collider data, RINO pretrains exclusively on jets from quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes and is evaluated on out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer to rare signal classes. In our controlled data-efficiency study, RINO matches fully supervised training on JetNet after finetuning on only 1% of the labeled data. With the full labeled dataset, RINO improves OOD classification accuracy on top-quark jets by 5.9% and, without retraining, improves AUC on the unseen Higgs boson decay channel $H \to 4q$ by 4.1% over the strongest SSL baseline. Scale-structure diagnostics reveal that DINO-style self-distillation permits our backbone to retain scale-dependent structure. Ablation studies show that this accounts for an 8.6% OOD accuracy gap with respect to alternative SSL paradigms such as SimCLR. Code is available at https://github.com/zichunhao/RINO.

title: Superpolynomial Lists for Reed-Solomon Codes over Binary Extension Fields
abstract: Recent work shows that ordinary Reed--Solomon codes over prime fields admit polynomial-size lists up to list-decoding capacity on every evaluation set. We show a contrasting phenomenon over binary extension fields. For every fixed rate $00$ such that, for all sufficiently large $h$, the full-field Reed--Solomon code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^h}$ has a received word with $n^{Ω_R(\log n)}$ codewords within relative distance $1-R-\varepsilon_R$. To our knowledge, these are the first superpolynomial ordinary Reed--Solomon list-size lower bounds at fixed positive rate and a fixed positive agreement gap above the rate. Thus capacity-approaching polynomial list size for Reed--Solomon codes is not uniform over the underlying field, and the obstruction occurs at every fixed rate. As a puncturing consequence, the same holds for primitive Reed--Solomon codes; the obstruction is also robust under controlled dense puncturing. The proof begins with an exact correspondence that turns certain binary Bose--Chaudhuri--Hocquenghem weight-enumerator coefficients into sizes of single Reed--Solomon lists. A classical binary weight family gives the initial quarter-rate construction, while a quadratic-form enumeration supplies its superpolynomial multiplicity. A common-kernel quotient/descent argument and common-root padding then extend the construction to all rates. We also determine the optimized agreement envelope achieved by the construction.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

title: Siam-ALS: An Explainable Siamese Deep Learning Framework for Early ALS Detection Using EEG and Eye-Tracking Signals
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous symptoms and reliance on clinical assessment, underscoring the need for objective, data-driven approaches that leverage patient-generated physiological signals. We propose Siam-ALS, an explainable Siamese deep learning framework that jointly models synchronized electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking (ET) signals. EEG captures ALS-related changes in brain activity, while ET provides information about oculomotor control, allowing the model to learn complementary patterns associated with ALS. The framework employs two modality-specific encoders: a convolutional EEG encoder that captures spatiotemporal neural patterns and an MLP-based ET encoder that models oculomotor dynamics. These modality-specific features are processed through weight-sharing Siamese branches and fused into a compact 64-dimensional joint embedding. A lightweight classifier is used to predict ALS, while pairwise metric learning helps the model learn more effective patterns from the small, diverse ALS datasets. Performance was evaluated on the public EEGET-ALS dataset using strict subject-level cross-validation, where Siam-ALS achieved an accuracy of 0.988 and an AUROC of 0.998, demonstrating strong performance compared with classical machine learning, DL, and non-Siamese fusion approaches. Cross-dataset evaluation on the independent BigP3BCI dataset achieved an AUROC of approximately 0.98, supporting the generalization capability of Siam-ALS across different BCI paradigms. evidence.title: Siam-ALS: An Explainable Siamese Deep Learning Framework for Early ALS Detection Using EEG and Eye-Tracking Signals
evidence.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) diagnosis remains challenging due to heterogeneous symptoms and reliance on clinical assessment, underscoring the need for objective, data-driven approaches that leverage patient-generated physiological signals. We propose Siam-ALS, an explainable Siamese deep learning framework that jointly models synchronized electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-tracking (ET) signals. EEG captures ALS-related changes in brain activity, while ET provides information about oculomotor control, allowing the model to learn complementary patterns associated with ALS. The framework employs two modality-specific encoders: a convolutional EEG encoder that captures spatiotemporal neural patterns and an MLP-based ET encoder that models oculomotor dynamics. These modality-specific features are processed through weight-sharing Siamese branches and fused into a compact 64-dimensional joint embedding. A lightweight classifier is used to predict ALS, while pairwise metric learning helps the model learn more effective patterns from the small, diverse ALS datasets. Performance was evaluated on the public EEGET-ALS dataset using strict subject-level cross-validation, where Siam-ALS achieved an accuracy of 0.988 and an AUROC of 0.998, demonstrating strong performance compared with classical machine learning, DL, and non-Siamese fusion approaches. Cross-dataset evaluation on the independent BigP3BCI dataset achieved an AUROC of approximately 0.98, supporting the generalization capability of Siam-ALS across different BCI paradigms. To enhance interpretability, six XAI methods were evaluated in the learned embedding space, with SHAP achieving the highest, though statistically comparable, fidelity in identifying important EEG and ET patterns that contribute to ALS predictions. Overall, Siam-ALS provides an accurate, generalizable, and explainable framework for multimodal ALS detection.

title: Necessity-First Computational Quantum Chemistry: The ZYQL Exact-Decision Language and Quantum-Witnessed Verification on Superconducting Hardware (thesis v0.1) and ZYQL software record v1.1.0
abstract: Doctoral-scale thesis draft and the guarded software record of ZYQL, a necessity-first trivalent exact-decision language (1 / 0 / REFUSED) for computational quantum chemistry, with the Hybrid Boundary Pattern (exact offline decision; QPU as witness; ML-DSA-44 sealed receipts) validated on three IBM Heron superconducting processors (ibm_fez, ibm_marrakesh, ibm_kingston). Includes signed experiment records: H2 exact ground state certified at -1.1456 Ha; Bell positive/separable negative hardware controls; GHZ ladder to 20 qubits (sparse); CHSH S=1.2822 certified refusal. Software carries the ZYGUARD guardian: refusal-before-compute for seven prohibited purpose classes, structural purity (no execution primitives), post-quantum traceable receipts. License note: code is MIT; the thesis text is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (dual licensing declared; the record-level license field reflects the dominant artifact, the software).

title: Project Prometheus
abstract: Executive Grant Proposal Summary Project Prometheus + Coherent Fusion + 729 Grid Architecture Toward Constraint Intelligence: The Next Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Infrastructure, and Autonomous Systems Principal Investigator: Anthony Jordan BlairOrganization: Proclus Dynamics ConsortiumProgram: Coherent Fusion Research InitiativeFlagship Project: Project Prometheus Vision The history of civilization can be understood as a succession of expanding intelligences. The Industrial Revolution amplified human physical capability. The Information Age amplified access to knowledge. Artificial Intelligence amplifies pattern recognition and decision-making. The next frontier may be more fundamental. Not the ability to process information. Not the ability to recognize patterns. But the ability to understand the underlying structures that make information and patterns possible in the first place. Project Prometheus proposes a new paradigm: Constraint Intelligence. A framework in which intelligent systems learn not only what is happening, but why particular futures are possible while others remain inaccessible. Today, artificial intelligence models learn correlations. Robots learn behaviors. Networks learn optimizations. Infrastructure learns efficiencies. Yet all remain constrained by a deeper limitation: They operate inside environments they do not fundamentally understand. They adapt to constraints. They do not discover the architecture of constraints themselves. Project Prometheus seeks to change that. Emerging from the broader Coherent Fusion Framework and its 729 Grid Architecture, the project investigates whether constraints can be identified, modeled, and ultimately treated as measurable organizational structures rather than passive limitations. If successful, this research represents a transition: From prediction to structure. From optimization to organization. From information intelligence to constraint intelligence. The Grand Challenge Modern civilization increasingly depends upon systems operating at scales and levels of complexity that exceed traditional human comprehension. These include: Artificial Intelligence Autonomous Robotics Large Language Models Smart Cities Transportation Networks Global Supply Chains Distributed Energy Systems Planetary-Scale Infrastructure Space-Based Autonomous Systems These systems generate unprecedented amounts of information. However, the greatest challenges no longer originate from a lack of data. They emerge from hidden constraints, structural instabilities, feedback loops, cascading failures, and emergent behaviors that remain difficult to identify before they occur. Current technologies are highly effective at learning patterns. They are far less effective at learning the architectures that generate those patterns. Project Prometheus explores whether a new generation of intelligent systems can move beyond pattern recognition and learn the governing structures of possibility itself. Scientific Foundation Project Prometheus serves as the mathematical and physical foundation of the broader Coherent Fusion initiative. At its core is a simple but profound question: Can coherent constraint architectures alter the transition structure of complex systems without violating the symmetries that govern them? To investigate this question, Project Prometheus develops a rigorous framework based upon exceptional points in PT-symmetric systems. Exceptional points represent singular transition boundaries where system behavior undergoes structural reorganization. Because they govern changes in stability, sensitivity, organization, and dynamics, exceptional points provide a natural laboratory for studying constraint-driven behavior. Phase I has produced: Proven Results A rigorous No-Go Theorem establishing fundamental limits on exceptional-point control. A classification of exceptional-point tuning mechanisms. A unified biorthogonal mathematical framework. A sector-mixing theorem revealing previously hidden structural limitations in many-body systems. Constructive Results A nonlinear self-consistent feedback mechanism capable of restoring exact linear exceptional-point tuning. A complete numerical verification architecture. A scalable framework for testing constraint-driven dynamics in larger systems. These results suggest a broader possibility: Constraints themselves may be treated as active computational objects. Connection to Coherent Fusion and the 729 Grid The broader Coherent Fusion program investigates how constraints organize behavior across multiple scales. Within that framework, the 729 Grid functions as an architectural map of state spaces, transformations, constraints, feedback loops, and emergent structures. The 729 Grid provides a way of viewing complex systems not as collections of isolated states, but as navigable landscapes of potential organization. Project Prometheus represents the first mathematically rigorous subsystem of that vision. It translates the abstract concepts of Coherent Fusion into a formal scientific framework that can be analyzed, tested, falsified, simulated, and potentially engineered. In this hierarchy: The 729 Grid provides the organizational architecture. Coherent Fusion provides the systems theory. Project Prometheus provides the mathematical foundation. Why This Matters for Artificial Intelligence The next generation of AI may require capabilities beyond prediction. Future intelligent systems must reason about: Hidden constraints. Dynamic constraints. Self-modifying environments. Emergent organizational structures. Long-horizon consequences. Adaptive possibility spaces. Project Prometheus introduces several potential directions for future AI architectures: Constraint-State Models Representing environments through governing constraints rather than raw observations. Self-Consistent Reasoning Updating internal models through recursive constraint feedback. Higher-Order Planning Reasoning over spaces of possible futures rather than isolated state transitions. Constraint Discovery Learning underlying organizational structures directly from data. Constraint Intelligence Understanding why outcomes occur rather than merely predicting that they will occur. Why This Matters for Robotics Future robots will increasingly operate in environments that cannot be fully specified in advance. Constraint-aware architectures may enable: Autonomous adaptation. Multi-agent coordination. Exploration of unknown environments. Real-time structural reasoning. Resilience under uncertainty. Self-adjusting task execution. Potential applications include: Manufacturing Industrial automation Autonomous construction Logistics Infrastructure maintenance Planetary exploration Human-robot collaboration Why This Matters for Infrastructure Infrastructure is increasingly becoming a complex adaptive system. Power grids, transportation networks, communication systems, logistics platforms, and sensor networks all exhibit large-scale emergent behavior. Constraint-aware architectures may provide new methods for: Failure prediction. Resilience analysis. Bottleneck detection. Critical-transition forecasting. Resource optimization. Coordinated infrastructure management. Potential impact areas include: Smart grids. Water systems. Transportation corridors. Supply-chain networks. Distributed energy systems. Planetary-scale sensing architectures. Why Fund Now Most frontier technology initiatives focus on: Larger AI models. More training data. Faster processors. Greater computational scale. Project Prometheus approaches intelligence differently. Rather than scaling prediction, it investigates the possibility of scaling understanding itself. The program has progressed beyond conceptual speculation and now possesses: A formal mathematical framework. Published theoretical results. A rigorous No-Go Theorem. A constructive alternative mechanism. Explicit falsification criteria. A complete verification architecture. Clearly defined Phase II milestones. This places the project at a unique stage where computation can determine whether the central hypothesis survives. The theoretical work exists. The framework exists. The next step is verification. Funding Objectives Phase II funding would support: Computational Verification Exceptional-point simulations. Many-body scaling studies. Thermodynamic extrapolation. Numerical theorem testing. Constraint Intelligence Research Constraint-learning algorithms. Constraint-state representations. Adaptive feedback systems. Higher-order reasoning architectures. Advanced AI Research Constraint-aware machine learning. Self-consistent planning systems. Multi-agent coordination frameworks. Long-horizon decision architectures. Robotics and Infrastructure Applications Autonomous systems integration. Constraint-aware robotics. Infrastructure resilience simulations. Distributed intelligence platforms. Open Scientific Infrastructure Research software. Computational toolkits. Verification pipelines. Public scientific outputs. title: Correcting Burst Errors with Applications to DNA-Based Data Storage
abstract: We introduce the problem of permutation burst error-correction, motivated by applications in molecular data storage with nanopore sequencing read platforms. A permutation burst of length $k$ is an error that affects a substring of length $k$ of a string of length $n$ by permuting its entries. Permutation burst errors can be corrected using classical burst error-correcting codes, such as Fire and Reed-Solomon codes. Here, we study how to reduce the redundancy of these classical codes by taking into account that the burst error preserves the weight of the substring. In addition, we further restrict our model to handle cyclic permutation bursts only, which are of independent practical and mathematical interest. Our main results include proving/establishing the following: a) for $k=o(\sqrt{n}),$ the redundancy of any permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n-k+\log \binom{2k-2}{k-2}+o(1).$ This result follows from McDiarmid's concentration bound; b) for $k \geq 9$ and $k=o\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}\right)$, the redundancy of any cyclic permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n +\log (k(k-1)-56)-\log\,80+o(1).$ c) the asymptotic redundancy upper bounds for the two types of substring errors that are twice the lower bound; d) constructions for both permutation burst and cyclic permutation burst errors that involve Varshamov-Tenegoltz type constraints or represent generalizations and extensions of Fire and other codes. In particular, we exhibit polynomially encodable and decodable codes that can correct cyclic bursts of length $\leq k$ using $\log n + k + 49\log k + O(\log \log k)$ redundant bits.

title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.

title: Gugak-VocalSet: A Multi-Genre Studio-Quality Dataset of Korean Traditional Singing with Sigimsae Annotations
abstract: We present Gugak-VocalSet, the first publicly available audio dataset for Korean traditional singing with dense annotations of sigimsae, a structured pitch contour system of vocal expressions. Gugak-VocalSet contains 24.5 hours of unaccompanied solo vocal recordings across 305 tracks of representative repertoire curated by the National Gugak Center, performed by 20 professional singers in a controlled studio environment with fixed key and tempo. In addition to genre, lyrics, and mood/timbre tags, the dataset provides a unified sigimsae ontology and approximately 68,000 segments (71,700 instances including multi-label) of audio-grounded sigimsae annotations; the ontology adopts a functional-position-based hierarchy designed for consistent application across genres, and 14 expert annotators specializing in Korean traditional music performed segment-level labeling accordingly. Baseline experiments on sigimsae classification and event detection show that domain-informed F0 representations remain competitive with, and on classification surpass, frozen probing of a general-purpose music foundation model, while pitch and spectral cues play complementary roles in event-level detection. Companion page: https://www.danbinaerin.com/Gugak-VocalSet/

title: Information Location under Matched Predictive Opportunity
abstract: Model rankings are difficult to interpret when benchmark tasks differ both in how predictable the target is and in where the predictive signal is located. We construct a finite-support synthetic testbed with a known binary posterior and the same public semantic facts available to every learner. In three core conditions, an identical two-point posterior marginal is determined by either a current warning, dependency topology, or the order of earlier warnings; a fourth topology-history interaction condition matches Bayes Brier opportunity but not the full posterior marginal. Across 2,304 development runs of specified tabular, static-graph, size-control, and graph-plus-GRU systems, rankings are not uniform: the temporal system has better mean size-integrated normalized regret than the static system in both ordered-history conditions, while the topology and interaction contrasts reverse direction across opportunity levels. Large tabular-static gaps also appear in the current-state control, where topology and ordered history do not determine the posterior, so rankings cannot be read as direct measures of structural-information use. Exact expected-risk evaluation removes sampled evaluation-label noise. In selected post-hoc replays, learned content pathways lose prediction-relevant distinctions although the underlying input information remains available; one selected failure is rescued by a persistent learning-rate reduction, whereas a one-step reduction and an analogous intervention in another selected trajectory are not. A planned confirmatory stage was not run because its precision target was infeasible within the replication cap. The results motivate separating predictive opportunity, posterior-determining information location, and stable learnability.

evidence.title: Information Location under Matched Predictive Opportunity
evidence.abstract: Model rankings are difficult to interpret when benchmark tasks differ both in how predictable the target is and in where the predictive signal is located. We construct a finite-support synthetic testbed with a known binary posterior and the same public semantic facts available to every learner. In three core conditions, an identical two-point posterior marginal is determined by either a current warning, dependency topology, or the order of earlier warnings; a fourth topology-history interaction condition matches Bayes Brier opportunity but not the full posterior marginal. Across 2,304 development runs of specified tabular, static-graph, size-control, and graph-plus-GRU systems, rankings are not uniform: the temporal system has better mean size-integrated normalized regret than the static system in both ordered-history conditions, while the topology and interaction contrasts reverse direction across opportunity levels. Large tabular-static gaps also appear in the current-state control, where topology and ordered history do not determine the posterior, so rankings cannot be read as direct measures of structural-information use. Exact expected-risk evaluation removes sampled evaluation-label noise. In selected post-hoc replays, learned content pathways lose prediction-relevant distinctions although the underlying input information remains available; one selected failure is rescued by a persistent learning-rate reduction, whereas a one-step reduction and an analogous intervention in another selected trajectory are not. A planned confirmatory stage was not run because its precision target was infeasible within the replication cap. The results motivate separating predictive opportunity, posterior-determining information location, and stable learnability.

title: A Four-Layer Artificial Life Avatar with a Drosophila Connectome as Its Instinct Layer
abstract: Background: Dialogue agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve high fluency in persona-based conversation, yet their internal states are entirely textual descriptions. When such an agent is "angry," the LLM is merely performing anger; no physical substrate corresponds to the emotion. This limitation produces context-dependent instability, non-differentiation of stimuli, and an absence of spontaneous behavior. Proposal: We propose a four-layer artificial life avatar, "Fuchan," in which the male whole-central-nervous-system connectome of Drosophila melanogaster, MaleCNS v1.0 (211,577 neurons, ~25.5 million synapses), serves as the instinct layer. Sensory inputs are propagated through the connectome via sparse matrix multiplication, and the resulting neural activity drives an LLM's language generation. The LLM is confined to verbalizing the instinctual state rather than performing it. Method: We conducted an exploratory observational study of a single session (1 hour 54 minutes: 13,390 telemetry samples; 66 LLM calls) involving a color-matching puzzle and an Ishihara-style color vision test. Results: We observed three emergent behaviors that were not designed: (1) test anxiety, surfacing as natural expressions such as "I'm not confident" and, notably, the negative form "I'm not that scared"; (2) trust building, where the user's encouragement "I won't hate you even if you make a mistake" produced a strong reward pulse (sugar=0.8) and a trust rise from 0.994 to 1.000; and (3) sleep with dream consolidation, in which 38 dialogue log entries were semantically compressed into a single memory ("Color Search with Kurui"). We also observed that biological constraints (the fly's poor red perception) surfaced not as a definitive "cannot see" but as sincere uncertainty, without hallucination. Conclusion: The four-layer architecture, implemented by a single author in less than one month, demonstrates that incorporating biological constraints into a computational system produces qualitatively different behavior from prompt-engineered personas.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Histologic Grading and Prognostication in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Scoping Review
abstract: This scoping review will map the existing evidence on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for histologic grading and prognostication in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). It will identify and characterize AI/ML approaches used for histologic grading and prediction of clinical outcomes such as recurrence and survival, summarize reported model performance, and examine comparisons with conventional histopathologic assessment where available. The review will also identify methodological and evidence gaps to inform future research and development of clinically applicable AI-based tools for OSCC assessment and prognostication.
