title: Prime polynomials in Legendre intervals over F_{2^k}[t], III: the hexad of a quartic linearised polynomial, the symplectic group Sp_4(F_2), and the Witt sums behind the constant X
abstract: Third part of a series on the variance of prime polynomials in Legendre intervals {f^2 + s : deg s ≤ d} over F_q[t], q = 2^k (Open Problem 8.2 of Part I, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23225896; Part II, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23252762). Part II reduced the degree-6 constant X to sums W'(λ_3, λ_5) of order-4 characters of the Hayes group, governed by the kernel of the linearised polynomial L' = λ_5^4 x^16 + λ_3^4 x^8 + x^4 + λ_3^2 x^2 + λ_5 x, on which the Frobenius was observed to act through S_6 ≅ Sp_4(F_2) with exact polynomial class counts. This paper explains that structure. The kernel of L' is the set of pairwise sums of the six roots of the sextic B = λ_5^2 u^6 + λ_3^2 u^2 + λ_5 u + 1 = u·A(u) + 1, where A is the Bluher quintic of Part II; the proof is the identity L' = x^4 B^2 + B + 1. Hence the Frobenius permutes the six roots, its S_6-class is the factorisation type of B over F_q, the symplectic form is the duad–syntheme pairing of the generalised quadrangle W(2), and the one-parameter family L + εx^4 corresponds to uA(u) + √ε, interpolating between the quadratic sums of A_6 and the order-4 sums of X. The number of Frobenius-stable symplectic structures of each type is 28|t|/|C|. First moments of the family u^6 + a u^2 + b u + b^2 are proved; the eleven class counts are verified for q ≤ 512 (odd k) and new polynomials, depending on k mod 4, are given for even k (q ≤ 1024). The order-4 sums are treated as Frobenius traces of rank-4 Witt–Artin–Schreier sheaves. Using the hexad, a multiplicity formula for Witt traces along towers and the moduli of Gauss sums of Z/4-valued quadratic forms, it is proved that every individual sum S''(λ) is a rational integer, that the normalised Frobenius eigenvalues are roots of unity, that in the class of 5-cycles the L-polynomial is (1 − η^5 q^{5/2} T^5)/(1 − η q^{1/2} T) with η a primitive 8th root of unity, so that W' = −q^7 unconditionally (+q^7 for even k), that for the six classes whose kernel lies in F_{q^4} the sum over F_{q^12} equals q^4 times the sum over F_{q^4}, and that the remaining classes have all S'' = ±4q^6. The closed form X = q^6 + q^5 (odd k) is thereby reduced conditionally to the class counts and to the Brown invariants of explicit small-field Z/4-valued forms, both stated precisely and verified exactly. Contents: paper (LaTeX source and PDF, 30 pages, four figures), self-contained Python verification code (hexad search, sextic identity, class counts, Witt sums and L-polynomials, trace identities, stable symplectic structures), exact data for q ≤ 1024, and a results summary. Code: MIT; paper, data, figures: CC BY 4.0. Repository: https://github.com/Ruqing1963/legendre-intervals-part3

title: Reproducibility repository for "Edge-preserving Bayesian neural networks via hierarchical sparsity-promoting priors"
abstract: Recovering piecewise-smooth functions with jump discontinuities from noisy, indirect, and incomplete data is a central task in computational inverse problems. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) with heavy-tailed weight priors have emerged as effective edge-preserving priors for such problems. However, posterior inference for these models remains computationally challenging, and existing approaches settle for point estimates obtained by directly optimizing heavy-tailed log-densities. We propose GSBL-BNNs, which model the neural network parameters hierarchically using sparsity-promoting priors from generalized sparse Bayesian learning (GSBL). The hierarchical formulation recovers several popular marginal priors, including Laplace and Student's $t$ (including Cauchy). A key modeling ingredient, novel among edge-preserving BNNs and native to the hierarchical formulation, couples each neuron's bias to its weights through a shared hyperparameter, so that the induced jump discontinuities are free to occur anywhere in the domain while the conditionally Gaussian structure underlying efficient inference is preserved. Furthermore, we develop a block-coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm for maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. This BCD approach alternates between standard network training with iteratively reweighted $\ell^2$-regularization and exact hyperparameter updates that are available in closed form for gamma and inverse gamma hyperpriors. Building on the BCD algorithm, we perform approximate Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification (UQ) using deep ensembles. Computational experiments---including signal denoising, deblurring, and inverting a two-dimensional hyperbolic conservation law---demonstrate that GSBL-BNNs deliver accurate edge-preserving reconstructions together with built-in UQ. Compared with Gaussian- and Cauchy-BNNs, they yield more accurate predictive means and avoid overconfident uncertainty estimates.

title: Effect of features burdened with classical error, misclassifications, Berkson error, and group-summary assignments on machine learning performance and interpretability
abstract: Abstract Measurement error is widespread in modern data pipelines, but its influence on predictive modeling and variable importance assessments in machine learning is often underestimated. Our study examines how input measurement error affects both prediction accuracy and interpretability across four common additive error types: classical error, misclassification of predictive features, Berkson error, caused by algorithmic or model-based assignment errors, and group-summary (aggregation) assignment errors. Using controlled Monte Carlo simulation experiments that cover regression and classification, we evaluate five popular machine learning models: generalized linear models, support vector machines, random forests, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptrons, across various error levels. To distinguish the effect of the error from optimization issues, hyperparameters are tuned separately for each dataset, and performance is measured using standard predictive metrics and permutation feature importance. Results show that measurement error generally reduces predictive performance and can significantly alter the ranking and estimated contribution of highly predictive features, with different degradation patterns depending on the error type and model. These findings clarify when performance declines might be mistaken for distributional shifts, among other things, and highlight the importance of diagnosing and correcting measurement error before drawing conclusions about model robustness, generalization, or variable relevance.

title: Learning Multimodal Sensor Fusion with JEPA Representations for Breathing Activity and Pose Recognition
abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.

title: TempoKV: Predictive KV Cache Quantization for Autoregressive Video Generation
abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models enable streaming generation of long videos but suffer from significant memory overhead due to the rapidly growing KV cache. Existing KV cache quantization methods are primarily designed for LLMs and transfer poorly to video models, where activations exhibit different statistics and strong spatiotemporal redundancy. We observe that the video KV cache is largely predictable over time, with a clear asymmetry. Keys are highly predictable from their temporal history, while values depend primarily on the current key and need a short history of preceding values. Based on these observations, we propose \textbf{\method}, a training-free predictive KV cache quantization framework for AR video generation. \method predicts keys and values according to their distinct dependencies and stores only the residuals at low precision. Both predictors are lightweight, calibrated once offline by linear regression on a small set of BF16 samples, and remain fixed across prompts and generation runs. Experiments on Self-Forcing, Causal Forcing, and LongCat-Video-13B show that \method consistently achieves higher generation quality than existing KV cache quantization methods at comparable or higher compression ratios, reaching up to $6.71\times$ KV cache compression with the best overall quality--efficiency tradeoff. Our code will be released on GitHub.

title: No Such Code: Certified Invariants for Quantum Codes, Circuits, and Measurement
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Four questions sit at the base of fault-tolerant quantum computing: whether a code with given parameters can exist, whether two circuits denote the same operation, how much entropy a measurement irreversibly produces, and whether a compiled gate still means what it should. They are normally answered by four disjoint techniques. We show they are one technique. In each case the answer is an invariant—the object a governing transformation leaves fixed—and that invariant can be held as a certificate a proof kernel checks and an operator-native substrate computes. The instruments are the quantum weight enumerator, whose shadow variant yields what is, to our knowledge, the first machine-checked nonexistence certificate for a quantum error-correcting code (no pure [[4, 1, 3]] stabilizer code, reduced to an integer impossibility); the spider normal form, unique both as a linear map and as a content-addressed tree, at the minimal axiomatic footprint of a proof assistant; the measurement boundary defect, whose logical entropy equals a kernel-counted cohomology dimension; and the reduction receipt, round-tripping a certified gate word to bare metal on two independent substrates. Everything downstream of the explicitly labelled modeling step in each domain is exact integer or rational arithmetic. The common shape—find the invariant the transformation fixes, and read it off as a certificate—turns four hard quantum questions into arithmetic a machine can hold. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Privacy Is a Bessel Inequality
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: How much noise must any differentially private mechanism add to keep a running count? The known answer — at least logarithmically much in the number of steps — is usually read as a fact about a clever construction, the binary tree. We argue it is something older and more structural: an instance of Bessel's inequality. Privacy forbids a mechanism from being accurate along a family of log2 T mutually orthogonal directions — the Haar wavelets of the prefix-sum workload — and orthogonality forces the individual costs to add with no cross-terms, so the total error energy is bounded below by the count of directions. A single two-point indistinguishability fact supplies the atom; an Assouad involution replaces the worst-case adversary with an average, converting a global optimization into a sum of local facts. We make this exact and machine-checked in Lean 4, unconditional over every mechanism, in the weighted-squared metric the argument natively controls; we cross-check the conclusion by an independent Fano / mutual-information route; and we anchor the abstract Haar measurement to the real prefix-count answer by a telescoping identity. The paper's deepest claim is metamathematical. We ask what kind of theorem a privacy lower bound is, and locate a sharp boundary in its constructive content: the universal statement is irreducibly classical — it inhabits exactly the three standard kernel postulates, and we show empirically that the rationals and finite sums alone already force them — while a concrete, integer-scaled witness of the same phenomenon is bare-metal constructive, carrying an empty kernel footprint, with the onset of the logarithmic growth — the error doubling as a second orthogonal scale is added — exhibited constructively. The frontier between "machine-verified classical" and "strictly constructive" is not a matter of effort. It is a measurable feature of the territory. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: A Traceable Case of Model-Initiated Concept Framing and Human-Led Revision in Natural Dialogue
abstract: This exploratory research note documents a naturally occurring case of model-initiated concept formation and human-guided revision in a Chinese-language human–AI dialogue. During an ordinary conversation, an AI system independently proposed a conceptual description of non-possessive intimacy centered on affection and bounded by autonomy. The human participant subsequently challenged an underlying assumption, leading to a revised distinction between personal affection and possessiveness. The observation raises a research question: Can meaningful conceptual distinctions emerge and be refined through ordinary human–AI interaction without additional model training or specialized experimental infrastructure? The study preserves the original observation, its conceptual development, and methodological limitations. It does not claim demonstrated theoretical novelty or generalizable model capabilities. This preliminary note is presented in English and Traditional Chinese, with selected original dialogue evidence. Further validation remains necessary.

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Optimized Image Biomarker Identification for Sinonasal Inverted Papilloma Diagnosis Using Image‐Enhanced Versus White‐Light Endoscopy
abstract: Objective: This study aims to compare image feature identification and diagnostic performance between artificial intelligence-aided image-enhanced endoscopy (using the Storz Professional Image Enhancement System, SPIES) and conventional white-light endoscopy (WLE) for sinonasal inverted papilloma (SIP). Methods: A total of 163 patients were investigated using Storz Professional Image Enhancement System (SPIES) endoscopy (SPIES Spectral A[SA]/Spectral B[SB]) and WLE. From each patient, one or two images (only in the presence of bilateral lesions) were obtained, and a large number of potential features were extracted from WLE, SA, and SB. Independent t-tests and LASSO methods were used to feature selection. Machine learning (ML) models were trained and evaluated for each channel of images. Results: The Random Forest (RF) algorithm on SPIES SB mode achieved superior performance: accuracy = 0.86, sensitivity = 0.89, specificity = 0.83, AUC = 0.86, and Kappa = 0.71. SB significantly outperformed SA (accuracy = 0.77) and WLE (accuracy=0.75). ROC analysis confirmed SB's diagnostic superiority (area under curve [AUC]: SB = 0.86 vs. SA = 0.77, WLE = 0.75). Conclusions: SPIES SB mode demonstrated the highest diagnostic accuracy and AUC for SIP identification, highlighting its potential as a superior imaging modality. SPIES endoscopy exhibits superior diagnostic accuracy and predictive performance compared to conventional WLE in the diagnosis of SIP. However, the single-center design and limited sample size necessitate validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts.

title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity
abstract: Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor--response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity--Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.

title: Interaction Nets That Carry Their Own Coherence
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Standard interaction nets are tested for the wrong thing. Confluence — the guarantee that the order of reduction does not change the answer — is almost always checked as a diamond (Church–Rosser): two one-step reductions of the same redex reconverge. But our nets are not standard. Boundary is a typed, open reduction calculus that compiles kernel-checked Lean proofs into interaction nets, and its confluence already lives one categorical level higher: each critical pair is a classifier square, each resolution is an admissible Squier join that carries its own legality receipt, and the whole convergent system is an idempotent free-compute closure. This document does three things. It reviews what makes our nets unique and why a diamond test under-measures them. It proposes a design and test methodology that checks confluence at its true level, by moving the critical-pair squares into Cubical Homotopy Type Theory — where the Kan filler hcomp is the admissible join, and the h-level tower is the confluence-coherence tower. Triaging the multiway-rewriting literature then sharpens the destination: confluence is not a ladder but a plane — a vertical coherence tower (where forks join: WCR1 through n-cell, the algebraic, topological, geometric, and logical coherences no rewriting system has had the instruments to reach) crossed with a horizontal multiway/branchial axis (where, under genericity, side effects, or measurement, forks deliberately do not), the two meeting at the quantum. The plan is staged and each stage is tested to completion; this is the map we update as we build. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Keep the Runtime, Derive the JIT Compiler: Runtime-Preserving Meta-Tracing with Two Coexisting Garbage Collectors
abstract: Meta-tracing frameworks derive a tracing JIT compiler from an interpreter, but implementations built with them commonly reimplement the object model and core library of an existing runtime as well. Meta-tracing constrains only the interpreter, not the values it manipulates. In runtime-preserving meta-tracing, a framework-written interpreter executes a production runtime’s bytecode over that runtime’s own values and delegates what it does not implement, so the runtime stays authoritative for object identity, method state and the core library. We state the host interface such an embedding needs and the invariants it must maintain, independently of the host language. The two collectors cannot see references stored in each other’s heaps. We keep host objects under the host collector and interpreter frames under the framework’s. During host marking, callbacks report the host values held by interpreter frames, compiled frames and suspended coroutines, and retained values stay at fixed addresses. Under stated coverage and collection premises, a model of the two heaps shows that host marking preserves every host object either executor can reach and relocates none that the framework reads. Exact marking additionally needs exact roots, exact reports and exact-cycle marking. Our realisation, RPyYARV, uses RPython and CRuby 4.0, with a host patch of 448 added lines and no machine- code backend of its own. It passes 99.1% of ruby/spec’s language examples, 97.9% of its core examples and all 1,568 C-API examples that CRuby passes. Its output matches CRuby’s under collection and compaction stress. Compaction is also where coverage violations surface, since coverage can be argued but testing can only falsify it. It runs 87 benchmarks, including Rails, RuboCop and HexaPDF unmodified, at 0.373 of CRuby’s time, 0.970 of YJIT’s and 0.610 of ZJIT’s in the geometric mean, at a tenth to a sixteenth of TruffleRuby’s memory.

title: Do Personalized Evaluation Functions Reflect Human Preferences? A Study of Weighted Proximity in Algorithmic Recourse
abstract: Algorithmic recourse focuses on providing individuals (end-users) negatively affected by ML-based decisions with recourse (actionable recommendations) that help them achieve a more favorable outcome in the future. Within this field, counterfactual explanations (CFEs) have gained popularity as a means of providing actionable recourse to end-users by identifying the minimal changes in their feature values needed to flip the ML model’s prediction to a more desirable one. Almost all prior work in CFEs rests on the assumption that minimizing (weighted) proximity (i.e., weighted L1 norm between the original input and the CFE) is a good proxy metric for capturing real-world human preferences with regard to the evaluation of prospective CFEs. Unfortunately, no prior work has empirically evaluated the effectiveness of weighted proximity in capturing real-world user preferences for evaluating CFEs. To address this research gap, this paper makes three novel contributions. First, we develop a novel two-phase study design that helps us effectively learn feature-specific weights for each individual end-user (in Phase 1) and evaluate the effectiveness of weighted proximity using those learned user-specific weights (in Phase 2). Second, we conduct the first-ever set of user studies (with 101 participants) that focus on evaluating the efficacy of global and personalized weighted proximity in capturing user preferences. Our experimental results show that global weighted proximity aligns with user preferences in only half the cases (53.21%), and personalized weighted proximity is not consistently better (56.91%). Finally, we conduct a series of sensitivity analyses to confirm that our findings are robust across different experimental settings and modeling choices.

title: Comparative Study of Canvas- and Coordinate-Based Geometry-Conditioned Neural Networks for Real-Time Prediction of Indoor Environments with Varying Room Dimensions
abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is computationally expensive for iterative building design. Deep learning surrogates offer faster predictions, but generalization across varying room dimensions remains challenging. This study compares two geometry-conditioned neural network surrogate models for rapid indoor airflow and temperature field prediction under varying room sizes. During the architectural design stage, this method is relevant for real-time assessment of whether conditioned supply air will effectively provide fresh and cool air throughout rooms with varying heights and lengths. The canvas-based neural network (CaNN) explicitly encodes room size by preserving different occupied regions within a fixed canvas, whereas the coordinate-based neural network (CoNN) uses normalized coordinate channels. Both employ U-Net autoencoders to separately predict airflow and temperature fields. Evaluation uses simplified rooms with varying heights and lengths as a controlled benchmark. The results show that CaNN achieves higher agreement with CFD results than CoNN, demonstrating its potential to support performance-driven building design.

title: Typed Evidence Fusion for Cross-Modal Enterprise Question Answering: Preserving Provenance, Currency and Cardinality Across Retrieval Modalities
abstract: Enterprises have accumulated a stack of partial solutions to the question-answering problem: semantic search over documents, knowledge graphs over master data, text-to-SQL over the warehouse, and increasingly a chat interface over each of them separately. Each works within its competence and fails outside it, and the failures are silent. Ask a document-RAG system for a total and it will find a sentence containing a number. Ask a text-to-SQL system why a figure moved and it will produce a query, not an explanation. The user cannot see which system they are talking to, so they cannot calibrate. This paper proposes a unified architecture in which retrieval modality is a routed decision rather than a deployment choice, and in which heterogeneous evidence (passages, graph paths, query result sets, computed aggregates) is carried in a typed representation that permits a single verification pass over all of it. The organising abstraction is a shared blackboard over which a planner, four specialist retrieval agents, a critic, and a synthesiser coordinate. We contribute: a typed evidence algebra with composition rules, which makes cross-modal evidence combinable rather than merely concatenable; a coverage-driven termination criterion that decides when to stop retrieving on the basis of what the question requires rather than a fixed step budget; a critic formulation that checks for the specific failure mode of cross-modal inconsistency, where a passage and a query result disagree; and an analysis of the cost–capability curve showing where marginal agent steps stop paying. We evaluate on EntQA-Bench, an executable benchmark released with this paper: a real SQLite warehouse of seven joined tables, 1,332 documents indexed with BM25, a 159-node entity graph, and 1,310 questions in seven classes by required modality, with gold answers computed from the sources. The results are measured. Flattening evidence to text costs accuracy: prose answers 87.6% of questions and a concatenated agent transcript 54.2%, against 100% for typed evidence, and on questions requiring all three modalities the transcript representation answers none. One claim from an earlier simulated draft does not survive. Typed evidence gives no accuracy advantage over plain JSON carrying values and confidences: both answer 100%, and the earlier figure of 8.3 accuracy points is withdrawn. What types buy is verification capability, which the untyped representations lack entirely: source disagreement is detected on 57.2% of injected conflicts against 0.0%, cardinality is reported correctly on 82.5% against 0.0%, and the weakest currency among combined sources is propagated on 100% against 0.0%. The revised claim is therefore narrower and, we think, more useful: types are what allow a cross-modal answer to be checked, not what make it correct.

title: Squeeze-Aware-YOLO: Early Channel Recalibration and Multi-Scale Fusion for Real-Time Traffic Sign Detection
abstract: Traffic sign detection plays a vital role in intelligent transportation systems, supporting the safe operation of advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles. Despite significant progress in real-time object detection, accurately identifying traffic signs under challenging conditions remains difficult. Variations in lighting, adverse weather, motion blur, and partial occlusion often reduce detection performance, especially for small or visually degraded signs where important spatial information can be lost. To address these challenges, we propose Squeeze-Aware-YOLO, a lightweight traffic sign detection framework that introduces a multi-branch bottleneck module combining convolutional kernels of different sizes with a Squeeze-and-Excitation mechanism to improve feature extraction and adaptive channel weighting. In addition, we integrate the Multi-Branch Auxiliary Feature Pyramid Network and Re-parameterized Heterogeneous Multi-Scale modules to strengthen multi-scale feature representation and feature fusion while preserving real-time inference efficiency for practical deployment. The proposed approach is evaluated on the Bangladeshi Traffic Sign Detection Dataset, the CSUST Chinese Traffic Sign Detection Benchmark 2021, and the German Traffic Sign Detection Benchmark, achieving mAP@0.5 scores of 74.7%, 79.4%, and 84.0%, respectively, while consistently outperforming recent state-of-the-art YOLO-based traffic sign detectors. These findings demonstrate that combining multi-scale receptive fields, channel attention, and enhanced feature fusion enables more accurate and robust traffic sign detection while maintaining the computational efficiency required for real-world deployment.

title: Riemannian Formulation of Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Solvers for Elliptic Problems: Energy-Norm Guarantees and Duct-Flow Applications
abstract: Sample-based quantum linear solvers measure quantum Krylov states $e^{-iAT}|b\rangle$ and reconstruct the solution of $Ax=b$ classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for positive-definite systems that arise from elliptic partial differential equations. We show that the sampling guarantees hold in any fixed basis with an efficient transform. We then replace the variational reconstruction by a Galerkin solve on the sampled set. For this reconstruction we derive expected and high-probability energy-norm error bounds, a sample complexity in terms of the smallest sampling probability on an essential set, a computable residual certificate, and a support-completeness theorem for the dephased outcome law. We formulate the method for elliptic problems on Riemannian cross sections. In two dimensions the stiffness matrix is metric-independent in conformal coordinates, and curved vessels lead to the same matrix class. Killing symmetries of the cross section give selection rules for the measurement outcomes, and the Lie derivative of the metric gives first-order bounds for geometric perturbations. We separate operator approximations, whose effect we bound, from sampler approximations, which affect coverage but not the target. As examples we treat the implicit step of pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts. In simulations of up to 12 qubits, the number of Fourier modes required for 1% error grows from 14 to 60 while the number of unknowns grows from 64 to 4096. A classical residual-greedy selection is nevertheless more efficient than quantum sampling in all cases studied, consistent with the low measured sampling efficiency. On a six-qubit trapped-ion processor, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model whose strength grows by about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity selection rule rejects shots at the predicted rate.

title: Channel Match: Calibrating Shape Latents for Few-Step 3D Generation
abstract: Recent native 3D generators achieve high-quality asset creation by modeling structured 3D latents with flow-based transformers, but their high-resolution generation remains computationally expensive due to costly iterative sampling. In this work, we introduce a few-step distillation framework for native 3D generation, enabled by continuous self-consistency training with a custom JVP FlashAttention kernel and an analytic velocity regression objective for sparse structured 3D latents. To stabilize joint optimization, we further introduce an adaptive loss weighting strategy that automatically balances them without manual tuning. Beyond acceleration, we reveal a previously overlooked failure mode of few-step native 3D generation: sampling-induced latent distribution drift preserves geometric correctness but disrupts downstream PBR texture synthesis, causing texture artifacts on geometrically valid assets. To address this issue, we propose Channel Match, a training-free adaptive per-channel latent calibration method that restores the latent distribution without modifying either generator. We validate our approach on TRELLIS.2 at the $1024^3$ resolution setting. Our two-step model achieves $4.5\times$ faster geometry sampling while maintaining geometry quality comparable to the many-step teacher, and Channel Match further improves rendering quality by recovering the latent interface between geometry and appearance generation.

title: RC-ENSO GPU ESN/DESN: selected 20-member ensemble
abstract: Twenty selected ESN/DESN members from a pool of 288 candidates, with CUDA-parallel training and deterministic forecasts. Benchmark models were trained on 1958–1999; 2002–2023 was used for member selection and correlation comparison. Reservoir configurations are W=0 and lr=1. Related paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01360-5. Code repository: https://github.com/zhangzejing/RC-ENSO.

title: Control bounds and calibration costs in finite-time Zeno discrimination — computational reproducibility resource (A32)
abstract: This dataset provides the computational reproducibility resource accompanying the manuscript “Control bounds and calibration costs in finite-time Zeno discrimination” by Matthias Jakob (Kolping-Schulen Neckarpark). The study investigates discrimination between absent and present generalized amplitude damping using a finite-duration sensor–auxiliary-qubit instrument. It includes imperfect preparation, noisy readout, auxiliary noise and calibration uncertainty, with decisions evaluated over continuous uncertainty sets. The archive contains numerical results, 176 stored control timing profiles, channel coefficient arrays, verification records and the complete computational source and dependency chain. Scripts and instructions are provided to verify content hashes, restore the nested scientific sources and reproduce the global error-floor calculation and selected independent checks. Earlier calculations and their verification provenance are retained in the dependency archives. The resource supports an analytic invariant-state lower bound for experiments without intermediate measurements, using the specified preparation family, fixed Hamiltonian direction and finite terminal meter. It also supports the separate comparison with the finite collection of stored control profiles and the analysis of calibration costs for known and unknown drive amplitudes. The analytic error floor uses exact rational outward rounding. Numerical Zeno guarantees, comparator enclosures and the separate terminal-meter tightening retain the floating-point error assumptions stated in the manuscript. Independent consistency checks are distinguished from formally validated interval computations.

title: AquaType
abstract: A Zhuyin input method for Mac that suggests the right words even when you press the wrong keys. Built on RIME (Squirrel), with a noisy-channel decoding engine that runs entirely on device. title: REFLEX: A Learned On-Board Reflex for Robust Autonomous Collision Recovery of Soft Quadrotors
abstract: Collision-resilient airframes allow quadrotors to survive impacts, but do not ensure autonomous post-collision recovery. Innovation gating in stock onboard estimators often rejects valid external velocity measurements after high-speed impacts, compromising recovery. We present REFLEX, a collision-recovery flight mode that runs entirely on the flight controller, requiring neither contact sensors nor a companion computer. Its proprioceptive recurrent policy stabilizes the vehicle without position, velocity, heading, or altitude estimates. The translational estimate is reinitialized while REFLEX is active, and a trust gate checks estimator consistency before returning control to the stock autopilot. The policy is trained in simulation using proximal policy optimization, with episodes initialized from post-impact states measured in 47 real collisions. In hardware experiments, REFLEX recovered 19 of 22 wall impacts at 5.03 $\pm$ 0.09 m/s, compared with 1 of 14 for the matched stock autopilot. These included 15 consecutive recoveries in a single flight. A separate exploratory flight demonstrated two additional recoveries at 6.02 and 6.05 m/s within the same flight, exceeding the previously reported velocity for autonomous wall-collision recovery by 64%.

title: Imitation Learning via Discrete and Rhythmic Primitive Composition
abstract: Long-horizon robotic manipulation is inherently composed of semantically meaningful sub-tasks. While Movement Primitives (MPs) can model these components, their composition typically relies on manual engineering or sample-inefficient reinforcement learning. Existing supervised methods are limited by the lack of MP labels in standard datasets and often fail to generalize across discrete and rhythmic movements. We propose Neural Dynamic Composition (NDC), a supervised framework to compose Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) using only raw trajectories for supervision, given a single example of each primitive. Our approach exploits parallel combinations of DMPs as a differentiable relaxation of categorical primitive selection, and utilizes a warp-invariant loss formulation to identify primitives despite spatial or temporal variations. A staged training curriculum is employed to learn the selection policy and DMP parameters, unifying discrete and rhythmic movements in one framework. Evaluated on 2D handwriting and 3D robotic tasks, our method outperforms baselines on most tasks and metrics. An ablation study demonstrates how each design choice contributes to the system's performance.

title: CondMSP: Condition-Informed and Resource-Aware Inorganic Materials Synthesis Planning
abstract: Materials synthesis planning (MSP) connects AI-driven materials discovery to experimental realization by proposing precursors, synthesis operations, and processing conditions for a target material. Existing approaches predict these components separately or in pairs and treat conditions only as a prediction target. Consequently, MSP remains centered on recipe prediction: it leaves unexplored how conditions can serve as process context for constructing synthesis routes, and it does not address which candidate routes should be executed under limited experimental resources. We propose CondMSP, which extends MSP from recipe prediction to execution-aware planning. CondMSP predicts temperature, time, and atmosphere by combining a joint predictor with variable-specific experts, and then uses these predictions both as process context, grounding the generation and retrieval of operation sequences, and as execution requirements, specifying which thermal stages can share a furnace run and at what cost. This specification is held fixed across all compared methods; within it, CondMSP ranks routes across precursor sets by a common utility and, under furnace budgets, jointly selects routes and allocates their thermal stages by constrained optimization. CondMSP improves condition and operation prediction and, under this shared constraint, raises reference-recipe recovery from 27.9% to 32.9% at three simulated furnace runs per target and from 34.7% to 40.0% at 30 trials, while a new evaluation set of 2,344 targets supports generalization beyond oxide-dominated training chemistry.

title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
abstract: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.

title: Nucleus Operators, Constructive Logic and Physical Possibility: A Unified Lean 4 Framework from Laws of Form to Constructor-Theoretic Cryptography
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: We present a unified formal framework connecting Spencer-Brown's Laws of Form (1969) to Constructor-Theoretic Cryptography via nucleus operators and Heyting algebras, fully mechanized in Lean 4 with Mathlib. The framework operates at three levels: (1) the nucleus operator R from locale theory, satisfying extensivity, idempotence, and meet-preservation, whose fixed-point locus ΩR = {x : R(x) = x} forms a Heyting algebra; (2) Laws of Form recast as nucleus application, where re-entry is the operator R and stable forms are fixed points; and (3) Constructor-Theoretic Cryptography, where physical possibility requires the dual polarity Φ P → P (soundness rather than inflation), enabling security proofs grounded in physical impossibility rather than computational hardness. We prove that superinformation media—where individual observables are clonable but their union is not—provably resist eavesdropping. The complete formalization comprises ~3000 lines of Lean 4 code with zero sorry proofs and no axioms beyond Lean's kernel. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

The framework operates at three levels: (1) the nucleus operator R from locale theory, satisfying extensivity, idempotence, and meet-preservation, whose fixed-point locus ΩR = {x : R(x) = x} forms a Heyting algebra; (2) Laws of Form recast as nucleus application, where re-entry is the operator R and stable forms are fixed points; and (3) Constructor-Theoretic Cryptography, where physical possibility requires the dual polarity Φ P → P (soundness rather than inflation), enabling security proofs grounded in physical impossibility rather than computational hardness. We prove that superinformation media—where individual observables are clonable but their union is not—provably resist eavesdropping. The complete formalization comprises ~3000 lines of Lean 4 code with zero sorry proofs and no axioms beyond Lean's kernel. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: The Degree-Two Shadow: Multiplicative Complexity as a Dimension
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Over the basis {AND, XOR, NOT} the exclusive-or and negation are, for most purposes, free; the conjunction is not. In secure multiparty computation, homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, and side-channel masking, the price of evaluating a Boolean map is set almost entirely by the number of AND gates it requires — its multiplicative complexity. Yet multiplicative complexity is notoriously hard to pin down: it is a minimum over an infinite family of circuits, and even for small maps the exact value is usually obtained, if at all, by a search whose result one is asked to trust. We identify the structure that makes the lower bound a matter of linear algebra rather than search. To each Boolean map we attach its degree-two shadow: the linear map that reads off the coefficients of the quadratic monomials in the map's algebraic normal form. This shadow is blind to the affine part of a circuit and therefore counts only what the AND gates create; because taking the shadow is a linear operation and each AND gate contributes at most one shadow vector, the shadows of a map's outputs must lie in a space whose dimension cannot exceed the number of AND gates. The multiplicative complexity of a map is therefore bounded below by the dimension of the span of its outputs' degree-two shadows — a rank, computed once, no search. We apply this to the nonlinear layer of the SHA-3 standard, the width-n Keccak χ map. Its outputs' shadows are the n quadratic monomials xi+1 xi+2 around a cycle; these are linearly independent precisely because 2 ̸= 0 in the index ring, so the shadow dimension is exactly n and no circuit computes χ with fewer than n multiplications. The standard one-per-output implementation meets this bound, so the multiplicative complexity of the Keccak nonlinear layer is exactly its width: MC(χn ) = n. The nonlinear layer of SHA-3 is AND-optimal, and not by accident of the width the standard fixes, but at every width. The lower-bound argument is a theorem checked by a proof assistant's kernel with no appeal to a solver; the exact value is established, kernel-checked, at every width a designer would use. What the result asserts about the territory beyond it is narrow and, we think, useful: a certificate of optimality for a cryptographic primitive can be a dimension, and a dimension travels. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: A 38-byte audio block with unequal BCH protection, a codec state field inside the error-correcting codeword, period-indexed keystream, a one-byte keyed tag checked after correction, re-arm gating, and in-band control bits (second version)
abstract: Each block is a fixed bit layout derived from (link mode, layout). It holds an 8-bit descriptor, every mix's codec bits for four 4-sample groups, per-mix codec resync fields, per-mix parity, and an 8-bit keyed tag. Protection is unequal: in the default mode a shortened binary BCH code per mix covers only the descriptor, the tag and the lowest-frequency sub-band codes of both channels; the other bands go unprotected. The tag is computed over the descriptor and the protected bits, then the BCH code is computed over the descriptor, the tag and the protected bits, then everything is XORed with a keystream indexed by the block's period number and the transmitter's salt. The receiver removes the keystream, corrects every mix's codeword, and only then checks the tag, so a hit the FEC repairs does not fail it. After any failed block the receiver re-arms: the next block that passes is still concealed and only the one after it plays. A random block therefore reaches the decoder only by passing a 1-in-256 test twice in a row. Modes without correction carry two parity bits per group per mix and tag the descriptor and those parity bits. A block whose descriptor names another plan is re-checked under that plan's layout and reported as a plan change only after two consecutive authenticated foreign blocks. Control blocks (a beacon each second, labels every ten seconds) are sent in the same modulation and framing, in place of an audio block; receivers conceal those periods without counting them as loss. Defensive publication, placed in the public domain as prior art. License: CC BY 4.0.

title: DeepSearch V3–V4: Execution Audit and Design of an AI-Agent System for Business Opportunity Research
abstract: Two whitepapers document DeepSearch, an independent AI-assisted research project on language-model agents for identifying and assessing business opportunities. V3 audits the pipeline’s architecture, decision rules and six recorded executions. It compares intended safeguards with actual behavior, examines how evidence supported decisions, and documents errors and limitations. No candidate in the recorded runs passed competitor screening, so later stages were not exercised. V4 proposes a redesign starting from business models already paid for abroad and assessing their transferability to Italy. It remains a design specification: it has not been implemented or tested, and no measured improvement is claimed. Both papers disclose AI assistance and distinguish recorded observations, design choices and hypotheses. They have not undergone human peer review.

title: Structural Cryptanalysis of a Middle-Graph Matrix Cipher and a Canonical Public Middle-Graph Encoding
abstract: Structural complexity in a graph-derived representation does not by itself establish cryptographic security. This paper performs a self-cryptanalysis of the authors’ own middle-graph matrix cipher from an earlier version of this manuscript; the attacked construction is not attributed to a previously published cipher. For a fixed key, the cipher right-multiplies a normalized weighted adjacency matrix of M(Sn+1) by an invertible secret matrix. We prove a ciphertext-visible row relation that, from one exact ciphertext, recovers every leaf parameter yi and the n secret key rows indexed by the edge vertices. A single ciphertext does not by itself reveal the message coordinates xi or zi; complete key recovery requires additional information such as known plaintexts and a full-column-rank stacked system. We give a concrete recovery algorithm and numerical example, an O(n3) arithmetic cost analysis, a perturbation bound for rounded ciphertexts, and experiments showing when integer parameter recovery survives decimal rounding. As a representation-only alternative, we define a canonical public byte-to-residue encoding and an optional expanded middle-graph matrix over F65521. The compact residue vector is the primary serialized object; the dense graph matrix is reconstructed only when a downstream graph or matrix algorithm actually consumes it. The map is public, deterministic, and reversible and is not claimed to provide confidentiality. Its clique identities can detect non-adversarial random corruption under an explicitly stated model, but they are not a form of authentication. If protected transport is required, then a standard AEAD scheme is applied as an independent security layer. This composition is included only to delimit the security boundary and not as a new cryptographic primitive. Benchmarks report the medians and interquartile ranges, compare the graph encoder with a simpler 16-bit baseline, and compare direct AES-GCM with encoding-plus-AES-GCM. The results show that the graph representation is justified only when its explicit graph structure is needed downstream; otherwise, direct authenticated encryption is simpler and faster.

title: FireNav: Decision-Oriented Reconstruction Evidence Routing for Vision-Language Navigation in Indoor Fire Environments
abstract: In real-world indoor fire environments, visual degradation severely impairs instruction grounding, waypoint prediction, and long-horizon exploration in vision-language navigation (VLN). Although image restoration offers a natural means to mitigate such visual degradation, existing methods primarily optimize reconstruction fidelity, which does not necessarily translate into better navigation decisions and may even corrupt task-critical cues when applied indiscriminately. In this paper, we present FireNav, a decision-oriented reconstruction evidence routing framework that aligns visual restoration with navigation utility in VLN. To advance this task, we first contribute FireVLN-Bench, a paired indoor fire navigation benchmark with clean references preserving task semantics, safety supervision, and matched settings for continuous navigation and robot execution with simulated dynamics. Our FireNav retains native visual tokens and treats latent reconstruction features as auxiliary evidence, where a lightweight router leverages visual features, task context, and prior execution states to determine whether such evidence should be admitted and how strongly it should contribute to the visual tokens. To learn when reconstruction is beneficial, we further introduce decision utility calibration, which compares action prediction losses with and without candidate evidence under the same state, thereby supervising evidence selection according to its contribution to waypoint, heading, and arrival prediction. Experiments demonstrate that FireNav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both navigation success and path efficiency across evaluation settings.

title: FENAS: A Few-Shot Meta-Ensembling Framework for Efficient Neural Architecture Search with Synergized Zero-Cost Proxies
abstract: Efficient neural architecture search (NAS) requires accurate performance estimation under limited evaluation budgets. Existing zero-cost proxies (ZCPs) provide fast training-free signals, but each proxy usually captures only a partial property of an architecture, leading to unstable rankings across datasets and search spaces. In contrast, GNN-based predictors can improve accuracy, but often depend on labeled architectures, graph encoders, and costly representation learning, which makes them less suitable for extreme few-shot settings. We propose FENAS, a topology-agnostic few-shot prediction framework that turns complementary initialization priors into robust ranking signals. Its core component, CAST, is a feature pipeline that combines copula alignment and synergy transformation. CAST maps heterogeneous ZCPs into a compact feature manifold, enabling lightweight meta-learners to produce reliable rankings from scarce supervision. On NAS-Bench-201, with only 0.5% labeled samples, FENAS achieves a Kendall's Tau ($τ$) of 0.70, outperforming representative topology-based few-shot predictors in this low-label regime. In closed-domain search, FENAS evaluates the NAS-Bench-201 space in approximately 1138 seconds and achieves competitive test accuracy. By providing a fast, reliable, and structurally simple evaluation mechanism, FENAS supports the design of automated neural architectures under limited evaluation budgets.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration in Communication Networks: A Systematic Review of Protocol Integration, Performance Trade-Offs, and Transition Readiness
abstract: The prospect of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) undermines the public-key primitives that secure virtually every layer of modern communication networks, from subscriber authentication in cellular cores to transport-layer key exchange. Adversaries already following a harvest-now, decrypt-later (HNDL) strategy make this threat actionable today for any traffic whose confidentiality must outlast a decade. Following NIST’s finalisation of the first post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards, ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) in August 2024, and the selection of HQC as a fourth key-encapsulation candidate in March 2025, research has shifted from algorithm design to network-level integration. This paper reports a PRISMA-2020-compliant systematic literature review of PQC migration in communication networks, structured around five research questions covering protocol and scenario coverage, quantitative performance impact, hybrid cryptography strategies, transition barriers, and open research gaps. Six databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, and MDPI) were searched (3229 records identified); after deduplication, title-keyword screening, full-text eligibility assessment, and a pre-specified quality appraisal (Q1–Q6, threshold ≥3/6) applied to 310 eligible studies, a final synthesis corpus of 141 studies (68 journal articles, 68 conference papers, 4 conference-derived book chapters, 1 workshop paper) was screened, quality-appraised, and synthesised narratively with supporting evidence tables. The review finds that transport-layer protocols (TLS 1.3, QUIC, DTLS 1.3) dominate the literature, that lattice-based ML-KEM/ML-DSA offer the most favourable latency–bandwidth–energy trade-off among standardised families, and that classical–PQC hybrid schemes are the de facto transition strategy across 5G/6G, IoT, VPN, and automotive scenarios, at the cost of 10–100× larger keys/signatures and 8–40% handshake latency overhead. Persistent barriers include constrained-device resource limits, immature hardware acceleration, incomplete IETF/3GPP standardisation, and public-key-infrastructure scaling. We propose a five-level PQC transition-readiness maturity model and identify large-scale field validation, PQC–QKD integration, and lightweight signature schemes as priority directions for future work.

title: Entropy-Regularized Mean-Field Games with Average-Reward Criterion: Span-Seminorm Contractions and Model-Free Learning
abstract: We study stationary discrete-time mean-field games with finite state and action spaces under the average-reward criterion, with an entropy-regularized objective and population-dependent dynamics and rewards. Under a minorization condition, the soft Q-operator is a span-seminorm contraction for the full transition kernel, so relative value iteration does not require the minorizing measure. When the Lipschitz constant of the kernel is below the minorization mass and the temperature exceeds an explicit threshold, the equilibrium fixed-point operator is a contraction: an equilibrium exists, its population distribution is unique, and a fixed-point iteration converges to it geometrically. We then learn the equilibrium model-free from a simulator, combining soft Q-learning at a fixed population distribution with an empirical transition kernel. We prove a finite-sample bound for soft Q-learning in the span seminorm, with temperature-independent constants, and derive convergence rates for the learned population distribution and policy. A congestion-aware routing game illustrates the results.

title: A Quantum Analogue of the Covering Lemma: Limits of Exact Anonymous Computation
abstract: Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.

title: An Attention-Guided Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Boundary Integral Computation in Physical Field Reconstruction
abstract: In practical engineering and scientific computing, a real physical system can be reduced to a boundary value problem, and the adequate boundary information to determine the interior spatial distribution and evolutionary state of the physical field can be solved with linear equations, alternatively, the the real physical problem can be treated with boundary problems with in adequate information problems in field of machine learning. This paper proposes a deep learning framework for the recovery of missing boundary information using an attention-guided graph neural network (GNN) surrogate. The framework extracts features from the physical information on the discretized boundary into a latent space, and the missing boundary quantities are then predicted by the network. Thus, the nonlinear mapping from known boundary quantities to missing boundary quantities is learned using a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture, while an attention mechanism is incorporated to better model the correlations among different types of boundary information. Furthermore, the interior physical field can be reconstructed using the conventional boundary element method (BEM) integral formulation. evidence.title: An Attention-Guided Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Boundary Integral Computation in Physical Field Reconstruction
evidence.abstract: In practical engineering and scientific computing, a real physical system can be reduced to a boundary value problem, and the adequate boundary information to determine the interior spatial distribution and evolutionary state of the physical field can be solved with linear equations, alternatively, the the real physical problem can be treated with boundary problems with in adequate information problems in field of machine learning. This paper proposes a deep learning framework for the recovery of missing boundary information using an attention-guided graph neural network (GNN) surrogate. The framework extracts features from the physical information on the discretized boundary into a latent space, and the missing boundary quantities are then predicted by the network. Thus, the nonlinear mapping from known boundary quantities to missing boundary quantities is learned using a variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture, while an attention mechanism is incorporated to better model the correlations among different types of boundary information. Furthermore, the interior physical field can be reconstructed using the conventional boundary element method (BEM) integral formulation. The effectiveness of the GNN-BEM framework is evaluated using numerical examples of the two-dimensional Laplace and Poisson equations, which demonstrate good performance in reconstruction accuracy, local detail preservation, and model stability. The results show that GNN-BEM provides a feasible computational framework for boundary information recovery and fast interior physical field reconstruction for partial differential equations under complex boundary conditions.

title: WisdomNet: trustable machine learning toward error-free classification
abstract: Misclassification is a critical problem in many machine learning applications. Since even the classifier models with high accuracy (e.g., > 95%) still introduce some misclassification error, it may not be possible to rely on the output of a classifier. In this paper, we introduce trustable learning, which prompts the learning model to yield only the true output, thus avoiding misclassifications. Whenever the model cannot decide the output accurately, the learning model should indicate that there could be a misclassification error if it is forced to classify, and hence, it should reject to make a decision or defer it to a human expert. Therefore, we develop a methodology for trustable learning and apply it to artificial neural networks and show that it is possible to develop a classifier with 0% misclassification error. We propose a novel neural network architecture named WisdomNet that could provide zero prediction error by introducing an additional neuron named as conjugate neuron that would indicate whether the network is able to classify the data correctly or not. The WisdomNet architecture can be applied to any previously built model, and we have evaluated WisdomNet with several network architectures such as multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network, and deep network on different data sets. The results show that the WisdomNet is able to reduce the classification error rate to 0%, while labeling the data is difficult to classify as `reject' at a low percentage of within around 10%.

title: VCF-RDFizer evaluation: benchmark harness and run records
abstract: The evaluation of VCF-RDFizer reported in VCF-RDFizer: From a VCF File to Explicit, Verifiable, and Policy-aware Semantic Genomic Data: every number, table, and figure in the manuscript and its supplement can be traced to a run record in this archive and recomputed from it. Contents benchmarks/: the benchmark harness, experiments 00-19, including the linked workflow (benchmarks/use_case/acmg/) and the shared-input converter comparison (benchmarks/converters/). benchmarks/README.md describes each experiment and the reported result it produced; benchmarks/DESIGN.md gives each experiment's design as run, organized by the manuscript's three research questions. The drivers that ran the experiments on each benchmark host are archived with their run records. benchmark-results/: the run records of every reported run, per host: commands, tool commits, image digests, timings, resource samples, validation reports, query results, comparisons, and logs. Generated graphs and indexes are not included. benchmark-results/README.md maps every reported result to its records. scripts/figure_data.py and scripts/build_site_data.py: compute every plotted and quoted value from the run records alone; scripts/test_build_site_data.py checks them against the manuscript. plugin-tests/: tests of VCF-RDFizer's linking and policy plug-ins on real data; site/: the results site, whose every number is computed from the run records. Inputs: the download command for every input VCF (README.md), their SHA-256 checksums (benchmark-results/input-checksums.tsv and vcf-input-sizes.json), and the scripts that derive the evaluated slices. Software: the core benchmark (experiments 00-13) ran VCF-RDFizer v3.1.0 (image ecrum19/vcf-rdfizer@sha256:1904e96dde12ab2e2e70d8ee1267765c293ab100a8bd1b14d5b009b2bf8e34aa); the linked workflow, regional and large-graph retrieval, the converter comparison, the consumer WGS validation run, and the index-storage measurement used VCF-RDFizer v3.3.1 (image ecrum19/vcf-rdfizer@sha256:3ad71b1a54612142e3be43b24e7e4a38551949cb641f4421bcae9bf051102993). The two releases write identical graphs: their conversions of the 100,000-record HG005 slice have the same 17,098,746 triples (sorted N-Triples SHA-256 661578e7…94ed). Not included: runs whose results the manuscript does not report (pre-release, superseded, stalled and failed runs, including those the supplement cites as evidence of corrected defects), which are on the GitHub repository's legacy branch; the manuscript, its figures and figure scripts, and the authors' working notes, which stay in the GitHub repository (BioMedSem_2026/, tool-docs/; marked export-ignore in .gitattributes); the source VCFs, which remain available from their providers (Genome in a Bottle, the 1000 Genomes Project, HGSVC2, precisionFDA, and the Personal Genome Project); the generated RDF graphs and indexes, which the archived commands regenerate; and the Docker images, which are pulled by digest. Licences: code under the MIT License (LICENSE); data and documents under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA), except the recorded MyVariant.info responses in benchmarks/use_case/acmg/myvariant-cache/, which remain under MyVariant.info's terms of use.

title: Stability-Driven Multistage Transformer–BiLSTM for Short-Term PV Power Forecasting
abstract: This study proposes an integrated short-term photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting framework, termed MSD-STB-OptFormer, to jointly address multiscale power fluctuations, unstable meteorological relevance, and model-parameter sensitivity. Successive variational mode decomposition (SVMD) first separates the original PV power series into components with different fluctuation characteristics, after which wavelet packet decomposition (WPD) further refines the reconstructed high-frequency component. A stability-driven feature-selection strategy then combines correlation-based redundancy screening with bootstrap perturbation and permutation importance to retain meteorological predictors with persistent predictive relevance. An improved whale migration algorithm (IWMA), incorporating fast random opposition-based learning and normal cloud mutation, is subsequently employed to optimize the hyperparameters of the Transformer-BiLSTM predictor. Second, a stability-driven feature selection strategy combines correlation-based redundancy screening with bootstrap-based stability evaluation to retain meteorological predictors with persistent predictive relevance. Third, an improved whale migration algorithm (IWMA), incorporating fast random opposition-based learning and normal cloud mutation, is used to optimize the hyperparameters of the forecasting model. Finally, the reconstructed multiscale components and selected meteorological features are fed into a Transformer-BiLSTM predictor, where self-attention captures long-range temporal dependencies and BiLSTM models bidirectional sequential dynamics; the component forecasts are subsequently aggregated to obtain the final PV power prediction. The framework is evaluated using real PV datasets under different seasonal and regional conditions. Comparative, cross-regional, capacity-normalized, and ablation analyses consistently show that the proposed framework improves forecasting accuracy, seasonal robustness, and generalization capability.

title: Preparing Routinely Collected Electronic Medical Record Data for Machine Learning in a South Australian Quaternary Hospital, 2020-2025: Development of an Interprofessional Translational Framework (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) are increasingly used to support machine learning (ML) in healthcare, yet comparatively little attention has been given to the translational work required to prepare routinely collected operational data before modelling can occur. OBJECTIVE This study examined the technical, clinical, and operational work required to prepare EMR data for downstream ML applications and developed an interprofessional translational preprocessing framework. METHODS An observational study was undertaken using routinely collected EMR data from 398,872 inpatient admissions at a South Australian quaternary hospital between 2020 and 2025. The preprocessing methodology integrated technical data preparation with workflow interpretation, interprofessional validation, and feature derivation to develop analytically meaningful and operationally interpretable model inputs. The study is reported in accordance with the RECORD guidelines. RESULTS Preprocessing identified recurrent challenges extending beyond conventional data cleaning, including incomplete structured documentation, workflow artefacts, high-cardinality variables, free-text dependence, and temporal instability. Many variables initially assumed to represent straightforward clinical or operational concepts instead reflected documentation practices, workflow behaviours, or administrative processes, requiring interprofessional interpretation before they could be reliably used for ML. These recurring activities informed development of a six-stage interprofessional translational framework spanning shared problem definition, data validity assessment, workflow interpretation, interprofessional validation, feature translation, and translation into action. CONCLUSIONS Preparing routinely collected EMR data for ML is not solely a technical exercise in data cleaning but an interprofessional translational process. The framework described provides a structured approach for preparing operational healthcare data for ML applications while preserving clinically meaningful and operationally interpretable representations of healthcare activity. Health systems seeking to realise value from AI should invest not only in technical modelling capability, but also in the organisational capability required to steward, interpret, validate, and translate routinely collected healthcare data into actionable intelligence.

title: CHEAR: Confusion-Hierarchy Evidence-Aware Reasoning for Cost-Efficient Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a new approach to wearable-sensor-based human activity recognition. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) further introduces similar motion examples and discriminative sensor knowledge, enabling decisions grounded in observations relevant to the current query. More evidence, however, does not necessarily mean better-organized evidence. When online prompts and LLM agents primarily orchestrate inference, decisions about which activities to compare and when to invoke discriminative knowledge remain concentrated at inference time. As the activity vocabulary grows, the model must repeatedly process more candidates and associated knowledge, whereas pruning candidates too early risks excluding the true activity. We propose confusion-hierarchy evidence-aware reasoning (CHEAR), which moves part of this knowledge organization offline. CHEAR constructs and validates an activity hierarchy from recurrent cross-subject retrieval errors and builds corresponding activity-pair knowledge. At inference time, the hierarchy orders candidate comparisons; the LLM retains candidates progressively, and local discriminative knowledge is accessed only for the remaining activities. Across eight datasets, CHEAR achieves 86.79\% mean cross-subject accuracy, a 75.91\% candidate reduction rate, and 96.44\% true-activity retention. Per-sample token use is 85.15\% lower on average than in a variant without the hierarchical structure. Mean accuracy across eight cross-dataset transfer directions is 88.81\%. These results show that organizing candidates and discriminative knowledge around observed activity confusions reduces online LLM input while maintaining recognition performance.

title: Enter, Quantum Magic, and Quantum Gravity: Readout, Recovery, and the Limits of Geometric Response
abstract: We formulate the proposed connection between quantum magic and matter-responsive geometry at a finite, already-prepared quantum carrier interface. The complete output is an isometry V from C to R tensor B, and residual response means that its complete complementary channel is not constant on the logical code. Exact recovery from R is equivalent to the absence of that response.The proposed unconditional implication from non-Clifford resources to residual response is false. We prove explicit counterexamples: a Clifford copying circuit has a nonconstant complement, whereas non-Clifford logical evolution—and even a fixed syndrome containing bipartite non-local magic—can coexist with a constant complement and exact logical recovery. We therefore separate magic, residual response, and physical geometric backreaction.For a specified controlled-rotation family, we construct a non-Clifford responding program and obtain the exact formulas: delta leak of theta equals sine theta divided by two, and epsilon rec R of theta equals one minus cosine theta, divided by two, for theta between zero and pi over two, inclusive. A general first-order residual-observable witness gives a quantitative sufficient condition for response under a declared deformation. A Pauli-compression criterion separately characterizes constant complements for Clifford encoders.Destructive Born–Lüders readout consumes measured quantum names and returns a classical interface. Readout-and-drop of an unobserved residual is exactly partial trace and does not further change the radiation channel. The four-Majorana recovery obstruction, finite-channel certificates, access-preserving endpoint continuity, and finite-proxy recurrence are retained with their proper scope. No metric, field-to-memory receiver, admitted analytic quantum coefficient, or gravitational backreaction theorem is constructed.

title: Minimal-Trust Proof Verification via Combinator Reduction
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: We present a system for independent verification of Lean 4 proofs that reduces the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) from approximately 50,000 lines of C++ to approximately 50 lines of code in any general-purpose language. The system compiles Lean 4 type-checking computations into SKY combinator terms—three reduction rules from classical combinatory logic (Schönfinkel 1924, Curry 1930). A compiled bundle encodes the complete type-checking computation as a self-contained combinator tree. An independent reducer applies the three rules until a normal form is reached; if the result decodes to K (Church-encoded true), the proof is valid. The compilation pipeline is formally verified: 146 theorems with zero sorry in Lean 4 establish that compilation preserves the semantics of type checking. Open-source reducer implementations in four languages (Python, Rust, TypeScript, Go) enable any party to verify a proof bundle without installing Lean 4 or trusting any upstream toolchain. A production service provides compilation, verification, STARK cryptographic attestation, and on-chain registration of verified proofs via Solidity smart contracts. We describe the architecture, its trust properties, and its applications to smart contract certification, regulatory compliance, cross-institutional proof sharing, and verification-as-a-service. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.
