title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards computed from the DLM's generated outputs based on answer correctness and constraint satisfaction. Moreover, through the lens of discrete flow matching (DFM), we interpret anchor placement as helping to reshape the initial velocity field that guides generation. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning across five DLM backbones show that AnchorDLM improves controllability and further yields gains in reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks.

title: Iterate on an LLM, Serve on an SLM
abstract: As frontier LLMs gain more capabilities, the cost to run them also goes up. At the same time, small language models (SLMs) also gain more capabilities but have largely been able to keep their cost stable, offering 5-40 times cheaper inference for the narrow, repetitive subtasks that agents decompose work into. However, the standing limiting factor is getting the correct behavior out of a small model in a fast, efficient, and economical way. Unfortunately, in most cases, zero-shot small models fail narrow production tasks. Furthermore, retraining one every time the behavior changes is too slow to iterate on. We propose doing both in sequence. First, develop the desired behavior in prompt space, on a frontier model, with immediate feedback from live traffic. Then, once the behavior converges, distill the recorded production behavior (not synthetic imitations of it) into an SLM through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We show a proper use case of this method through a scheduling agent for home-care agencies that fans out a single yes/no safety decision per caregiver-shift pair on GPT-5.4-nano. A LoRA-tuned Qwen3-8B trained on 11.6k recorded production decisions reaches 0.913 agreement, while the teacher (GPT-5.4-nano), re-run on its own recorded prompts, agrees with itself only 72.7% of the time, pointing to the fact that the SLM may also be more consistent. Furthermore, when the two disagreed, a blinded professional scheduler sided with the student 48-29. Finally, we find that the SLM has approximately 2.5 times lower median latency and is a fraction of the cost. We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

We believe this lifecycle of quick building, live feedback, and cheap inference is a blueprint for others building similar systems.

title: DDBench: Benchmarking Deduction from Distributed Evidence
abstract: Teams of agents often need to solve problems using evidence scattered across their members. Reaching a shared answer requires exchanging clues and drawing the right deductions. A final accuracy score records whether a team succeeds. Explaining team performance requires separating evidence requirements, reasoning difficulty and communication delays. Here we introduce DDBENCH, a benchmark that makes these requirements measurable in the same task. Its six-agent detective-inspired and generic constraint puzzles have verified unique answers that no individual agent can determine alone. Exact checks identify the smallest groups with enough evidence and the steps needed under a fixed deduction procedure. Paired comparisons of rule-based solvers show how extra communication rounds and checks of possible answers turn partial progress into complete, correct solutions. On identical puzzles, networks with the same number of links achieve 0% (path) and 100% (star) team accuracy after four rounds. A separate search track measures progress when standard deduction leaves alternatives to test. Round-by-round traces expose intermediate progress. Checks for unintended clue patterns identify shortcuts relevant to future learned evaluations. DDBENCH enables reproducible comparisons of how teams combine private evidence and complete deductions under limited resources.

title: Relational Rebinding Principle (RRP)
abstract: This paper proposes the Relational Rebinding Principle (RRP), a conditional systemic principle describing how a prior state, representation, relation, or functional association may influence the subsequent functional assignment of a current carrier when a measurable relational correspondence exists. The motivating phenomenon is a linguistic case in which a previously encoded meaning associated with the term "poor" may subsequently influence the functional interpretation of a different carrier whose name contains the same or a sufficiently corresponding relational component. The proposed framework does not treat this linguistic case as proof of a universal law. Instead, it uses the case as a canonical phenomenon from which an abstract and testable architecture is constructed.The framework separates prior state, current carrier, relational correspondence, activation, functional assignment, criterion, medium, and observable output. Security is therefore not treated as a primitive criterion. Instead, the criterion is represented by a general variable K_{t}, while the medium or contextual implementation is represented by M_{t}. The architecture is independent of the number of interacting systems in the mathematical sense that the same operator structure can be instantiated for arbitrary finite N, while applicability remains conditional on explicit structural requirements.The theory is also formulation-independent with respect to linear, nonlinear, discrete, continuous, network, simple, complex, conscious, and non-conscious implementations, provided that the required state, relational, functional, and observable conditions are present. This does not imply that every system must exhibit the effect. Null and counterexample regimes are explicitly incorporated.The mathematical architecture is formulated as a sequence from prior encoding to relational correspondence, activation, functional assignment, output, and subsequent state transition. A baseline model is introduced to quantify the functional shift attributable to prior relational activation. Synthetic simulations are specified as tests of mathematical behavior rather than empirical proof. The manuscript therefore separates observation, interpretation, mechanism, mathematical representation, simulation, and empirical validation. The final sections establish falsifiability conditions, competing explanations, scope limitations, cross-domain constraints, and an anti-pseudoscience audit.

title: Unified Graph Convolutional Neural Network with PPMI-Informed Graphs and MuRIL Embeddings for Hate Speech Detection in Indian Code-Mix Text
abstract: The widespread use of social media has led to a rise in online bullying and abusive language. Huge amounts of content are created on social media daily, creating a challenge for platforms to manually detect and remove offensive posts, making automated detection systems essential. This challenge is even greater in multilingual countries such as India, where code mixing is prevalent. This paper investigates the effectiveness of graph-based representations for hate speech and offensive (HOS) language detection in social media posts written in code-mixed low-resource languages. We conducted experiments on seven openly available datasets spanning Kannada-English, Malayalam-English, Tamil-English, and Hindi-English code-mixed languages. The main goal is to identify the most effective edge-weight computation method for hate speech detection across the target languages by conducting a comprehensive comparative analysis of different edge construction techniques. We construct sentence graphs with MuRIL word embeddings as nodes and compare three edge-weighting schemes—Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI), Sequence Graph Transform (SGT), and raw co-occurrence processed through a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN)—concatenated with a MuRIL sentence embedding for classification. The highest test-set accuracies and the corresponding best weighted F1 results obtained for PPMI were 82.00%, 73.89% for HASOC Malayalam 2020, 65.26%, 65.81% for HASOC Malayalam 2021, 75.37%, 75.37% for HASOC Tamil, 72.7%, 72.68% for HASOC Hindi-English, 63.36%, 55.58% for EACL Kannada, 92.05%, 89.94% for EACL Malayalam, and 73.84%, 63.62% for EACL Tamil. Further, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of sentence representation quality and model performance and provided detailed mathematical and empirical analysis of the different graph representations.
